labs.title: Null pointer dereference

blocks.output:
about to read through a null pointer...
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
exit=139
(We never reach "x = ..." — it died on the read.)

-ex run -ex bt -ex 'print p' -ex 'info locals' \
      ./bin/01_null_deref

Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x000000000040049c in main () at 01_null_deref.c:104
104     int x = *p;        // <-- THE BUG
#0  0x000000000040049c in main () at 01_null_deref.c:104
$1 = (int *) 0x0
p = 0x0
x = 0

How to read each command:
  run         -> runs the program inside gdb; it stops the instant the
                 signal is delivered, ON the faulting instruction.
  bt          -> backtrace (call stack). Here just frame #0 = main, and
                 it names the exact file:line (01_null_deref.c:104).
  print p     -> shows p == 0x0. The smoking gun: we read *through* 0.
  info locals -> all locals in the frame; confirms p=0x0 (x not set yet).
(`set debuginfod enabled off` suppresses gdb's interactive prompt asking
 whether to download missing debuginfo from the Fedora server — see
 README "debuginfod".)

==46685== Invalid read of size 4
==46685==    at 0x40049C: main (01_null_deref.c:104)
==46685==  Address 0x0 is not stack'd, malloc'd or (recently) free'd
==46685== Process terminating with default action of signal 11 (SIGSEGV)
==46685==  Access not within mapped region at address 0x0
How to read it:
  "Invalid read of size 4"  -> a 4-byte (int) load that touched memory
                               it should not have.
  "Address 0x0 is not ..."  -> 0x0 isn't stack/heap/recently-freed: it is
                               simply unmapped. => NULL deref.

ASan variant (faster; also dumps registers):

==46704==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000
==46704==The signal is caused by a READ memory access.
==46704==Hint: address points to the zero page.
    #0 0x4e9ea1 in main .../01_null_deref.c:104:13
"Hint: address points to the zero page" == NULL (or near-NULL) deref.

steps.title: LOOK AT THE LLVM IR (uses the local LLVM clang, v23)

blocks.output:
Relevant IR inside main:
      store ptr null, ptr %2, align 8      ; p = NULL
      %5 = load ptr, ptr %2, align 8       ; tmp = p   (== null)
      %6 = load i32, ptr %5, align 4       ; *** = *p   <-- FAULTS HERE
  `%6 = load i32, ptr %5` is the dereference: load 4 bytes from the pointer
  we just loaded (null). opt -passes=verify reports the IR is *well formed*
  — verification checks STRUCTURE, not that a pointer is valid at runtime.
  (META-LESSON: a verifier is not a bug finder.)

ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  Here they nearly coincide, but the crash SITE is the load (`*p`) while the
  root CAUSE is the earlier assignment `int *p = NULL;`. The load merely
  exposes the bad VALUE set earlier. In real code the NULL usually comes
  from a function that returned NULL (malloc/fopen/lookup) far from the
  deref — walk the backtrace and `print` the pointer to find WHERE it
  became NULL.

tryIt.text:
Change `int x = *p;` to `*p = 5;` (a WRITE). Re-run under gdb/valgrind:
  it now says "Invalid write" / "WRITE memory access". Same root cause,
  different access kind.
============================================================

blocks.text: segfault

`p` is set to NULL (`int *p = NULL;`) and then
             dereferenced (`int x = *p;`). Reading the int at virtual
             address 0 is forbidden — the kernel never maps page 0 —
             so the CPU raises a fault. (Buggy line: `int x = *p;`.)

"Segmentation fault (core dumped)", shell exit code 139
        (139 = 128 + signal 11 = 128 + SIGSEGV). Deterministic:
        address 0 is *never* mapped, so it crashes every run.

Give p real storage, or guard the deref:
    int v = 42; int *p = &v;             // point at a real object
or  if (p) { int x = *p; ... }            // never deref without a check

labs.title: Uninitialized / wild pointer (nondeterministic UB)

steps.title: REPRODUCE (run it MANY times; watch the exit code change)

commands: for i in $(seq 1 16); do ./bin/02_uninit_wild_ptr; echo -n "$? "; done; echo
blocks.output:
216 248 168 232 120 200 88 168 120 152 216 40 248 200 56 184
^ representative — YOURS WILL DIFFER, and that is exactly the bug. The
  values are all multiples of 8 because they are the low byte of a
  16-byte-aligned stack address. No 139 here: it never crashed.

FORCE the crash (deterministic SIGSEGV) and pin ASLR to prove causation:

commands: for i in $(seq 1 8); do ./bin/02_force; echo -n "$? "; done; echo
for i in $(seq 1 6); do setarch -R ./bin/02_uninit_wild_ptr; echo -n "$? "; done; echo
blocks.output:
120 120 120 120 120 120
^ `setarch -R` disables ASLR: now the address is fixed, so the exit code
  is IDENTICAL every run. That proves the run-to-run variation was ASLR.

steps.title: LOCATE WITH GDB (and SEE the "gdb disables ASLR" effect)

blocks.output:
-ex 'break 132' -ex run -ex 'print p' \
      -ex 'print/x *(unsigned char*)p' -ex 'info locals' \
      ./bin/02_uninit_wild_ptr
Breakpoint 1, main () at 02_uninit_wild_ptr.c:132
132         unsigned char v = *(unsigned char *)p;  // <-- THE BUG
$1 = 0x7fffffffd718 "\030\327\377\377\377\177"
$2 = 0x18
p = 0x7fffffffd718 "\030\327\377\377\377\177"
v = 0 '\000'

blocks.text:
Run that gdb line TWICE: `print p` shows the SAME address both times,
because gdb sets `disable-randomization on` by default:

blocks.output:
Disabling randomization of debuggee's virtual address space is on.
CONSEQUENCE: addresses are STABLE under gdb but DIFFER from a bare native
run (where ASLR is on). So "the address gdb shows" is not "the address
you crashed at natively". To reproduce the native layout under gdb:
    (gdb) set disable-randomization off
How to read the commands:
  break LINE       -> stop just before the deref so we can inspect p.
  print p          -> the wild pointer's value (a random stack address).
  print/x *(...)p  -> the byte we are about to return, in hex.
  info locals      -> shows p (and v, still garbage) in this frame.

steps.title: CONFIRM WITH VALGRIND (--track-origins=yes is the hero here)

blocks.output:
==56945== Use of uninitialised value of size 8
  ==56945==    at 0x400471: main (02_uninit_wild_ptr.c:132)
  ==56945==  Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation
  ==56945==    at 0x4004A0: reader (02_uninit_wild_ptr.c:121)
  How to read it:
    "Use of uninitialised value of size 8" -> the 8-byte POINTER we deref
       is itself uninitialized. Note valgrind does NOT say "Invalid read":
       the ADDRESS is valid (mapped stack) — it only caught the bug through
       uninitialized-VALUE tracking. (META-LESSON #3 again, made concrete.)
    "Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at reader" ->
       --track-origins walked the value back to WHERE it was born. Without
       --track-origins you only learn THAT it's uninitialized, not where.

  On the forced build valgrind ALSO reports the bad address:

==56951== Use of uninitialised value of size 8
  ==56951==    at 0x40047F: main (02_uninit_wild_ptr.c:132)
  ==56951== Invalid read of size 1
  ==56951==    at 0x40047F: main (02_uninit_wild_ptr.c:132)
  ==56951==  Address 0x1ffffff708 is not stack'd, malloc'd or (recently) free'd

ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  The crash SITE (forced build) is the deref in main. The ROOT CAUSE is in
  reader(): `keep` is never initialized. valgrind's --track-origins points
  straight at reader() — the *birthplace* of the bad value — not at main
  where it was used. Trace the value backward to its origin, not forward to
  the crash.

tryIt.text:
1) Run the default build under `gdb` with `set disable-randomization off`
     and confirm the printed `p` now changes between gdb runs.
  2) Build with `-fsanitize=memory` (clang MSan) if available — it is
     purpose-built to catch exactly this "use of uninitialized value".
============================================================

blocks.text: UB / wild read  (the headline meta-lesson bug)

`reader()` returns a pointer variable `keep` that it never
                initialized. `main` dereferences it (`*(unsigned char*)p`).
                Reading an uninitialized variable is Undefined Behavior.
                Buggy line: the `unsigned char v = *(unsigned char*)p;`.

WHY THIS PARTICULAR SHAPE (read this — it IS the lesson):
  A fresh program's stack pages are ZERO-FILLED by the kernel, so a naive
  `char *p; *p;` just reads 0 and behaves like a NULL deref (boring,
  deterministic). To show REAL uninitialized garbage I first "dirty" the
  stack: writer() leaves an ASLR-randomized address in a stack slot, then
  reader() — built with the SAME frame shape — reads that same slot WITHOUT
  initializing it. So `p` ends up holding a *real, valid, but random* stack
  address. That is the textbook wild pointer.

SYMPTOM (this is the whole point — it is NONDETERMINISTIC):
  - Default build: it does NOT crash. `p` is a valid (mapped) stack
    address, so the read succeeds and the program's exit code is the byte
    it happened to read — which is a byte of an ASLR'd address, so it is
    DIFFERENT ALMOST EVERY RUN. (META-LESSON #3: a wild pointer that lands
    on valid memory passes silently — "no crash" != "no bug".)
  - Forced build (-DFORCE_CRASH): we push `p` 16 MiB past the stack top
    into an unmapped page, so it reliably SIGSEGVs (exit 139).

Initialize the pointer to something real before use:
    char *keep = &some_real_object;   // in reader()
or return a defined value. Never read an object before assigning it.

labs.title: Integer divide by zero (SIGFPE)

blocks.output:
computing 100 / 0 ...
Floating point exception (core dumped)
exit=136

-ex run -ex bt -ex 'print b' -ex 'info locals' \
      -ex 'x/i $pc' ./bin/03_divzero
Program received signal SIGFPE, Arithmetic exception.
0x00000000004004b1 in main (argc=1, argv=0x7fffffffd888) at 03_divzero.c:87
87      int q = a / b;            // <-- THE BUG
#0  0x00000000004004b1 in main (argc=1, argv=0x7fffffffd888) at 03_divzero.c:87
$1 = 0
a = 100
b = 0
q = 0
=> 0x4004b1 <main+65>:  idivl  -0x18(%rbp)
How to read each command:
  run         -> stops on SIGFPE, right at the faulting instruction.
  bt          -> the call stack; names main and 03_divzero.c:87.
  print b     -> b == 0: the divisor is the problem.
  info locals -> a=100, b=0, confirming the operands.
  x/i $pc     -> disassemble the faulting instruction: it is an `idiv`
                 (signed integer divide). Proof it's an INTEGER, not FP,
                 fault despite the "Floating point exception" wording.

steps.title: VALGRIND IS THE WRONG TOOL HERE (and that's a lesson)

blocks.output:
==57274== Process terminating with default action of signal 8 (SIGFPE): dumping core
  ==57274==  Integer divide by zero at address 0x1002D8A124
  ==57274==    at 0x4004B1: main (03_divzero.c:87)
  valgrind/memcheck tracks MEMORY errors. A divide-by-zero is an arithmetic
  fault, not a bad memory access, so memcheck adds nothing — it just lets
  the SIGFPE through. Reach for a sanitizer instead:

03_divzero.c:87:15: runtime error: division by zero
  SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior 03_divzero.c:87:15
  UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer:DEADLYSIGNAL
  ==57286==ERROR: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: FPE on unknown address 0x00000042dfae
      #0 0x42dfae in main /home/adit1713ya/debug_lab/03_divzero.c:87:15
  exit=1
  UBSan instruments the divide and prints the exact file:line:column and a
  plain-English "division by zero" BEFORE the hardware fault. This is the
  right tool for arithmetic UB.

blocks.text:
ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  The crash site is the divide. The root cause is that `b` was allowed to
  become 0 (here: program run with no extra args -> argc-1 == 0). In real
  code, validate denominators at their SOURCE, not at the divide.

tryIt.text:
Run `./bin/03_divzero 5` (one arg => b==1). It prints q=100 and exits 0 —
  same code, no bug, because the input no longer drives b to 0. Bugs that
  depend on input are why you reproduce with the EXACT failing input.
============================================================

blocks.text: arithmetic fault (SIGFPE) / UB

`a / b` is evaluated with b == 0. Integer division by
             zero is Undefined Behavior in C; on x86-64 the DIV/IDIV
             instruction raises a hardware exception (#DE), delivered as
             SIGFPE. Buggy line: `int q = a / b;`.
             (`b` comes from argc so the compiler can't fold it away and
              the divide really executes at runtime.)

"Floating point exception (core dumped)" — note the name is
        a misnomer: it is an INTEGER divide fault. Shell exit 136
        (136 = 128 + 8 = 128 + SIGFPE). Deterministic.

labs.title: Stack array out-of-bounds write

steps.title: REPRODUCE (note: the plain build "succeeds" — that's the danger)

blocks.output:
buf[0]=0 (looks fine?!)
exit=0
^ Silent corruption. Nothing told you buf[4..8] were written OOB.

A stack canary makes it LOUD (corruption detected at function return):

*** stack smashing detected ***: terminated
Aborted (core dumped)
exit=134                              # 134 = 128 + 6 (SIGABRT)

steps.title: LOCATE WITH GDB (on the canary build — read the backtrace)

commands: gdb -q -batch -ex 'set debuginfod enabled off' -ex run -ex bt \
blocks.output:
./bin/04_stack_oob_write.canary
*** stack smashing detected ***: terminated
Program received signal SIGABRT, Aborted.
0x00007ffff7e243cc in __pthread_kill_implementation () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#0  0x00007ffff7e243cc in __pthread_kill_implementation () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#1  0x00007ffff7dca15e in raise () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#2  0x00007ffff7db16d0 in abort () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#3  0x00007ffff7db273b in __libc_message_impl.cold () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#4  0x00007ffff7eb0f19 in __fortify_fail () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#5  0x00007ffff7eb22a4 in __stack_chk_fail () from /lib64/libc.so.6
#6  0x00000000004004ed in main () at 04_stack_oob_write.c:113
How to read it:
  bt  -> read it bottom-up. Frame #6 is YOUR code: main at line 113 —
         the closing brace / RETURN. Frames #5..#0 are the canary tripwire
         firing: __stack_chk_fail -> __fortify_fail -> abort -> raise.
  KEY: the canary is checked at function RETURN (line 113), so gdb points
       you at the return, NOT at the overflowing write (line 111). The
       canary tells you "something smashed the stack", not WHERE. (See
       ROOT CAUSE below — escalate to ASan for the exact write.)

steps.title: VALGRIND MISSES IT; ASAN NAILS IT (the headline tool lesson)

blocks.output:
buf[0]=0 (looks fine?!)
  exit=0
  ^ valgrind/memcheck reports NOTHING. memcheck has no red zones around
    STACK arrays, so an overflow that stays within the mapped stack page is
    invisible to it. META-LESSON: "valgrind clean" != "no bug".

==NNNNN==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address 0x.... at pc 0x....
  WRITE of size 4 at 0x.... thread T0
      #0 0x... in main .../04_stack_oob_write.c:111:16
  Address 0x.... is located in stack of thread T0 at offset 48 in frame
      #0 0x... in main .../04_stack_oob_write.c:108
    This frame has 1 object(s):
      [32, 48) 'buf' (line 109) <== Memory access at offset 48 overflows this variable
  ... Shadow bytes around the buggy address: ...
  =>0x............: f1 f1 f1 f1 00 00[f3]f3 00 00 ...
  exit=1
  How to read ASan:
    "stack-buffer-overflow" + "WRITE of size 4" -> a 4-byte (int) write past
       an array on the stack, at .../04_stack_oob_write.c:111 column 16.
    "[32,48) 'buf' ... offset 48 overflows" -> buf occupies bytes 32..47 of
       the frame (16 bytes = 4 ints); the access at offset 48 is one int too
       far. ASan names the VARIABLE and the exact write — far more precise
       than the canary or gdb.
    Shadow legend: f1 = left redzone, 00 = addressable (buf's 16 bytes),
       f3 = right redzone (poisoned guard). The [..] marks the byte hit.
       ASan surrounds every stack array with poisoned redzones; touching one
       is an instant, pinpointed error — which is why ASan catches what
       valgrind misses here, and ~10x faster too.
    (ASan addresses are ASLR-randomized: representative — yours will differ.)

ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  Three different tools point at three different lines, and understanding why
  IS the lesson:
    - Plain build: no crash at all (corruption is silent).
    - Canary build / gdb: aborts at the RETURN (line 113) — that's when the
      smashed canary is *checked*, long after the damage.
    - ASan: the WRITE itself (line 111) — the true root cause.

blocks.text:
The corruption happens at line 111; everything downstream is a delayed
  symptom. Always prefer the tool that flags the WRITE, not the aftermath.

tryIt.text:
Change `i <= 8` to `i <= 4` (write just ONE past the end). Re-run the ASan
  build: it STILL fires on buf[4] — ASan's redzone catches even a 1-element
  overflow that the plain build and valgrind sail right past.
============================================================

blocks.text: stack error / buffer overflow

`buf` has 4 ints (valid indices 0..3) but the loop runs
             `i <= 8`, so it writes buf[4]..buf[8] — up to 5 ints PAST
             the end of a stack array. Buggy line: `buf[i] = i;` for i>=4.

DANGEROUSLY QUIET. With default flags on this box it does
        NOT crash and exits 0 — the writes land in adjacent stack
        padding. (This is the trap: "it ran fine" is not "it's
        correct".) A stack canary turns it into an abort at RETURN;
        ASan reports the exact overflowing write.

labs.title: Heap buffer overflow

blocks.output:
stored, p[7]=k
exit=0
^ Silent again — the plain build gives no hint p[8] was out of bounds.

steps.title: LOCATE WITH GDB (gdb alone won't catch a silent overflow)

blocks.text:
Because the plain run doesn't fault, `gdb run` just exits 0. gdb is for
the CRASH; for a silent heap overflow you either (a) reach for valgrind/
ASan (STEP 3), or (b) set a hardware WATCHPOINT on the byte after the
block to catch the write. Demo of a watchpoint:

blocks.output:
-ex 'break 90' -ex run -ex 'print (void*)&p[8]' \
      -ex 'watch *(char*)(p+8)' -ex continue -ex bt ./bin/05_heap_overflow
Breakpoint 1, main () at 05_heap_overflow.c:90
90      p[8] = '!';                       // <-- THE BUG
$1 = (void *) 0x404318       # addr of the OOB byte (representative)
Hardware watchpoint 2: *(char*)(p+8)
Old value = 0 '\000'
New value = 33 '!'           # 33 == '!': the OOB write just happened
main () at 05_heap_overflow.c:91
#0  main () at 05_heap_overflow.c:91
(watch *ADDR -> gdb stops the instant that memory changes; it reports the
 NEXT line 91 after the store, so look one line up for the writer.)

==58983== Invalid write of size 1
  ==58983==    at 0x4004C0: main (05_heap_overflow.c:90)
  ==58983==  Address 0x4a6a048 is 0 bytes after a block of size 8 alloc'd
  ==58983==    at 0x4840B26: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:447)
  ==58983==    by 0x4004A8: main (05_heap_overflow.c:87)
  How to read it:
    "Invalid write of size 1"            -> a 1-byte store to memory it
                                            shouldn't touch.
    "0 bytes after a block of size 8"    -> the address is immediately after
                                            an 8-byte heap block => overflow
                                            by one. valgrind even shows the
                                            malloc call site (line 87).

==58990==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x7b46f87e0018 at pc 0x4e9f06
  WRITE of size 1 at 0x7b46f87e0018 thread T0
      #0 0x4e9f05 in main .../05_heap_overflow.c:90:10
  0x7b46f87e0018 is located 0 bytes after 8-byte region [0x7b46f87e0010,0x7b46f87e0018)
  allocated by thread T0 here:
      #0 0x4a5bd8 in malloc
      #1 0x4e9e58 in main .../05_heap_overflow.c:87:15
  ASan and valgrind agree: a 1-byte WRITE 0 bytes after an 8-byte block,
  at line 90, allocated at line 87.

blocks.text:
ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  There is no crash site on the plain build — that's the danger. The root
  cause is the off-by-one index p[8] against a size-8 allocation. The tools
  tie the bad WRITE (line 90) back to the ALLOCATION (line 87), which is
  exactly the pair you need to reason about a heap overflow.

tryIt.text:
Change `malloc(8)` to `malloc(9)` and keep `p[8]='!'`. Both valgrind and
  ASan go quiet: the access is now in bounds. Then make it `p[9]` and watch
  them fire again, now "1 bytes after a block of size 9".
============================================================

blocks.text: heap error / buffer overflow

`p = malloc(8)` gives 8 valid bytes (p[0..7]) but we write
             p[8] — one byte PAST the block. Buggy line: `p[8] = '!';`.

Usually SILENT on a plain run: a 1-byte overflow lands in
        the allocator's padding, so it "works" and exits 0. The
        corruption only bites later (heap metadata, the next block).
        valgrind and ASan both pinpoint it immediately.

Either allocate room for the index you use (`malloc(9)`), or don't write
past the end (`p[7] = '!';`). Size allocations to the data, and index
strictly < size.

labs.title: Use after free

blocks.output:
x = 206240
exit=0
^ It "succeeded" but x is GARBAGE that changes every run (e.g. 206240,
  253135, 224352) — it's the freed chunk's tcache pointer, not 42.

blocks.text:
The plain run doesn't fault, so escalate to a sanitizer (STEP 3) to make
it deterministic. Under gdb you'd typically run the ASan build so the
tool stops you at the use:

./bin/06_use_after_free.asan
... ASan halts the program; bt shows main at 06_use_after_free.c:86 ...
(Running a sanitizer build *inside* gdb is the everyday combo: ASan finds
 it, gdb lets you poke around the frame at the moment it fires.)

==58996== Invalid read of size 4                 (heap addrs representative)
  ==58996==    at 0x4004C4: main (06_use_after_free.c:86)
  ==58996==  Address 0x4a6a040 is 0 bytes inside a block of size 4 free'd
  ==58996==    at 0x4843E43: free (vg_replace_malloc.c:990)
  ==58996==    by 0x4004BF: main (06_use_after_free.c:85)
  ==58996==  Block was alloc'd at

blocks.text:
How to read it — valgrind gives you the FULL life story of the block:
    "Invalid read of size 4 ... inside a block of size 4 free'd" -> you read
       a 4-byte int from memory that was freed.
    "free'd at ... main (...:85)"  -> WHERE it was freed.
    "Block was alloc'd at ... (...:83)" -> WHERE it was born.
  Those three lines (use 86, free 85, alloc 83) are the whole bug.

blocks.output:
used p[0]=0x55; now leaking 100 bytes
exit=0
^ Looks perfectly healthy. That's why leaks survive code review.

steps.title: GDB IS THE WRONG TOOL (know when NOT to reach for it)

blocks.text:
There is no crash, so `gdb run` just exits 0 — gdb shows you nothing.
gdb is for FAULTS (signals, wrong values), not for "memory that was never
given back". For leaks, go straight to valgrind --leak-check or LSan.

blocks.output:
==61827== 100 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 1
  ==61827==    at 0x4840B26: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:447)
  ==61827==    by 0x400488: main (08_memory_leak.c:77)
  How to read it:
    "100 bytes in 1 blocks"     -> size and count of the leaked allocation.
    "definitely lost"           -> no pointer to it survives => a true leak.
    "at malloc ... by main (...:77)" -> the ALLOCATION call stack: the
       leak is the block born at line 77. valgrind points at where it was
       allocated (you decide where it SHOULD have been freed).
  --leak-check=full -> per-leak stack traces (not just a summary count).
  --show-leak-kinds=all -> also list "indirectly lost", "possibly lost",
       and "still reachable" blocks, not only "definitely lost".
  THE FOUR LEAK KINDS:
    definitely lost  -> no pointer at all => fix it.
    indirectly lost  -> only reachable via an already-lost block.
    possibly lost    -> only an interior pointer remains (suspicious).
    still reachable   -> a pointer exists at exit (often "intentional",
                         e.g. a global cache) — usually benign.

  ASan/LeakSanitizer finds it too, automatically at process exit:

==61836==ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks
  Direct leak of 100 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
      #0 0x... in malloc
      #1 0x... in main .../08_memory_leak.c:77:15
  SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 100 byte(s) leaked in 1 allocation(s).

  No crash site at all. The "root cause" is a missing free on the path that
  loses the last pointer. The tool reports the ALLOCATION site (line 77)
  because that's the block's identity; the FIX lives wherever ownership
  ends.

tryIt.text:
Add `free(p);` before return — both valgrind and LSan go silent ("All
  heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible"). Then `free(p); free(p);`
  turns it into bug #07 (double free).

blocks.text: leak

`malloc(100)` allocates a block that is never `free`d. When
             `p` goes out of scope at return, the only pointer to the
             block is lost — the memory stays allocated until the process
             exits. Buggy line: `char *p = malloc(100);` (with no free).

NONE at runtime: exits 0, output normal. A leak is invisible
        to a single run; it only hurts long-running programs (memory
        grows without bound). You need a tool to even see it.

just shows you *a* value (gdb won't tell you it's uninitialized). For

  The symptom shows up in main (the deref, line 84) or even deep inside

             variable. `local` ceases to exist when `get_ptr` returns, so

  The crash SITE is an arbitrary deep frame where the stack finally ran out
  — its exact address/depth is meaningless and changes every run. The ROOT

y = -2147483648
exit=0
^ No crash, no warning at runtime. The wrong answer is the only symptom.

gdb runs to a clean exit; `print y` would just show -2147483648. There is
no signal and no invalid memory, so gdb has nothing to catch. Arithmetic
UB is a job for a sanitizer, not a debugger.

blocks.output:
12_signed_overflow.c:75:15: runtime error: signed integer overflow:
      2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'
  SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior 12_signed_overflow.c:75:15
  y = -2147483648
  exit=0
  How to read it:

  And the contrast that proves the point:

y = -2147483648
  (valgrind says NOTHING.)
  META-LESSON: valgrind/memcheck only sees MEMORY errors. Signed overflow is
  a pure arithmetic/UB issue with no bad memory access, so memcheck is blind
  to it. Sanitizers and valgrind are COMPLEMENTARY, not interchangeable —
  pick by the SYMPTOM (see the README cheat-sheet).

ROOT CAUSE vs CRASH SITE:
  There is no crash. The "site" and the cause are the same expression, but
  the deeper cause is trusting that `INT_MAX + 1` wraps. It is UB; treat it

`x = INT_MAX` then `x + argc`. Since argc >= 1, this is
             INT_MAX + 1, which overflows a signed int. Signed overflow
             is Undefined Behavior in C (unlike UNSIGNED, which wraps by
             definition). Buggy line: `int y = x + argc;`.
             (argc is used so the compiler can't constant-fold it away.)

SILENT. On this machine it "wraps" to INT_MIN and prints
        -2147483648, exit 0 — it LOOKS like it works. But it is UB:
        the compiler is entitled to assume signed overflow never
        happens and optimize accordingly, so at -O2 the same code
        can do something entirely different. Never rely on the wrap.

labs.title: Hand-written IR: verifier says VALID, program crashes
labs.source:
; ============================================================
; IR LESSON 2: a pointer SILENTLY TRUNCATED through a 32-bit slot
; ------------------------------------------------------------
; Hand-authored LLVM IR (opaque pointers, LLVM 21/23 compatible). It takes a
; valid 64-bit pointer, ptrtoint's it to i64, TRUNCATES to i32 (dropping the
; high 32 bits of the address), stores those 32 bits, reloads them, and rebuilds
; a pointer via inttoptr. On x86-64 a stack address looks like 0x00007ffff7....
; so chopping the high half yields a bogus address -> the final store SIGSEGVs.
;
; THE LESSON (this is the whole point):
;   `opt -passes=verify` calls this IR **VALID**. Verification checks STRUCTURE
;   (types of each instruction's operands, dominance, well-formed CFG), not
;   whether your pointer arithmetic is *sane*. With OPAQUE pointers, `ptr`
;   carries no element/width type, so a 64->32 truncation of an address is just
;   "an i64 truncated to i32" — perfectly well-typed. The size mismatch that
;   destroys the pointer is INVISIBLE to the verifier. A verifier is not a bug
;   finder; "verified" only means "well-formed".
;
; WORKFLOW (run from ir/, with the LOCAL LLVM on PATH):
;   export PATH=/home/adit1713ya/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin:$PATH
;   llvm-as lesson2_truncptr.ll -o lesson2.bc          # assemble .ll -> .bc
;   opt -passes=verify lesson2_truncptr.ll -disable-output && echo VALID
;                                                       # => prints VALID (!)
;   llc -filetype=obj lesson2_truncptr.ll -o lesson2.o # IR -> object
;   clang lesson2.o -o lesson2_exe                      # link
;   ./lesson2_exe ; echo "exit=$?"                      # => SIGSEGV, exit 139
;   lli lesson2_truncptr.ll ; echo "exit=$?"            # JIT-run the IR: same SIGSEGV
;   opt -passes=debugify lesson2_truncptr.ll -S -o lesson2.dbgfy.ll
;                                                       # attach per-instr lines,
;                                                       # then llc+gdb to map the
;                                                       # fault to an IR line.
; (See ir/README.md for the REAL captured output of every command above.)
; ============================================================

target triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"

define i32 @main() {
entry:
  ; a real 4-byte object we intend to write to
  %target = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 123, ptr %target, align 4

  ; a 32-bit slot -- TOO SMALL to hold a 64-bit pointer
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4

  ; address-of target as a 64-bit integer
  %as_int = ptrtoint ptr %target to i64
  ; *** TRUNCATE 64 -> 32: silently drops the high half of the address ***
  %trunc  = trunc i64 %as_int to i32
  ; stash the truncated address in the 32-bit slot (well-typed; semantically wrong)
  store i32 %trunc, ptr %slot, align 4

  ; read it back and rebuild a pointer from the 32 surviving bits
  %back32 = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  %back64 = zext i32 %back32 to i64
  %badptr = inttoptr i64 %back64 to ptr        ; high 32 bits are now ZERO

  ; write through the broken pointer -> almost certainly SIGSEGV
  store i32 456, ptr %badptr, align 4          ; <-- THE BUG (faults here)

  ret i32 0
}

the ROSETTA STONE for one crash.
------------------------------------------------------------
One faulting operation, written once in C, exists at EVERY level:

labs.title: The debugify line-number trap

blocks.text:
map a runtime fault to the EXACT IR instruction
                      with `opt -passes=debugify` — and its TRAP.
------------------------------------------------------------
`debugify` stamps a synthetic !DILocation onto EVERY IR instruction, with
the line number = the instruction's ORDINAL (1st instr -> line 1, 2nd -> 2,
...). It is NOT the physical line in the .ll text file.

gdb will faithfully say e.g. "debugify_trap.nodbg.ll:15", but if
you `list 15` gdb opens the .ll and prints whatever TEXT physically sits on
line 15 — usually a blank line or an unrelated instruction. The "15" names
the 15th INSTRUCTION (the faulting one), not source line 15. You resolve it
by reading the !dbg / !DILocation metadata, not by trusting `list`.

`opt -passes=verify` attaches NO debug info, so a fault in that
build gives only "main+offset" with no line at all.

We give the function several arithmetic steps before the null store so the
faulting instruction gets a satisfyingly large ordinal.

Build & trace (see cross_level/README.md for REAL output):
  clang -O0 -S -emit-llvm debugify_trap.c -o debugify_trap.nodbg.ll   # NO -g
  opt -passes=debugify debugify_trap.nodbg.ll -S -o debugify_trap.dbgfy.ll
  llc -filetype=obj debugify_trap.dbgfy.ll -o debugify_trap.dbgfy.o
  clang debugify_trap.dbgfy.o -o debugify_trap_dbgfy
  gdb ... ./debugify_trap_dbgfy     # -> "...nodbg.ll:N" where N is the ordinal
============================================================

labs.title: Crash site vs root cause: walk the SSA def-use chain backward
labs.source:
; ============================================================
; CROSS-LEVEL LESSON 3: CRASH SITE vs ROOT CAUSE — trace backward.
; ------------------------------------------------------------
; The instruction that SIGSEGVs is innocent. The real defect is upstream.
; Here a valid 64-bit pointer is destroyed long before it is used:
;
;   ROOT CAUSE (here):   %chopped = trunc i64 %addr to i32   ; keep only low 32 bits
;                        store i32 %chopped, ptr %slot       ; write 4 bytes into slot
;   ...
;   CRASH SITE (here):   store i32 456, ptr %wild            ; deref the wrecked pointer
;
; %slot is a 4-byte (i32) alloca, but we reload it with `load ptr` -- an 8-BYTE
; load. That reads the 4 bytes we wrote PLUS 4 bytes of ADJACENT stack, so the
; high half of the rebuilt pointer is garbage. The pointer is wild -> the final
; store faults (SIGSEGV, deterministically on this box).
;
; To debug this you START at the faulting store and walk the SSA def-use chain
; BACKWARD (every value names the instruction that produced it):
;
;   store i32 456, ptr %wild        <- crash site; who made %wild?
;     %wild     = load ptr, ptr %slot          <- 8-byte load from a 4-byte slot!
;       store i32 %chopped, ptr %slot          <- only 4 bytes were ever written
;         %chopped = trunc i64 %addr to i32    <- *** ROOT CAUSE ***
;           %addr  = ptrtoint ptr %target to i64
;
; TWO things this proves:
;   * `opt -passes=verify` calls this VALID. Opaque `ptr` carries no width, so
;     "trunc i64 to i32" then "load i64" is structurally fine. Verified != correct.
;   * `valgrind --track-origins=yes` (on the native exe) reports
;     "Use of uninitialised value of size 8" and traces the origin back to the
;     stack slot whose high 4 bytes we never wrote — i.e. straight to the trunc.
;
; Build & run (from cross_level/, local LLVM on PATH):
;   opt -passes=verify truncptr_rootcause.ll -disable-output && echo VALID
;   llc -filetype=obj truncptr_rootcause.ll -o tr.o && clang tr.o -o truncptr_ir
;   ./truncptr_ir ; echo exit=$?
; (REAL output for every step is in cross_level/README.md.)
; ============================================================

target triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"

define i32 @main() {
entry:
  ; a real 4-byte object we intend to write to
  %target = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 123, ptr %target, align 4

  ; a 4-byte (i32) slot -- too small to hold a 64-bit pointer
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4

  ; address-of target as a 64-bit integer
  %addr    = ptrtoint ptr %target to i64
  ; *** ROOT CAUSE: keep only the low 32 bits of the address ***
  %chopped = trunc i64 %addr to i32
  ; write those 4 bytes into the 4-byte slot (well-typed; semantically lossy)
  store i32 %chopped, ptr %slot, align 4

  ; reload as an 8-BYTE pointer from the 4-byte slot: the high 4 bytes come from
  ; ADJACENT stack -> uninitialised garbage
  %wild = load ptr, ptr %slot, align 8

  ; CRASH SITE: store through the wrecked pointer -> SIGSEGV
  store i32 456, ptr %wild, align 4

  ret i32 0
}

labs.title: The noise floor — measure the MACHINE before the code
labs.teaches:
Before you can say "my change made it 8% faster" you must know how much
the SAME code varies run-to-run on THIS machine, and why. This lab runs a
fixed, memory-free, CPU-bound workload 30 times and reports the spread.
Three things dominate the spread on a laptop:
  1. WHICH core you land on. This CPU is hybrid: P-cores (CPUs 0-7, two
     SMT threads per core) and E-cores (CPUs 8-15). The same loop is
     ~1.9x slower on an E-core. The scheduler moves you between them.
  2. FREQUENCY. The governor is `powersave`: the clock ramps up during the
     first reps. (Turbo is disabled on this laptop, no_turbo=1, which
     removes one more source of variance that most machines have.)
  3. INTERFERENCE: interrupts, other processes, the SMT sibling thread.

blocks.output:

0.92 IPC means the core spent most of each cycle waiting for the previous
iteration. And 60.1M cycles in 28.8 ms means the core ran at ~2.09 GHz
during the fast reps: that is the clock powersave gave us, no turbo.

blocks.text:
a dependent multiply-xorshift chain (each iteration needs the
 previous result), so it measures core latency, not memory or the vector
 unit. Deterministic: same answer every run.

min   = the least-disturbed run. For a CPU-bound loop this is the most
          reproducible statistic and the one to compare A vs B on.
  p50   = typical. p99/max = the disturbances (frequency ramp, migration,
          interrupts). "spread" = max/min: on a quiet pinned P-core after
          warm-up it is ~1%; unpinned it can be >2x.
  Rule: if the difference between A and B is smaller than the spread of A
        alone, you have not measured anything yet.

THE RULES THIS LAB ESTABLISHES (every later lab assumes them):
  R1. Pin (tools/pin.sh). Prefer a P-core. Never compare P-core vs E-core
      numbers to each other.
  R2. Warm up: discard the first reps, or run long enough that the ramp is
      a small fraction of the total.
  R3. Repeat and report min/p50/p99, never a single number or a mean.
  R4. Same binary, same input, same core for A and B. Interleave A/B runs
      (ABAB) so slow drift (thermal) affects both.
  R5. Count instructions AND cycles with perf stat: a change that cuts
      instructions but not cycles is not a speedup; one that cuts cycles
      but not instructions changed the microarchitectural behaviour.

low-latency boxes do all of them):
  sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance      # no ramp
  echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/intel_pstate/no_turbo   # no turbo
  kernel cmdline isolcpus= nohz_full= rcu_nocbs=  # isolate cores from the scheduler
  IRQ affinity (/proc/irq/N/smp_affinity)         # keep interrupts off the core

labs.title: Hardware counters — cycles, instructions, branches, misses
labs.teaches:
Wall time tells you THAT something is slow. Counters tell you WHY:
  branch-misses  -> the CPU guessed the wrong direction and threw work away
  cache misses   -> the core waited for memory
  IPC            -> instructions retired per cycle: how busy the core was
Two workloads, each with a "good" and a "bad" twin:
  branch-sorted vs branch-random : SAME instructions, SAME data volume,
                                   13x the time. Only one counter differs.
  stride-1 vs stride-16          : an order of magnitude FEWER instructions,
                                   yet only 1.5x less time — and the
                                   counters look nothing alike.

blocks.text: completely different:

blocks.output:
163,189,726      cpu_core/cycles/u
         565,339,998      cpu_core/instructions/u          #    3.46  insn per cycle
          83,934,670      cpu_core/L1-dcache-loads/

111,093,819      cpu_core/cycles/u

          10,534,311      cpu_core/L1-dcache-loads/

           4,425,578      cpu_core/LLC-load-misses/
  Read it:
  - Both loops walk the same 64 MB array 10 times: 640 MB from DRAM either
    way (the array is far bigger than the 18 MB L3). Same bytes moved.
  - stride-1 executes 11x more instructions (it touches all 16 ints per
    line, vectorized 4-wide) at 3.46 IPC and shows ALMOST NO MISSES: 16K
    LLC misses for 10M cache lines. That is not because the data was in
    cache — it was not — but because the hardware PREFETCHER saw the
    sequential stream and fetched every line before the load asked for
    it. Counters count DEMAND misses. A prefetched line is a hit.
  - stride-16 touches one int per line. The prefetcher keeps up less well
    with a 64-byte stride: 66% of loads miss L1 and 4.4M of the 10M lines
    miss LLC on demand, so the core waits: IPC 0.48. It still finishes
    faster (45 vs 78 ms) because it does 1/11 of the instructions, but
    nowhere near 11x faster: the cost is moving lines, not executing loads.
  Two lessons: (1) memory-bound code can show HIGH IPC and ~zero misses
  when the prefetcher hides the latency; the tell is that time scales with
  bytes, not instructions. (2) "cache misses" counters count what the core
  waited for, not what came from DRAM. For bytes-from-DRAM you need the
  uncore/memory-controller events (or just compute GB/s from bytes/time:
  640 MB / 78 ms = 8.2 GB/s here).

HOW TO READ perf stat OUTPUT:
  - Lines are `count  event  # derived metric`. Derived metrics (insn per
    cycle, % of all branches) are computed by perf from the raw counts.
  - perf stat counts the WHOLE process, setup included. Make the timed loop
    dominate (10 passes here; the fill is <5% of instructions) or the
    counters describe your setup code. (First draft of this lab used
    qsort on 16M bytes: 4 seconds of sorting made the "sorted" run look
    30x worse than random. Always sanity-check counts against expectations.)
  - On this hybrid CPU each event is listed twice (cpu_core/ and cpu_atom/);
    the PMU your process did not run on shows <not counted>. Pin first.
  - `-r 5` repeats and prints mean +- stddev. If you ask for more events
    than the PMU has counters, perf time-multiplexes them and prints a
    "(xx.xx%)" scaling note: those counts are ESTIMATES.
  - `perf list` shows event names. Generic names (cache-misses) map to
    vendor events differently per CPU; for serious work use the specific
    ones (L1-dcache-load-misses, LLC-load-misses, dTLB-load-misses) or raw
    cpu_core/event=…,umask=…/ from the vendor's event list.

labs.title: From "the binary is slow" to the hot LINE of source
labs.teaches:
The everyday investigation loop on a real (optimized, C++, possibly
stripped) binary:
  sample -> hot SYMBOL -> hot INSTRUCTIONS -> hot SOURCE LINE,
and the traps on the way:
  T1. Inlining: the hot function does not appear in the profile at all,
      because at -O2 it was inlined into its caller (which was inlined
      into ITS caller). The samples are charged to whatever symbol is
      left standing — here, `main`.
  T2. Mangling: C++ symbols look like _Z9normalizeRKNSt7__cxx11... — you
      need c++filt (or the tool's -C / --demangle) to read them.
  T3. Stripped binaries: no symbols -> perf shows raw addresses. You
      recover names from a separate debug file (.debug + gnu_debuglink),
      and you learn that perf keeps its own cache of binaries by build-id.

labs.title: Microbenchmark pitfalls — measuring the wrong thing
labs.teaches:
A microbenchmark is a program whose ONLY purpose is to be measured, and
the optimizer does not know that. Six ways the number lies, each with the
fix, all demonstrated by ONE binary and proven by reading its machine code:
  dce         the result is unused -> the loop is deleted -> "0 ns"
  constfold   the input is a compile-time constant -> answer is a literal
  closedform  even with an opaque input, some loops become a formula
  keep        the fix: opaque input (argv) + BENCH_KEEP(result)
  volatile    the WRONG fix: `volatile` forces a store per iteration and
              forbids vectorization: you measure a program nobody ships
  warmup      first-touch page faults inflate the first pass
  timer       the clock itself has a cost and a resolution

    40109f:	cmp    %rax,%rcx

  A real loop over an opaque n, vectorized: two 64-bit loads, sign-extend
  (pcmpgtd + punpckldq is how baseline SSE2 widens int -> long), two paddq,
  four elements per iteration. 0.44 ns/element = 256 MB in 30 ms = 8.6 GB/s,
  i.e. this loop is memory-bandwidth bound on this laptop, and no amount of
  AVX would change the number (try -march=native: TRY THIS #4 in lab 02).

  Now `volatile`:

401100:	movslq (%rdi,%rcx,4),%rdx
    401104:	add    %rdx,-0x8(%rsp)
    401109:	movslq 0x4(%rdi,%rcx,4),%rdx
    40110e:	add    %rdx,-0x8(%rsp)
  Scalar, and every element does a read-modify-write of the stack slot
  holding the volatile accumulator: a store-to-load dependency of ~5 cycles
  per element. 3.5 ns/element, 8x slower than the shipped code. You did
  not measure "summing an array"; you measured "volatile". This is the
  most common wrong benchmark on the internet.

HOW TO READ THE `warmup` ROWS:
  pass 1 touches 256 MB of fresh pages: every 4 KiB page costs a minor page
  fault (the kernel allocates and zeroes a page on first write). pass 2 pays
  only memory bandwidth. Here 3.2x; on another run it was 10x — the
  first-touch cost depends on what the kernel has to do (zeroing, page
  reclaim, huge pages: THP is `madvise` on this box, so no). That is the
  "warm-up" every benchmark framework discards. If your real workload runs
  ONCE on fresh memory, pass 1 IS the real cost: then measure pass 1 on
  purpose, and consider MAP_POPULATE / pre-faulting (lab 05).

HOW TO READ THE `timer` ROWS:
  clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) is a vDSO call: no kernel entry, but ~27 ns
  here. rdtsc ~12 ns; rdtscp+lfence (serialized, lab 05) ~24 ns. None can
  time a 1 ns operation: put N of them in a loop and divide, or accept the
  resolution floor. Everything you time includes the timer's cost once;
  subtract it only if it is a meaningful fraction. (Numbers are for this
  CPU; measure yours with `timer` before trusting sub-100 ns results.)

THE -O0 TRAP (the opposite lie):
dce              85.941 ms     1.281 ns/iter   sum unused -> loop deleted

constfold         0.002 ms     1.564 ns/iter   constant input -> answer computed at build time
  closedform       70.666 ms     1.053 ns/iter   opaque input, but SCEV replaced the loop by a formula

blocks.text:
At -O0 the dead loop "costs" 86 ms and the polynomial loop 71 ms.
  Neither program exists in production. -O0 numbers describe the compiler's
  worst-case scaffolding, not your algorithm. Benchmark what you ship.

tryIt.text:
1. Move BENCH_KEEP(r) INSIDE the loop of sum_keep. How much slower? Why?
     (It forces the running sum into a register/memory each iteration and
     blocks vectorization — the same disease as volatile, milder.)
  2. Change sum_squares to `s += i * i * i`. Does SCEV still find a closed
     form? (Read the asm.) What about `s += a[i] * i`?
  3. Run `keep` with n = 1M (4 MB, fits in L2) and n = 4M (16 MB, L3):
     watch ns/element drop as the loop stops being DRAM-bound.
============================================================

blocks.text: ./bin/04_microbench_pitfalls dce|constfold|keep|volatile|warmup|timer|all [n]

K1. Inputs come from outside the compiler's sight (argv, a file, a
    volatile read ONCE before the loop). Sizes included.
K2. Every result is consumed: BENCH_KEEP(result) after the loop, not
    inside it.
K3. Never make the accumulator volatile. If you must stop a loop from
    being vectorized/reassociated, use a barrier or a `-fno-…` flag, and
    KNOW that you changed the program.
K4. Read the asm of the timed region once. If it is not what you meant
    to measure, the number is meaningless no matter how stable.
K5. Report timer overhead and warm-up separately from the result, and
    benchmark the optimization level you ship.

labs.title: Tail latency — p50 is a lie, p99.9 is the product
labs.teaches:
Throughput benchmarks (labs 01-04) time a whole loop. Latency-critical
systems (trading, audio, control, request serving) care about EACH
iteration, and specifically about the worst ones. This lab times one
million iterations of a ~1 us operation INDIVIDUALLY with the serialized
TSC, and shows:
  - the distribution is not a bell curve: a tight body plus a long tail
  - what puts events in the tail (page faults, preemption, migration,
    SMT sharing, interrupts) and how to SEE each one from user space
  - which mitigations you can apply yourself (pre-fault, pin, no
    allocation/syscalls in the loop) and which need the kernel

blocks.text:
Read it: p50 (992 ns) is the honest cost of 8 serialized DRAM misses. But
p99.9 is 39x that and the max is 360 us: one iteration in a thousand is
slower than a thousand normal ones. The histogram has a second hump at
8-65 us (4.5K samples) that the body does not explain. The counters say
why: 32,772 minor page faults DURING the loop. The table is 16,384 pages
and each fresh page costs TWO faults: the first read maps the shared zero
page, the first write then allocates a real page (copy-on-write). Each
fault is a trip through the kernel: a few microseconds, sometimes tens.

blocks.output:
8 dependent loads            48      999     1530     3350     7554    87091     1162.7
tail: p99/p50 = 3.4x   p99.9/p50 = 7.6x   max/p50 = 87x
during loop: minor page faults=6  voluntary ctxsw=0  involuntary ctxsw=10  migrations seen=0
  [  4096,   8191] 4818
  [  8192,  16383] 593
  [ 16384,  32767] 61
  [ 32768,  65535] 4

blocks.text:
The page-fault hump is gone (6 faults, none in the table). p99.9 fell
from 38.7 us to 7.6 us: a 5x improvement of the metric that matters,
from a change that does not touch the hot loop at all. What remains in
the tail: 10 involuntary context switches (the scheduler took the CPU
away mid-iteration), timer/network interrupts, and the SMT sibling.

steps.title: PRE-FAULT AND PIN TO A P-CORE

blocks.output:
8 dependent loads            48      994     1555     3682     7691    77662     1171.6
tail: p99/p50 = 3.7x   p99.9/p50 = 7.7x   max/p50 = 78x
during loop: minor page faults=6  voluntary ctxsw=0  involuntary ctxsw=7  migrations seen=0
Honest result: on this laptop pinning alone does not move p99.9 (7.7 vs
7.6 us) — there were no migrations in the unpinned warm run either — and
the max swings between ~40 and ~100 us from run to run in both modes.
What is left is preemption and interrupts, and without root you cannot
remove them. That IS the finding: "the residual tail is not in my code;
it needs an isolated core." Knowing where your responsibility ends is
part of the skill.

steps.title: MAP_POPULATE DOES THE PRE-FAULT FOR YOU

blocks.output:
8 dependent loads            44     1000     1517     3502     7729    82889     1169.4
during loop: minor page faults=4  voluntary ctxsw=0  involuntary ctxsw=9  migrations seen=0
Same result as warm, no loop to write: MAP_POPULATE (or mlock, or
MADV_WILLNEED) makes the kernel fault the whole mapping in at mmap time.
This is what allocators in latency-critical systems do at startup.

tryIt.text:
1. Start a busy loop on the SMT sibling (`taskset -c 3 yes >/dev/null &`)
     and rerun STEP 3. Watch p50 AND the tail move; kill it after.
  2. Add `free(malloc(64))` inside the timed iteration. Find it in the
     histogram, then confirm with `ltrace -c`.
  3. `madvise(table, TABLE_BYTES, MADV_HUGEPAGE)` right after the mmap in
     populate mode (THP is `madvise` on this box). Compare p50: fewer TLB
     misses per lookup. Then `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses:u` both ways.
  4. Shrink TABLE_BYTES to 1 MB (fits in L2): p50 falls ~5-10x; does the
     tail? The tail is not about your code.
============================================================

blocks.text:
8 dependent random read-modify-writes in a 64 MB table (each
 address depends on the previous value, so the 8 misses serialize). That
 is a stand-in for "look something up in a big order book / hash map":
 ~125 ns per DRAM miss x 8 = ~1 us.

./bin/05_tail_latency [cold|warm|populate] [iterations]
        cold      table from calloc, NEVER touched before the timed loop
        warm      table written once before the loop (page faults paid up front)
        populate  table from mmap(MAP_POPULATE) (kernel pre-faults it)

Buckets are powers of two in ns. A healthy latency-critical loop has one
  or two adjacent buckets holding >90% of samples and a tail that decays
  FAST. A second hump is a DIFFERENT mechanism (here: page faults), not
  "noise". Name every hump; the counters printed below the table are how.

THE SOURCES OF TAIL LATENCY (and how to see each):
  page faults        getrusage(ru_minflt) delta; perf stat -e page-faults;
                     fix: pre-fault, MAP_POPULATE, mlock, hugepages (MADV_HUGEPAGE)
  preemption         /proc/self/status nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches; perf sched (root);
                     fix: pin, SCHED_FIFO (root), isolcpus (root), fewer runnable threads
  migration          sched_getcpu() changing mid-run; fix: pin
  SMT sibling        a busy sibling steals execution units; fix: leave the sibling idle
  frequency changes  powersave governor / turbo; fix: performance governor (root)
  interrupts         /proc/interrupts per-CPU deltas; fix: IRQ affinity (root)
  allocation/syscall in the loop   strace -c, ltrace -c; fix: preallocate, never call
                     the kernel on the hot path (that is the whole point of
                     busy-polling and kernel-bypass NICs)
  TLB misses         perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses; fix: hugepages (a 64 MB
                     table is 16K 4-KiB pages but only 32 huge pages)

p50 / p99 / p99.9 / max and the sample count, with the
 conditions (pinned to what, warm or cold, governor). "Average latency
 1.2 us" is not a result. "p99.9 went from 38.7 us to 7.6 us because the
 table was pre-faulted; the remaining tail is preemption, verified by the
 involuntary-switch counter" IS a result.

labs.title: Stride — the cache line is the unit of memory traffic
labs.teaches:
Memory does not move bytes; it moves 64-byte LINES. The same number of
accesses costs 8x more when each access lands on a different line, and
4x more again when each lands on a different 4 KiB page. This lab walks a
256 MB array with strides from 1 byte to 8 KiB, doing the SAME number of
loads (32M) each time, and reports ns per access.

blocks.output:
stride    ns/access line-traffic MB/s   note
         1        0.563           1777   several accesses per 64-byte line
         2        0.572           3494   several accesses per 64-byte line
         4        0.641           6236   several accesses per 64-byte line
         8        1.117           7162   several accesses per 64-byte line
        16        1.287          12435   several accesses per 64-byte line
        32        2.333          13719   several accesses per 64-byte line
        64        4.304          14869   one access per line
       128        7.963           8038   one access per line, prefetcher stride
       256        9.930           6445   one access per line, prefetcher stride
       512        8.480           7547   one access per line, prefetcher stride
      1024        8.265           7744   one access per line, prefetcher stride
      2048       10.748           5954   one access per line, prefetcher stride
      4096       17.658           3624   one access per 4 KiB page (TLB)
      8192       17.831           3589   one access per 4 KiB page (TLB)

HOW TO READ IT (three regimes):
  1. stride 1..32: 64/stride accesses share a line. Time per access grows
     slowly because most accesses hit the line that the previous access
     just pulled in. The loop is instruction-bound at stride 1 (0.56 ns is
     about one dependent add per access) and becomes line-bound by 32.
  2. stride 64..2048: every access is a new line, so time per access is
     the cost of streaming lines from DRAM: ~4.3 ns per line at stride 64 =
     14.9 GB/s of line traffic, which is this laptop's practical single-
     core bandwidth. From 128 on, fewer lines per page are touched and the
     L2 streamer prefetcher (which works within a 4 KiB page) has fewer
     lines to run ahead on, so per-line cost roughly doubles.
  3. stride >= 4096: every access is a new PAGE: a TLB miss and a page walk
     per access, and the prefetcher does not cross page boundaries. 17.7 ns
     per access, 4x the stride-64 cost, for the SAME number of loads.
  "line-traffic MB/s" = lines actually fetched x 64 bytes / time. It tells
  you how much of the memory system you are using; ns/access tells you
  what your loop pays. Both matter: the first is a ceiling, the second is
  your bill.

tryIt.text:
1. Halve the array to 128 MB and to 16 MB: at 16 MB (fits L3) stride 64
     gets much cheaper; stride 4096 stays expensive (still 4096 pages).
  2. `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses:u` at stride 64 vs 4096: predict the
     ratio before you run it.
  3. Change the access to a store (`a[idx] = i`) and re-run: stores need
     the line too (read-for-ownership), plus write-back traffic.
============================================================

blocks.text:
C1. Count LINES, not bytes. A struct field you don't need still costs a
    full line when it sits between two you do (lab 03).
C2. Sequential within a page is the fast case; the prefetcher is your
    best friend and it stops at 4 KiB boundaries (huge pages extend it:
    lab 06).
C3. Random access pays a line AND often a page per access. Reduce it
    with layout (sort, pack, index) before reaching for prefetch hints
    (lab 05).

labs.title: Working set — measure L1, L2, L3, DRAM and the TLB yourself
labs.teaches:
The classic pointer-chasing experiment: follow a random cyclic
  permutation through an array of size S, so every load depends on the
  previous one (no overlap, no prefetching), and plot ns per load against
  S. The steps in the curve ARE the memory hierarchy of this machine, and
  one of the steps is not a cache at all.

WHY A RANDOM CYCLE (Sattolo's algorithm): a single cycle visiting every
  slot once, in random order. Sequential order would let the prefetcher
  hide everything; independent random loads would let out-of-order
  execution overlap them (lab 05). Dependent random loads measure LATENCY.

steps.title: RUN IT (pinned to a P-core; 20M dependent loads per size)

tryIt.text:
1. Pin to an E-core (`-c 8`) and rerun: different L1/L2 sizes appear.
  2. `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses:u,L1-dcache-load-misses:u,LLC-load-misses:u`
     at 1 MiB, 8 MiB and 64 MiB. Match each counter to a step of the curve.
  3. Add `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` on the array (THP is `madvise` here) and
     watch the 16 MiB point drop toward true L3 latency.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- 8 KiB..32 KiB: 2.4 ns = 5 cycles at ~2.1 GHz. L1 hit latency. (4 KiB
  shows 4.4 ns: a 512-slot cycle is so short the loop overhead and the
  first-iteration effects dominate; ignore the smallest point.)
- 64 KiB..1 MiB: 3.8 -> 11.9 ns. L2 (1.25 MB on a P-core here). The
  rise inside L2 is the L1 dTLB running out (~96 entries x 4 KiB = 384 KB)
  and part of the accesses paying an L2 TLB lookup.
- 2..8 MiB: 24 -> 82 ns. L3 latency is ~40-50 cycles (~20-25 ns), and
  you can see that at 2 MiB. Beyond that the number climbs far above any
  L3 latency because the STLB (2048 entries x 4 KiB = 8 MB of reach) is
  exhausted: every load now ALSO walks the page table, and the page-table
  entries themselves compete for cache. That is the step that is not a
  cache: it is virtual memory.
- 32 MiB+: 128 -> 184 ns. DRAM latency (~100 ns) plus page walks that
  increasingly miss in cache too. The 512 MB point is the honest cost of
  a random dependent access in a large table on this laptop.
Compare with `lscpu` / `getconf -a | grep CACHE`: L1d 48 KiB and L2 1.25 MB
per P-core (getconf reports the E-core's 32 KiB / 2 MB cluster; lscpu
sums both kinds), L3 18 MB shared. The curve found them without
documentation. That is the point: you can characterize an unknown
machine (a cloud instance, a phone SoC) in a minute with this program.

W1. "Fits in cache" is per level and per core; know your machine's
    numbers (run this on every new box before believing any benchmark).
W2. A dependent random access costs ~130-180 ns here. Design structures
    so that the common path does one such access, not five (open
    addressing, flat arrays, B-trees over binary trees).
W3. Beyond ~8 MB of random reach, 4 KiB pages cost a page walk per
    access; huge pages move that cliff to gigabytes (lab 06).

labs.title: AoS vs SoA — line utilization decides bandwidth (and a trap)
labs.teaches:
The same 8M records as an Array of Structs (32-byte Order) and as a
Struct of Arrays (one array per field), under three access patterns:
  field       sum ONE field across all records      -> SoA should win
  all-fields  touch every field of every record     -> both stream everything
  random      read whole records in random order    -> AoS should win
plus a trap that catches most people the first time: a loop that "should
be bandwidth-bound" is actually bound by a floating-point dependency
chain, and the layout change cannot show its full benefit until the
compiler is allowed to reassociate.

blocks.output:
AoS: sum one field             17.58 ms   2.096 ns/rec      3.8 GB/s useful
SoA: sum one field              8.78 ms   1.047 ns/rec      7.6 GB/s useful
AoS: touch all fields          27.19 ms   3.241 ns/rec      6.5 GB/s useful
SoA: touch all fields          15.50 ms   1.847 ns/rec     11.4 GB/s useful
AoS: random record            157.53 ms  18.779 ns/rec      1.1 GB/s useful
SoA: random record            334.67 ms  39.896 ns/rec      0.5 GB/s useful
("useful GB/s" counts only the bytes the loop needed, not the lines it
 actually moved.)

225,439,202      cpu_core/cycles/u
       403,963,143      cpu_core/instructions/u          #    1.79  insn per cycle
        16,926,793      cpu_core/L1-dcache-loads/
         1,510,460      cpu_core/L1-dcache-load-misses/  #    8.92% of all L1-dcache accesses

tryIt.text:
1. Add an AoSoA layout (struct of 8-record blocks) and run all three
     patterns: it should sit between the two extremes everywhere.
  2. Make `price` a float and `qty` an int16_t: the record shrinks to 24 or
     16 bytes. Re-measure the AoS field sum: line traffic drops with size.
  3. `perf stat -e L1-dcache-load-misses:u` on `random` for both layouts:
     SoA should show ~4x the misses per record.
============================================================

blocks.text:
field: AoS reads 32-byte records to use 8 bytes: 4x the line traffic.
  8M x 32 B in 17.6 ms = 15.5 GB/s of lines: AoS is at this laptop's
  bandwidth ceiling (lab 01 measured ~15 GB/s). SoA moves 4x fewer
  bytes, yet is only 2x faster, 1.05 ns per record. Why not 4x?
THE TRAP: look at the SoA loop's asm:
  addsd (%rdi,%rax,8),%xmm0 ; addsd 0x8(%rdi,%rax,8),%xmm0 ; ... (8 per iteration)
  Eight scalar double adds into ONE register: a dependency chain. Adding
  doubles in a different order changes rounding, so without permission
  the compiler must keep the program order, and the loop is bound by
  the FP-add latency (2 cycles on this core: 1.05 ns), not by memory.

blocks.output:
AoS: sum one field             17.26 ms   2.057 ns/rec      3.9 GB/s useful
SoA: sum one field              4.03 ms   0.481 ns/rec     16.6 GB/s useful

blocks.text:
With reassociation allowed the loop becomes packed `addpd` into several
  accumulators, and SoA now runs at 16.6 GB/s useful: the full 4.3x that
  the layout promised. AoS did not move: it was bandwidth-bound already.
  Lesson: a layout change only pays when the loop is bound by the thing
  the layout fixes. Check what the loop is bound by first (codegen lab 02
  shows the -Rpass remarks and the pragma that allows reassociation for
  one loop instead of the whole program).
all-fields: both layouts read every byte. SoA still wins 1.75x: four
  sequential streams with unit stride vectorize and prefetch well; AoS
  handles 32-byte structs with mixed types, less vectorizable.
random: AoS 18.8 ns, SoA 39.9 ns. One random record is ONE line in AoS
  and FOUR lines (four arrays) in SoA: SoA loses 2x. Random access by
  record wants the record together.

L1. Lay data out for the loop that dominates: scans of a few fields ->
    SoA; random access to whole records -> AoS; both -> AoSoA (blocks
    of 8-16 records in SoA form) or a hot/cold split (hot fields in a
    compact array, cold fields elsewhere).
L2. Before crediting a layout change, confirm the loop is memory-bound
    (bytes moved / time near the machine's bandwidth). If it isn't,
    find the real bound: an FP chain, a branch, a division.
L3. "Useful bytes / time" is the honest bandwidth metric; lines moved /
    time is the ceiling. The gap between them is your waste.

labs.title: False sharing — independent data, shared line, shared cost
labs.teaches:
Coherence works on whole 64-byte lines. If two cores write two DIFFERENT
variables that happen to share a line, each write must first pull the
line away from the other core (request-for-ownership), and the line
ping-pongs between them. The variables are logically independent; the
hardware cannot tell. This lab has N threads each incrementing its OWN
counter 100M times, with the counters (a) adjacent, (b) padded to one per
line, and for comparison (c) all threads on the SAME counter.
labs.build:
(cd cache && ./build.sh)   -> bin/04_false_sharing (-pthread)
Threads pin themselves to CPUs 2, 4, 6, 0: four DIFFERENT physical
P-cores (siblings are 2-3, 4-5, 6-7, 0-1). Pinning to siblings would
measure something else (shared L1).

blocks.output:
configuration                                  ms ns/increment
1 thread, own counter (baseline)            886.6         8.87
2 threads, adjacent counters (FALSE)       5081.3        50.81
2 threads, padded counters                  872.6         8.73
2 threads, SAME counter (true sharing)     3636.8        36.37
4 threads, adjacent counters (FALSE)      10762.9       107.63
4 threads, padded counters                  885.6         8.86
4 threads, SAME counter (true sharing)     7728.1        77.28
sizeof(Plain)=8 sizeof(Padded)=64  &plain[1]-&plain[0]=8 bytes

tryIt.text:
1. Change `cpus` to {2, 3, 4, 5} (SMT siblings share an L1) and rerun:
     false sharing gets cheaper (same L1) but the baseline gets slower
     (the siblings compete for one core's execution units).
  2. Replace atomic_fetch_add with a plain `(*ctr)++` (a data race, but
     instructive): the line still bounces, and the count is wrong.
  3. Spread the 4 counters 16 bytes apart instead of 8: still one line,
     still slow. Then 64: fixed. The threshold is the line, not proximity.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- Baseline: one atomic increment (lock xadd) is ~8.9 ns when the line
  stays in this core's L1.
- Padded: 2 or 4 threads, each on its own line: 8.7-8.9 ns. Perfect
  scaling; the threads never interact.
- Adjacent (false sharing): 50.8 ns with 2 threads, 107.6 ns with 4: 6x
  and 12x slower, for the SAME instructions on DIFFERENT data. Every
  increment waits for the line to travel from another core's cache (a
  cross-core transfer is ~40-100 ns), and the more cores, the longer the
  queue.
- Same counter (true sharing): 36 and 77 ns. Note that false sharing was
  as bad or WORSE than genuinely sharing one counter. The hardware
  mechanism is identical (line ping-pong); the only difference is that
  the true-sharing version is at least doing what you asked.

sections.title: HOW TO FIND IT IN REAL CODE

blocks.text:
- A scaling experiment: run the same per-thread work with 1 thread, then
    N threads on separate cores. If per-op cost rises with N although the
    threads "don't share anything", suspect a shared line.
  - `perf c2c record` / `perf c2c report` (needs root here) names the
    cache lines and the offsets within them that bounce between cores.
  - Typical culprits: arrays of per-thread counters or flags; a struct with
    one hot field written by thread A next to one written by thread B; a
    lock word next to the data it protects; the head and tail indices of a
    queue (concurrency lab 02).

THE FIX (and its cost):
  alignas(64) on each concurrently-written hot variable, or
  std::hardware_destructive_interference_size (C++17; the value is a
  compiler/target constant and can differ between compilers, so many
  codebases hardcode 64 and static_assert it). Padding costs memory and
  cache footprint: pad what is WRITTEN concurrently, not everything. Data
  that is only read can share lines freely: readers don't bounce lines.

labs.title: Memory-level parallelism, and when software prefetch helps
labs.teaches:
A DRAM access costs ~140 ns (lab 02) but the core can have many in
flight at once. Latency-bound code (each load depends on the previous)
pays the full cost every time; throughput-bound code overlaps them.
Three experiments on the same 128 MB random cycle:
  1. K independent dependent chains: ns per load falls almost linearly
     with K (memory-level parallelism, MLP).
  2. ONE chain with "jump pointers": each node also stores the node D
     steps ahead, so we can prefetch it. Software prefetch turns a
     latency-bound walk into a throughput-bound one: 7-10x.
  3. Independent loads whose addresses are already in an array: software
     prefetch does NOTHING, because the out-of-order core already sees
     the addresses and overlaps the loads itself.

       1        144.7

== 2: ONE chain with jump pointers (D=8): prefetch the node D steps ahead ==
no prefetch               140.2 ns/load

== 3: independent loads with addresses in an index array: prefetch distance ==

tryIt.text:
1. D = 2 and D = 4: prefetch too close to its use hides little.
  2. Shrink BYTES to 8 MB (L3) and rerun: MLP gains shrink because L3
     latency is short and the chain is limited by other things.
  3. `perf stat -e cycles:u,instructions:u` on chains=1 vs chains=16:
     instructions identical, cycles 10x apart. IPC is the tell.
============================================================

blocks.text:
1. 1 chain = 145 ns per load: pure latency. 16 chains = 12.3 ns: the
   core keeps ~12 misses in flight (the load buffer / fill buffers set
   the ceiling; on this core it flattens around 10-16). Same total
   work; the only difference is DEPENDENCY. This is the single most
   important idea for data-structure performance: independent lookups
   should be issued together (batching), not one after another.
2. The jump-pointer trick: the address of node i+D is known at node i,
   so `__builtin_prefetch` issues its miss D steps early. With D=8,
   140 -> 21 ns; with D=16, 156 -> 15 ns, approaching the 16-chain
   throughput. This is how B-trees, skip lists and hash tables get
   "prefetchable": you store or compute the next-next address early.
   Cost: 8 bytes per node and one extra load (from the same line).
3. When addresses come from an index array, the loads are already
   independent: the core issues them back to back and prefetching
   changes nothing (11.1 vs 11.4 ns). Software prefetch only helps when
   the hardware could NOT have known the address in time. Adding
   prefetches to code like this costs instructions and can hurt.

M1. Latency-bound code is limited by dependency, not by bandwidth. Ask
    "how many misses can be in flight?" before "how fast is memory?".
M2. Restructure for independence first: batch lookups, process K keys
    at once, use breadth over depth.
M3. Prefetch only when (a) the loads are dependent AND (b) you can
    compute the address at least one memory latency (~140 ns = the
    time for D steps of the hot loop) ahead. Measure; the wrong distance
    or a prefetch the hardware already did is pure overhead.

labs.title: TLB reach and transparent huge pages
labs.teaches:
Every load translates a virtual address. The TLB caches translations:
~96 first-level entries and 2048 second-level entries here, so with
4 KiB pages random access beyond ~8 MB misses the TLB on nearly every
load and pays a page walk (several dependent memory reads of its own).
A 2 MiB huge page covers 512x the memory per entry. Linux can give you
huge pages transparently (THP): this box is in `madvise` mode, so you
ask with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) and, since 6.1, can force the matter
with MADV_COLLAPSE. This lab does dependent random loads over a region
with 4 KiB pages vs huge pages, prints how many huge pages you actually
got, and counts dTLB misses.

blocks.output:
mode=4k   region=1024 MB  huge after fault=0 MB, after MADV_COLLAPSE=0 MB (rc=0 ok) | dependent random loads: 226.3 ns/load
         4,967,751      cpu_core/dTLB-load-misses/       #   92.89% of all dTLB cache accesses
         5,347,937      cpu_core/dTLB-loads/

mode=huge region=1024 MB  huge after fault=324 MB, after MADV_COLLAPSE=324 MB (rc=12 Cannot allocate memory) | dependent random loads: 188.9 ns/load
         3,417,438      cpu_core/dTLB-load-misses/       #   64.90% of all dTLB cache accesses
         5,265,403      cpu_core/dTLB-loads/

blocks.text:
Read it: with 4 KiB pages 93% of the 5M dependent loads miss the TLB
(each is a fresh random page). Asking for huge pages got only 324 MB of
the 1 GiB as huge pages, and MADV_COLLAPSE could not finish the job
(ENOMEM: the kernel has no free 2 MiB-contiguous physical chunks on this
busy laptop). Result: a third of the loads hit huge pages, misses drop to
65%, time drops 226 -> 189 ns. Partial success, honestly reported by
the program itself: NEVER assume you got huge pages; measure
AnonHugePages (/proc/self/smaps) and the miss rate.

steps.title: SMALLER REGIONS, WHERE THP SUCCEEDS COMPLETELY

blocks.output: mode=4k   region=256 MB  huge after fault=0 MB,   after MADV_COLLAPSE=0 MB   (rc=0 ok) | dependent random loads: 146.7 ns/load
mode=huge region=256 MB  huge after fault=256 MB, after MADV_COLLAPSE=256 MB (rc=0 ok) | dependent random loads: 129.9 ns/load
mode=4k   region=64 MB   ...                                                          | dependent random loads: 142.1 ns/load

mode=huge region=64 MB   huge after fault=64 MB, ... (rc=0 ok)                       | dependent random loads: 127.8 ns/load
  Read it: with the whole region on huge pages (128 entries cover 256 MB,
  no misses), a dependent random load costs ~128-130 ns = DRAM latency.
  With 4 KiB pages it costs ~142-147 ns: the page walk adds ~15-17 ns
  here, because for a 256 MB region the page-table entries (512 KB of
  them) stay cache-resident. For the 1 GiB region they don't, and the
  4 KiB cost climbs to 226 ns: a walk that misses cache is ~100 ns on
  top of the data miss. TLB cost is not a constant; it depends on whether
  the page tables themselves are hot.

WHEN HUGE PAGES MATTER (and when they don't):
  - Random access over a working set beyond ~8 MB (STLB reach): yes:
    10-40% on latency-bound code, more when page tables miss cache.
  - Sequential streaming: little; the hardware prefetcher and the STLB
    keep up, and the walk cost is amortized over 64 loads per page.
  - Fits in L2/L3 and under 8 MB: nothing to gain.

blocks.text:
Costs: 2 MiB granularity wastes memory for small objects; THP
  `always` can cause allocation stalls and khugepaged CPU use, which is
  why latency-sensitive systems prefer `madvise` (this box) plus explicit
  madvise/MAP_HUGETLB on the big tables, or hugetlbfs reserved at boot
  (root) so the pages are guaranteed instead of best-effort.

tryIt.text:
1. Run the 1 GiB `huge` case right after a reboot (little fragmentation):
     you will likely get all 1024 MB and ~130 ns.
  2. Replace the dependent chain with independent random loads (drop the
     `p[idx] +`): the TLB cost mostly vanishes behind memory-level
     parallelism (lab 05). TLB misses hurt latency-bound code most.
  3. `cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled` and `.../defrag`;
     read what `madvise` and `defer+madvise` mean for a latency-critical
     process.
============================================================

blocks.text:
T1. Beyond ~8 MB of random reach with 4 KiB pages, count a page walk per
    access. Huge pages move the cliff to gigabytes.
T2. THP is best-effort. Check AnonHugePages and dTLB-load-misses; on a
    fragmented machine you may get a fraction, or nothing.
T3. For guaranteed huge pages in production: hugetlbfs / MAP_HUGETLB
    reserved at boot (root), pre-faulted, mlocked.
