labs.title: What common C++ idioms compile to at -O2 (read, don't guess)
labs.teaches:
Twelve small functions, each a C++ idiom that people argue about in
performance reviews. The build emits their assembly at -O0, -O2 and -O2
-march=native; this header shows the -O2 output so you can see what the
compiler actually did. The skill: open the .s file, find the function
(`awk '/^_Z.../,/\.Lfunc_end/'`), ignore .cfi/.p2align noise, read.
labs.build:
(cd codegen && ./build.sh)   -> bin/01_idioms.O2.s, .O0.s, .native.s
  (-fno-asynchronous-unwind-tables removes the .cfi_* directives so the
   output is readable; it changes nothing about the instructions.)

WHAT -O2 EMITTED (from bin/01_idioms.O2.s, AT&T syntax, x86-64 baseline):

  min_branch(a,b) = a<b ? a : b            -> NO branch: a conditional move
      movl  %esi, %eax
      cmpl  %esi, %edi
      cmovll %edi, %eax
      retq
    (At -O0 the same function is 15 instructions with a jge and two spills.
     "Branchless min" hand-tricks are re-inventing this; lab 04 measures.)

  div10(x) = x / 10                         -> multiply by the magic constant, shift
      movl  %edi, %ecx
      movl  $3435973837, %eax               # 0xCCCCCCCD = ceil(2^35 / 10)
      imulq %rcx, %rax
      shrq  $35, %rax
    Division by a constant never divides. A 3-cycle multiply replaces a
    ~20-cycle div. Division by a VARIABLE stays a div: hoist it.

  is_pow2(x) = x && !(x & (x-1))            -> bit tricks; with -march=native: popcnt
      testl %edi, %edi ; je .LBB2_1 ; leal -1(%rdi),%eax ; testl %eax,%edi ; sete %al
    native: popcntl %edi, %eax ; cmpl $1, %eax ; sete %al

  sum_vec(const vector<int>&)               -> vectorized (SSE2) loop, 4 ints per step
      movq (%rsi,%rax,4), %xmm2 ; movq 8(%rsi,%rax,4), %xmm3
      pcmpgtd %xmm2, %xmm4 ; paddq %xmm2, %xmm0 ; ... ; addq $4, %rax ; cmpq %rax, %r8
    The range-for over a vector is two pointer loads (begin/end) and a
    plain loop; no abstraction survives to the machine code.

  zero(p, n): for i: p[i] = 0              -> jmp memset@PLT (loop idiom recognized)
      testq %rsi, %rsi ; je ; movq %rsi,%rdx ; xorl %esi,%esi ; jmp memset@PLT
    Your loop became a library call (a tail call, even). This is why
    "hand-written memset loops are faster" claims are always wrong at -O2.

  call_virtual(Base&, x)                   -> load vptr, load slot 0, indirect jump
      movq (%rdi), %rax ; movq (%rax), %rax ; jmpq *%rax
    Two dependent loads then an indirect branch (predicted by the BTB).
    The cost that matters is the missed INLINING of the callee, not these
    three instructions (HFT module, "virtual calls").

  call_std_function(const std::function&, x)   -> null check + indirect call
      cmpq $0, 16(%rdi) ; je .throw ; leaq 4(%rsp),%rsi ; callq *24(%rdi)
    std::function costs an indirect call through its invoker plus a check,
    and the argument is passed by ADDRESS (spilled to the stack: movl %esi,
    4(%rsp)). Prefer templates or function_ref in hot paths.

  call_lambda(x): lambda(y){ y*3 }(x)      -> leal (%rdi,%rdi,2), %eax
    The lambda vanished. Zero cost, fully inlined, x*3 as one lea.

  switch_dense(k) 0..7                     -> a table LOAD, no jump table needed
      cmpl $7, %edi ; ja default ; movl .Lswitch.table(,%rax,4), %eax
    Because every case returns a constant, clang built a lookup table of
    RESULTS. The "replace switch with a table" advice is done for you.

  switch_sparse(k) {1,100,10000,1000000}   -> a compare tree (binary search)
      cmpl $9999, %edi ; jg ; cmpl $1, %eax ; je ; cmpl $100, %eax ; ...
    Sparse cases can't be a table; you get log2(n) compares. Dense enums
    starting at 0 are the cheap kind.

tryIt.text:
1. Add `int64_t mul_add(int64_t a, int64_t b, int64_t c) { return a*b+c; }`
     and check for a single `imul` + `add` (x86 has no integer FMA). Then
     the same for double with -march=native: vfmadd.
  2. Add a function that returns a std::string by value; read the SSO
     handling. Then std::string_view: two registers.
  3. Give Base::f a `final` override in a derived class and call through a
     `Derived&`: the virtual call becomes direct (devirtualization).
============================================================

blocks.text:
For each function: predict the instructions BEFORE you look. Then look.
Then compare -O2 with -O2 -march=native (popcnt, AVX2 in sum_vec) and
with -O0 (everything through memory). The habit this builds, reading the
asm for the 20 lines that matter, is what separates "I think the
compiler will..." from "it emits...". Use tools/asmdiff.sh for any
function under any two flag sets.

labs.title: Vectorization remarks — why a loop did or did not vectorize
labs.teaches:
The loop vectorizer explains itself if you ask. Seven loops, each a
classic reason for vectorizing or not: may-alias pointers, restrict, a
floating-point reduction (illegal to reorder), the same reduction with a
per-function permission, a loop-carried dependence, an early exit, and a
gather. The remarks name the reason; the timings show what it costs; and
one surprise shows that "more ISA" can make a loop SLOWER.

blocks.output:
axpy          : remark: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 2)
axpy_restrict : remark: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 2)
dot           : remark: loop not vectorized: cannot prove it is safe to reorder floating-point
                operations; allow reordering by specifying '#pragma clang loop vectorize(enable)'
                before the loop or by providing the compiler option '-ffast-math'
dot_pragma    : remark: vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, interleaved count: 2)
prefix        : remark: loop not vectorized: unsafe dependent memory operations in loop.
                Use #pragma clang loop distribute(enable) to allow loop distribution ...
find_neg      : remark: loop not vectorized: Cannot vectorize potentially faulting early exit loop
gather        : remark: loop not vectorized: cannot identify array bounds
main's loops  : vectorized (the fill loop)

blocks.text:
Read it: width 4 = four floats per 128-bit register; interleave 2 = two
independent vector accumulators/streams per iteration. `axpy` vectorized
even though y and x may alias: clang emitted a RUNTIME overlap check and
two versions of the loop (versioning). `restrict` removes the check.

blocks.output:
axpy, axpy_restrict, dot_pragma : vectorized loop (vectorization width: 8, interleaved count: 4)
gather                          : vectorized loop (vectorization width: 8, interleaved count: 1)

blocks.text:
With AVX2 the width doubles, and `gather` now vectorizes (vpgatherdd
exists), while the cost model still refuses to interleave it.

steps.title: MEASURE (1M floats = 4 MB, L3-resident, 200 reps, pinned)

blocks.output:
axpy               0.603 ns/elem
  axpy_restrict      0.364 ns/elem
  dot (scalar)       0.985 ns/elem
  dot_pragma         0.244 ns/elem

axpy               0.431 ns/elem
  axpy_restrict      0.377 ns/elem
  dot (scalar)       1.940 ns/elem      <-- SLOWER than baseline
  dot_pragma         0.230 ns/elem
  Read it:
  - dot vs dot_pragma: 4x. The scalar reduction is a chain of dependent
    adds (2 cycles each on this core); the vector version keeps 8 partial
    sums (4 lanes x 2 interleave) and adds them at the end.
  - axpy vs axpy_restrict at baseline: 0.60 vs 0.36. The versioned loop
    pays its overlap check and a less favourable code layout; `restrict`
    (or `__restrict`, or passing spans you know are disjoint) is free
    speed when it is TRUE. When it is false, it is undefined behaviour.
  - THE SURPRISE: `dot (scalar)` got 2x SLOWER with -march=native. The asm:
      baseline: mulss (%rsi,%rcx,4),%xmm1 ; addss %xmm0,%xmm1 ; ...
      native:   vfmadd132ss (%rsi,%rcx,4),%xmm0,%xmm1 ; vfmadd231ss ... ; ...
    clang's default -ffp-contract=on fused the multiply-add into an FMA.
    FMA has 4-cycle latency here; the separate add had 2, and the multiply
    was off the critical path. Fewer instructions, longer dependency chain,
    half the speed. Lesson: the chain, not the instruction count, bounds a
    reduction; and "enable FMA" is not automatically a win.

THE VECTORIZER'S CHECKLIST (what the remarks are checking):
  1. Countable trip count (no early exit; find_neg fails here).
  2. No loop-carried dependence (prefix fails: a[i] needs a[i-1]).
  3. Memory does not overlap, or a runtime check can prove it (axpy).
  4. Operations are vectorizable on this target (gather needs AVX2).
  5. Reordering is allowed (FP reductions need reassociation permission).
  6. The cost model says it is profitable (interleave count 1 for gather).

tryIt.text:
1. Compile with -ffp-contract=off -march=native: dot (scalar) returns
     to ~1 ns. Now you have proof the FMA was the cause.
  2. Change `find_neg` to count negatives without returning early: it
     vectorizes. Compare the two remarks.
  3. `#pragma clang loop vectorize_width(8)` on axpy at baseline: the
     vectorizer can't (no AVX); read the remark it gives you.
============================================================

blocks.text:
V1. Always ask: -Rpass=loop-vectorize -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize
    -Rpass-analysis=loop-vectorize. Never guess from the source.
V2. Grant permissions narrowly: `restrict` on the pointers you know,
    `#pragma clang fp reassociate(on)` on the function you accept, not
    -ffast-math on the whole program (it also changes NaN/inf handling).
V3. Verify the effect with a measurement AND by reading the loop body;
    a vectorized loop that runs slower (FMA chain, gather scatter cost)
    is not a success.

labs.title: llvm-mca — latency-bound vs throughput-bound, predicted then measured
labs.teaches:
llvm-mca simulates a loop body on a model of the CPU's pipeline and
reports how many cycles per iteration the DEPENDENCIES and the PORTS
allow. It cannot see memory misses or branches, but for the arithmetic
core of a loop it answers the question "is this bound by latency or by
throughput?" before you run anything. Two loops doing the same
multiply-add work: one recurrence (every iteration waits for the
previous product) and four interleaved recurrences.

(cd codegen && ./build.sh)   -> bin/03_llvm_mca, bin/03_llvm_mca.s (with LLVM-MCA-BEGIN/END markers)
The markers come from `__asm__ volatile("# LLVM-MCA-BEGIN name")` in the
source: they survive into the .s as comments and delimit regions.

dependency. Iteration 1's imul waits (======) for iteration 0's add: the

blocks.output:
chain1    2.287 ns/elem
  chain4    0.508 ns/elem
  Ratio measured: 4.5x. Ratio predicted: 6.03 / 1.5 = 4.0x. The model got
  the SHAPE right (latency-bound vs throughput-bound, ~4x) and the
  direction of every conclusion you would draw from it.

WHERE THE MODEL IS WRONG, AND WHY THAT IS FINE:
  At ~2.1 GHz, 2.287 ns = 4.8 cycles per element, not 6. The real chain is
  imul (3) + add (1) = 4 cycles: the LOAD in `addq (mem),%rax` is not on
  the chain (its address does not depend on %rax), so the core issues it
  early and only the 1-cycle add waits. mca charges the fused load+add its
  full 6-cycle latency to the chain: a known limitation of modelling a
  micro-fused instruction as one unit. Similarly chain4 measured 1.07
  cycles/elem vs 1.5 predicted. Use mca for RELATIVE questions ("is it the
  chain?", "would 4 accumulators help?", "which port is saturated?") and
  the machine for absolute numbers.

     different conclusions? (imul latency is 3 on all; add-from-memory
     differs.)
  2. Make chain8 (eight recurrences). mca: Block RThroughput 8.0, Total
     Cycles ~8 per 8 elements = 1.0/elem: now PORT-bound. Measure it.
  3. Replace the multiply by an add: chain latency 1+1; how many chains
     until the ports (Block RThroughput) become the limit?
============================================================

blocks.text:
cache misses (it assumes every load hits), branch mispredicts, the
frequency, the front-end on real code layout, and anything across the
region boundary. A loop that mca says runs at 1 cycle/iter and the
machine runs at 100 is memory-bound: go to the cache track.

A1. For an arithmetic loop, run mca before optimizing: if Total Cycles
    >> Iterations x Block RThroughput, you are latency-bound and need
    more independent chains (accumulators), not faster instructions.
A2. Read the Instruction Info latencies: the longest dependent path
    through the loop is your speed limit.
A3. Confirm with cycles/element from perf stat; expect mca to be within
    ~30% on the absolute, and right on the ratio.

labs.title: Branch vs cmov — the compiler chooses the shape, the data decides the cost
labs.teaches:
"Branchless is faster" is not a rule; it is a measurement that depends
on (a) whether the compiler actually produced branchless code and (b)
whether the branch would have been predictable. Four functions on the
same data:
  select_naive   s += c[i] ? a[i] : b[i]       as people write it
  select_cmov    load both, then select         the shape that gets if-converted
  select_branch  a REAL branch, forced with an asm barrier
  compact        out[j] = in[i]; j += keep[i]   branchless stream compaction
run on a random condition (unpredictable) and a periodic one (predictable).

steps.title: RUN IT (two passes, pinned; 4M elements, L2/L3-resident)

blocks.output:
random condition       naive  7.35   cmov  1.02   forced-branch  7.56   compact  1.54   (ns/elem)
predictable condition  naive  0.97   cmov  1.75   forced-branch  1.20   compact  1.06   (ns/elem)
random condition       naive  7.29   cmov  1.49   forced-branch  7.51   compact  1.13   (ns/elem)
predictable condition  naive  0.98   cmov  0.73   forced-branch  1.66   compact  0.78   (ns/elem)

blocks.text:
select_naive: a BRANCH, on the pointer, not a cmov:
    cmpl  $0, (%rdx,%r9,4)
    movq  %rsi, %rcx
    je    .LBB0_8
    movq  %rdi, %rcx            # rcx = c[i] ? a : b   ... then load (%rcx,%r9,4)
  Clang chose to branch and load only one side. Reasonable in general
  (loading both sides could touch memory you never needed), fatal on
  random data: 7.3 ns/elem = a mispredict every other element.
select_cmov: loading both sides first made the select if-convertible,
  and then VECTORIZABLE. There is no cmov at all: a 128-bit blend:
    movq (%rdi,%rax,4),%xmm3 ; movq (%rsi,%rax,4),%xmm5 ; movq (%rdx,%rax,4),%xmm7
    pcmpeqd %xmm1,%xmm7 ; pand %xmm7,%xmm5 ; pandn %xmm3,%xmm7 ; por %xmm5,%xmm7
  Four elements per step, no control flow, 1.0-1.5 ns on random data:
  5-7x faster than the branch. Same source semantics; different shape.
select_branch: the asm barrier keeps a real jcc; it tracks `naive`.
compact: branchless by construction, and clang found a neat trick:
    movl  (%rsi,%r8,4), %r10d ; movl %r10d, (%rdi,%rax,4)    # unconditional store
    cmpl  $1, (%rdx,%r8,4) ; sbbq $-1, %rax                   # j += (keep != 0) via carry
  The store always happens (to out[j], overwritten next time if not
  kept) and the index advances via subtract-with-borrow. ~1 ns/elem
  regardless of the data. This is how you write a filter for
  unpredictable predicates.

tryIt.text:
1. Compile with -march=native: the blend becomes 256-bit (vpblendvb);
     does random-condition cmov get faster? (It is probably already
     bandwidth/latency-bound on the three loads.)
  2. Make `a[i]` expensive: `a[i] * a[i] / 7`. On predictable data the
     branch now wins clearly: it skips the work half the time.
  3. Sort `c_rand` (all zeros then all ones) and rerun: the "random" rows
     become the predictable ones. That is the classic interview question,
     and now you own the counter that proves it (lab perf/02).
============================================================

sections.title: HOW TO READ THE PREDICTABLE ROWS

blocks.text:
With a periodic condition (512 true, 512 false) the branch predictor is
right almost always, and naive/branch cost 1.0-1.7 ns: about the same as
the branchless versions, within run-to-run noise (cmov shows 1.75 in one
pass and 0.73 in the next: that spread IS the noise floor of a 4M-element
loop on this laptop, lab perf/01). So: on predictable data, nothing to
gain; on unpredictable data, 5-7x. The data decides, and you can measure
predictability directly: `perf stat -e branch-misses:u`.

B1. Never assume the compiler emitted a cmov. Read the loop. The shape of
    the source (load-both vs load-one) changes its decision.
B2. Branchless wins when the condition is unpredictable AND both sides
    are cheap and safe to evaluate. It loses when one side is expensive,
    or when the branch was predictable and the select adds latency to a
    dependency chain.
B3. Prefer formulations the vectorizer can take (load both, blend) over
    hand-written bit tricks; and check `perf stat -e branch-misses`
    before and after.

labs.manifestTitle: Branch vs cmov vs blend: the compiler chooses the shape, the data decides the cost
labs.evidence: Naive form compiled to a branch (7.3 ns random); load-both form vectorized (1.0-1.5 ns); compact via sbb trick

labs.title: Inlining across translation units — separate compilation vs LTO
labs.teaches:
The optimizer works one translation unit at a time. A tiny hot function
defined in another .cpp is a CALL: no inlining, no vectorization of the
loop around it, no constant propagation into it. Link-time optimization
(LTO) merges the units before optimizing, and the call disappears. This
lab is two files: 05_lib.cpp defines `scale`, this file calls it 200M
times.

commands: for b in 05_separate 05_lto 05_lto_thin; do printf "%-14s " $b; ../tools/pin.sh -q ./bin/$b; done
blocks.output:
05_separate    1.317 ns/call
05_lto         0.968 ns/call
05_lto_thin    0.947 ns/call

blocks.text:
separate:
  4004e3:  call   400590 <_Z5scalel>       # one call per iteration
  4004e8:  add    %rax,%r13
  4004f1:  jne    4004e0 <main+0x50>
lto:
  400524:  paddq  %xmm2,%xmm5              # scale() inlined, then the loop VECTORIZED
  400553:  paddq  %xmm5,%xmm8
  ...
  400577:  add    $0xfffffffffffffffc,%rcx
  40057b:  jne    400520 <main+0x90>
With the definition visible, `scale` was inlined into main and the whole
accumulation loop became packed 64-bit adds, four per step. The 1.3 ns
was never "the cost of a call" (a predicted call is a few cycles); it
was the cost of everything the call PREVENTED.

steps.title: ASK THE INLINER (remarks come from the LINK step under LTO)

blocks.output: 05_main.cpp:8:19: remark: '_ZL8bench_nsv' inlined into 'main' with (cost=35, threshold=487) ...
<unknown>:0:0: '_Z5scalel' inlined into 'main' with (cost=-15025, threshold=337)

blocks.text:
Read it: under LTO the inlining decision happens inside the linker's
optimization pipeline, so the remark must be requested through the
linker (-Wl,-mllvm,-pass-remarks=inline with lld). The cost is hugely
negative: inlining `scale` makes the caller SMALLER after
simplification, so it is a certain win. Cost/threshold is the inliner's
currency; -Rpass-missed=inline tells you when it refused and why.

tryIt.text:
1. Mark `scale` `__attribute__((noinline))` in 05_lib.cpp and rebuild
     the LTO binary: it returns to ~1.3 ns. Inlining, not linking, was it.
  2. Put `scale` into a shared library (-shared -fPIC) and call it through
     the PLT: measure; then compare with -fno-plt / -Bsymbolic.
  3. Run the PGO steps above and diff `-Rpass=inline` output with and
     without the profile: look for "hot callsite" in the remark text.
============================================================

sections.title: WHAT LTO COSTS AND WHEN IT MATTERS

blocks.text:
- Full LTO merges everything into one module: best optimization, slow
    serial link, lots of memory. ThinLTO summarizes per module, imports
    only what it needs, links in parallel: nearly the same result here
    (0.947 vs 0.968) at a fraction of the build cost. Default to ThinLTO.
  - It matters when hot paths cross TU boundaries through small functions:
    accessors, math helpers, comparators, allocators. It does nothing for
    a hot loop that is already in one TU, or for calls into a shared
    library (the boundary is the .so, not the TU: header-only or
    static-link the hot helpers instead).
  - The alternatives without LTO: put the small function in a header
    (`inline`), or make it a template. That is why performance libraries
    are header-heavy.

PGO IN ONE PARAGRAPH (try it):

blocks.output:
With a profile the inliner raises its threshold at HOT call sites and
  lowers it at cold ones, and lays out hot blocks together. On branchy
  code PGO is often the single largest win available; on this tiny loop it
  cannot beat LTO's inlining across the TU wall.

blocks.text:
I1. When a profile shows a small function called millions of times, the
    cost is the missed inlining. Check whether the call crosses a TU or
    a shared-library boundary before touching the function's body.
I2. Use -Rpass=inline / -Rpass-missed=inline (via the linker under LTO)
    to see decisions instead of guessing from the source.
I3. ThinLTO by default for release builds; header/template for the
    handful of helpers that must inline everywhere; PGO when branches
    and layout dominate.

labs.title: A data race that "works", one that doesn't, and what TSan sees
labs.teaches:
Two threads increment the same counter 2M times each. Four versions:
  collapsed  plain `counter++` in a loop, as written        -> passes! (why?)
  racy       the same, with a barrier so each ++ really executes
  atomic     std::atomic fetch_add(relaxed)
  mutex      std::mutex around the increment
plus the same binary under ThreadSanitizer. The lesson is not "races
give wrong answers"; it is that a race is undefined behaviour that may
give the RIGHT answer for reasons that will change with the next
compiler flag, and that a tool sees what tests cannot.

commands: for i in 1 2 3; do ./bin/01_race_tsan collapsed; done
blocks.output:
collapsed expected 4000000 got 4000000 OK  (0.3 ms, 0.1 ns/increment)
collapsed expected 4000000 got 4000000 OK  (0.3 ms, 0.1 ns/increment)
collapsed expected 4000000 got 4000000 OK  (0.3 ms, 0.1 ns/increment)

commands: for i in 1 2 3; do ./bin/01_race_tsan racy; done
blocks.output:
racy      expected 4000000 got 2043416 WRONG  (8.9 ms, 2.2 ns/increment)
racy      expected 4000000 got 2031633 WRONG  (4.1 ms, 1.0 ns/increment)
racy      expected 4000000 got 2097535 WRONG  (13.1 ms, 3.3 ns/increment)

atomic    expected 4000000 got 4000000 OK  (154.8 ms, 38.7 ns/increment)
mutex     expected 4000000 got 4000000 OK  (427.9 ms, 107.0 ns/increment)

0000000000400840 <_ZL14racy_collapsedv>:
  400840:  addq   $0x1e8480,0x283d(%rip)        # 403088 <_ZL13plain_counter>
  40084b:  ret

blocks.text:
The optimizer turned two million increments into ONE add of 2,000,000
(0x1e8480). Each thread performs a single read-modify-write; the window
for the two to interleave is a few nanoseconds, so they almost never
collide and the answer comes out right. It is still a data race, still
undefined behaviour, and -O0 or a slightly different loop body brings
the wrong answers back. Passing tests prove nothing about races.

steps.title: THE RACE THAT SHOWS: half the increments are lost (2.0M of 4.0M

blocks.text:
survive). Each thread does load-add-store; when both load the same
value, one store overwrites the other. Note it is not "slightly off":
about half is lost, because the two threads run in lockstep on the
same line. And it took 1-3 ns per increment, faster than the correct
versions: wrong answers are cheap.

blocks.output:
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=56417)
    Write of size 8 at 0x000001899760 by thread T2:
      #0 racy() .../concurrency/01_race_tsan.cpp:12:72
    Previous write of size 8 at 0x000001899760 by thread T1:
      #0 racy() .../concurrency/01_race_tsan.cpp:12:72
  SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race .../01_race_tsan.cpp:12:72 in racy()
  racy      expected 4000000 got 2089718 WRONG  (183.8 ms, 45.9 ns/increment)

WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=56425)
      #0 racy_collapsed() .../01_race_tsan.cpp:11:78

Read it: TSan reports the two conflicting accesses with their stacks,
  INCLUDING for the collapsed version whose output was correct. It does
  not need the race to misbehave: it tracks happens-before relations
  (via locks and atomics) and flags any pair of unordered conflicting
  accesses. Cost: ~5-15x slower, 5-10x memory; run your test suite under
  it regularly, not in production.

THE COSTS (this machine, two threads on two P-cores):
  atomic relaxed fetch_add   38.7 ns/increment   the line ping-pongs between cores (cache lab 04)
  std::mutex lock/unlock    107.0 ns/increment   two atomics plus, under contention, futex sleeps (lab 04 here)

blocks.text:
Both are "correct"; both are slow because they SHARE. The fast fix is
  per-thread counters combined at the end: no sharing on the hot path.

tryIt.text:
1. Build `collapsed` at -O0 and run it three times: wrong answers appear.
  2. Make the counter `volatile`: still a race (TSan still fires), still
     wrong. volatile is not a synchronization primitive.
  3. Give each thread its own counter (padded, cache lab 04) and sum at
     the end: correct, and ~1 ns per increment.
============================================================

blocks.text:
R1. Any two unsynchronized accesses to the same location, at least one
    a write, from two threads = data race = UB. Not "a stale read".
R2. Tests cannot find races; TSan can. Build with -fsanitize=thread in
    CI for every multi-threaded target.
R3. The correct fix is usually to not share (partition, message-pass),
    then atomics, then locks. Measure the contention (lab 04).

labs.title: SPSC ring buffer, three ways — memory orders, padding, cached indices
labs.teaches:
The single-producer single-consumer queue is the workhorse of low-latency
systems: one thread pushes, one pops, no locks, no CAS. Three versions
of the same queue move 50M items between two P-cores:
  naive    seq_cst everywhere, head and tail adjacent (same cache line)
  padded   acquire/release on the shared indices, each on its own line
  cached   padded + each side keeps a private copy of the other's index
and then the padded/cached queue on two SMT siblings of ONE core.
The TSan build proves the acquire/release version is race-free.

steps.title: RUN IT (three runs; producer CPU 2, consumer CPU 4)

blocks.output:
producer on CPU 2, consumer on CPU 4, 50000000 items, capacity 4096
naive            148.2 ns/item     6.7 M items/s
padded            17.7 ns/item    56.4 M items/s
cached            33.6 ns/item    29.8 M items/s
-- same physical core, two SMT threads (CPU 2 and 3): --
cached/SMT         2.6 ns/item   383.8 M items/s

padded            42.2 ns/item    23.7 M items/s
cached            30.2 ns/item    33.1 M items/s
cached/SMT         2.4 ns/item   413.1 M items/s

padded            22.8 ns/item    43.9 M items/s
cached            28.9 ns/item    34.6 M items/s
cached/SMT         2.4 ns/item   420.0 M items/s

tryIt.text:
1. Change QueuePadded's release/acquire to relaxed: TSan reports a race
     on buf[] (the slot write is no longer ordered before the index).
     Run it without TSan: it will probably still "work". That is R1 of lab 01.
  2. Make the item 64 bytes (a struct): the buffer traffic now dominates;
     compare padded vs cached again.
  3. Pin producer and consumer to an E-core pair (8 and 9): slower
     cores, and no SMT: the "same core" row disappears.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- naive: 148 ns/item. Every push does a seq_cst store (xchg: a full
    fence and a store-buffer drain) AND head/tail share one line, so every
    operation on either side pulls the line across cores (false sharing,
    cache lab 04). Both mistakes, 5-8x.
  - padded vs cached: 17.7 / 42.2 / 22.8 ns for padded across three runs,
    33.6 / 30.2 / 28.9 for cached. The honest reading: on this laptop they
    are within each other's run-to-run variance; the cached variant is
    more STABLE (its worst run is 34 ns; padded's is 42 ns), the padded
    variant has the best single run. The cached-index trick reduces
    reads of the other side's line from one-per-operation to one-per-
    batch; it pays most when the producer and consumer run at similar
    speed with the queue partly full, which is workload-dependent. Do not
    copy the "cached is 2x faster" claim from a blog; measure YOUR
    producer and consumer.
  - SMT siblings: 2.4-2.6 ns/item. The two threads share one L1, so the
    lines never leave the core: 10-15x faster than across cores. In real
    systems this is a design choice (co-locate the hottest pair on one
    core's siblings) with a cost (they share execution units).

THE ORDERS, AND WHY (see QueuePadded):
  producer: t = tail.load(relaxed)            // my own index: nobody else writes it
            if (t - head.load(acquire) == CAP) full   // acquire: see the consumer's slot reads as done
            buf[t & mask] = v
            tail.store(t + 1, release)         // release: the slot write happens-before any acquire of tail
  consumer: mirror image.
  The release/acquire pair on the index that PUBLISHES is the only
  synchronization needed; seq_cst adds a fence for nothing (x86: xchg vs
  mov; lab 03). relaxed on your own index is safe because it has a
  single writer. TSan agrees: 0 warnings.

both read the same tail and write the same
 slot. You need an atomic claim (fetch_add/CAS on tail) plus a per-slot
 sequence number so the consumer can tell "claimed" from "filled" (the
 bounded MPMC design), or one SPSC queue per producer. Nothing in this
 file is safe for that; its speed comes precisely from the 1:1 contract.

Q1. Never let the producer's and consumer's written variables share a
    line. alignas(64) on head and tail, and keep the buffer off those
    lines too.
Q2. release on the publishing store, acquire on the reading load, relaxed
    on your own index. seq_cst is a fence you did not need.
Q3. Measure with YOUR item size and speed ratio; the classic
    micro-optimizations (cached indices, batching) are workload-dependent.
Q4. Prove race-freedom with TSan, not by reasoning alone.

labs.title: What each memory_order compiles to on x86-64 and AArch64
labs.needs: clang -S for both targets (aarch64 via tools/a64.sh sysroot)
labs.teaches:
The C11/C++11 memory orders are abstract; the cost is concrete and
depends on the architecture's memory model. Thirteen tiny functions,
one operation each, compiled for x86-64 (TSO: strong), AArch64 v8.0
(weak, exclusives) and AArch64 v8.1+ (LSE atomics). No running needed:
this lab is entirely about reading the .s files build.sh emits.
labs.build:
(cd concurrency && ./build.sh)   -> bin/03_x86.s, bin/03_aarch64.s, bin/03_aarch64_lse.s

THE TABLE (one line per function, from the three .s files):

  function        x86-64 (TSO)                          AArch64 v8.0 (exclusives)                     AArch64 v8.1 LSE
  ------------    ----------------------------------    -------------------------------------------   ----------------------------
  load_relaxed    movl (%rdi),%eax                      ldr  w0,[x0]                                  (same)
  load_acquire    movl (%rdi),%eax                      ldar w0,[x0]                                  (same)
  load_seqcst     movl (%rdi),%eax                      ldar w0,[x0]                                  (same)
  store_relaxed   movl %esi,(%rdi)                      str  w1,[x0]                                  (same)
  store_release   movl %esi,(%rdi)                      stlr w1,[x0]                                  (same)
  store_seqcst    xchgl %esi,(%rdi)                     stlr w1,[x0]                                  (same)
  add_relaxed     lock xaddl %eax,(%rdi)                loop: ldxr; add; stxr; cbnz                   ldadd  w8,w0,[x0]
  add_acqrel      lock xaddl %eax,(%rdi)                loop: ldaxr; add; stlxr; cbnz                 ldaddal w8,w0,[x0]
  cas_seqcst      lock cmpxchgl %edx,(%rdi); sete       loop: ldaxr; cmp; b.ne; stlxr; cbnz; clrex    casal  w8,w2,[x0]; cmp; cset
  fence_release   (nothing)                             dmb ish                                       (same)
  fence_seqcst    lock orl $0,-64(%rsp)                 dmb ish                                       (same)
  plain_load      movl (%rdi),%eax                      ldr  w0,[x0]                                  (same)
  plain_store     movl %esi,(%rdi)                      str  w1,[x0]                                  (same)

HOW TO READ IT, x86:
  - relaxed, acquire, release and even seq_cst LOADS are plain movs: TSO
    already forbids the reorderings those orders forbid. The atomic
    versions differ from plain_load only in what the COMPILER may do
    (no tearing, no caching in registers, no reordering with other
    atomics); the hardware instruction is identical.
  - store_seqcst is xchg: an implicitly locked instruction, i.e. a full
    fence that drains the store buffer. It is the one order that costs on
    x86, ~20-40 cycles, and it is the default. (Lab 05 shows why it exists:
    without it, StoreLoad reordering is visible.)
  - RMWs are lock-prefixed regardless of order: on x86 every atomic RMW
    is already sequentially consistent. relaxed buys nothing on x86 for
    fetch_add; it buys a lot on AArch64.
  - fence_seqcst is `lock orl $0,(%rsp)`: a locked no-op used as a cheaper
    mfence. fence_release emits nothing: the compiler barrier is enough.

HOW TO READ IT, AArch64:
  - The memory model is weak: plain ldr/str may reorder with anything.
    acquire and release are separate INSTRUCTIONS: ldar (load-acquire),
    stlr (store-release). They cost real cycles and they are exactly what
    you asked for; relaxed gets the cheap ldr/str.
  - seq_cst maps to the SAME ldar/stlr as acquire/release: the pair is
    RCsc (sequentially consistent with each other) by design, so seq_cst
    is not more expensive than acq/rel on AArch64. The cost cliff is
    between relaxed and everything else, the opposite of x86.
  - v8.0 RMWs are load-exclusive / store-exclusive LOOPS (ldxr/stxr): the
    store fails and retries if another core touched the line in between.
    The a/l suffixes add acquire/release: ldaxr/stlxr. Under contention
    these loops livelock-ish and burn cycles.
  - v8.1 LSE replaces the loop with ONE instruction: ldadd / cas / swp,
    with al suffixes for acq_rel (ldaddal, casal). That is why every Arm
    server core since Neoverse N1 has LSE and why -moutline-atomics exists
    (aarch64 lab 03). The x86 lock-prefix and LSE are the same idea:
    the RMW is done by the cache system, not by a retry loop.
  - fences are dmb ish (data memory barrier, inner-shareable domain):
    both release and seq_cst fences are the same full barrier here; the
    compiler does not have a cheaper one-directional fence to reach for.

tryIt.text:
1. Add `exchange` and `fetch_or`: x86 xchg / lock cmpxchg loop (or is
     not a lock-able single instruction with a result), AArch64 swp / ldset.
  2. Compile for -march=armv8-a with -moutline-atomics: every RMW becomes
     `bl __aarch64_ldadd4_relax`: a runtime-dispatched helper (aarch64 lab 03).
  3. Compile for x86 with -mcx16 and use a 16-byte atomic: lock cmpxchg16b.
============================================================

blocks.text:
O1. On x86, relaxed vs acquire/release changes NOTHING in the
    instructions except for stores at seq_cst (xchg). Use acq/rel to
    document intent and to keep the code correct on Arm; do not expect a
    speedup on x86 from "relaxing" loads.
O2. On AArch64, relaxed is genuinely cheaper; acq/rel/seq_cst cost the
    same. Choose by correctness (lab 05 shows when seq_cst is required).
O3. Prefer RMW instructions over CAS loops (fetch_add over
    compare_exchange in a loop): on both architectures they are single
    instructions that cannot fail.
O4. When in doubt, compile with -S for both targets and READ. It takes
    ten seconds and settles most arguments.

labs.title: Mutex vs spinlock vs atomic — uncontended and contended, with the syscalls counted
labs.teaches:
What a lock costs when nobody else wants it, and what it costs when
two or four cores do. Three ways to protect a counter increment:
  std::mutex        glibc's futex-based mutex
  spinlock (TTAS)   test-and-test-and-set with `pause`, no kernel
  atomic add        no lock at all: the increment IS the atomic
10M critical sections split across 1, 2 or 4 threads on separate P-cores.

blocks.output:
lock                 1 thread    2 threads    4 threads   (ns per critical section, 10000000 total)
std::mutex               25.2         79.1        100.6
spinlock(TTAS)           13.5         43.7         79.8
atomic add               11.8         24.3         27.9

steps.title: COUNT THE SYSCALLS (mutex only, all three thread counts)

blocks.output:
std::mutex               29.0         66.6         74.9
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
100.00    1.593456          12    127650     35711 futex
127,650 futex calls for 30M critical sections in total (the 1-thread run
makes none): about 0.6% of the contended acquisitions went to the
kernel. The rest were resolved by glibc's short adaptive spin before
sleeping. 35,711 "errors" are EAGAIN: the waiter found the lock already
released when it tried to sleep. (strace itself slows syscalls ~100x,
lab systems/02, so the timings under strace are not comparable.)

tryIt.text:
1. Run the 4-thread mutex case with `taskset -c 2,3` (two SMT threads
     for four threads: oversubscribed): watch ns/section explode and
     futex calls climb.
  2. Remove `_mm_pause()` from Spin::lock: the spinning thread hammers
     the line and slows the HOLDER down; measure the 2-thread case.
  3. Make the critical section 1 us long (spin on rdtsc): now the mutex's
     sleeping waiters are the right choice and the spinlock burns cores.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- Uncontended std::mutex: 25 ns for lock+increment+unlock. That is two
  atomic RMWs (a CAS to lock, an exchange to unlock) on a line that
  stays in this core's L1, and NO syscall. "Mutexes are slow because
  they call the kernel" is false for the uncontended case.
- Uncontended spinlock: 13.5 ns: one exchange (acquire) and one plain
  store (release). About half the mutex; the mutex's extra cost is its
  second RMW and the bookkeeping for waiters.
- atomic add uncontended: 11.8 ns: a single lock xadd.
- Contended, 2 threads: everything jumps 2-3x because the LINE holding
  the lock (or the counter) now bounces between cores (cache lab 04);
  4 threads: 4-7x. The atomic add scales best because it holds the
  line for one instruction; the spinlock next; the mutex worst,
  because a waiter that spins for a while and then sleeps pays a futex
  syscall and a wake-up (microseconds) whenever it loses the spin.
- Note the mutex's 4-thread number (100 ns) is only 25% worse than its
  2-thread number: the queueing is dominated by the line transfer, and
  the adaptive spin keeps most acquisitions out of the kernel. The
  disaster case (thousands of ns) needs oversubscription: more runnable
  threads than cores, so a lock HOLDER gets preempted while holding.

std::mutex   default. Correct under oversubscription (sleeping waiters
             free the core), ~25 ns uncontended, adaptive spinning built in.
spinlock     only when: critical sections are tens of ns, threads are
             pinned to dedicated cores (never preempted while holding),
             and you have measured the mutex's spin-then-sleep as a
             problem. Always with `pause` and a test-before-test-and-set.
atomic       when the critical section IS one RMW. Otherwise consider
             not sharing at all: per-thread state combined later, or an
             SPSC queue (lab 02) to hand work to one owner.

K1. Uncontended locks are ~10-30 ns and syscall-free. Contention costs
    come from the cache line, then from sleeping. Measure with 1, 2, 4
    threads before believing any claim.
K2. Count futex calls with `strace -f -c -e trace=futex` to see how
    often you actually sleep. If it is often, the critical section is
    too long or the lock is too hot: shard it.
K3. Spinlocks require pinned, non-preempted threads; without that
    guarantee a preempted holder makes every waiter burn a core for a
    scheduler quantum.

labs.title: The store-buffer litmus test — see x86 reorder with your own eyes
labs.teaches:
The one reordering x86 permits, made visible, and the one memory order
that forbids it. Two threads:
    Thread 1: x = 1;  r1 = y;          Thread 2: y = 1;  r2 = x;
Under sequential consistency, at least one thread must see the other's
store: r1 == r2 == 0 is impossible. On real hardware each store sits in
its core's STORE BUFFER for a while, and the following load reads the
other variable from cache before that store is globally visible. Both
loads can return 0. This is the "StoreLoad" reordering that TSO allows,
and it is why memory_order_seq_cst exists. One million trials, three
memory orders.

steps.title: RUN IT (threads pinned to CPUs 2 and 4)

blocks.output:
relaxed                    r1==r2==0 in 87632 of 1000000 trials
acquire/release            r1==r2==0 in 246171 of 1000000 trials
seq_cst                    r1==r2==0 in 0 of 1000000 trials

7  xchgl %ecx, _ZL1x.0(%rip)      <- seq_cst stores: xchg = store + full fence
      7  xchgl %ecx, _ZL1y.0(%rip)

blocks.text:
The relaxed and acquire/release versions store with a plain `movl $1`
(lab 03: on x86 a release store IS a plain store); only seq_cst uses
xchg, which drains the store buffer before the next load can execute.

tryIt.text:
1. Pin both threads to SMT siblings (2 and 3): the rate drops (shared
     store buffer? no: shared L1 and different timing) but does not reach 0.
  2. Replace the seq_cst stores with relaxed stores plus
     atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst) between the store and the load: 0 again
     (`lock orl` from lab 03).
  3. Cross-compile the litmus for aarch64 (tools/a64.sh) and run it under
     qemu: user-mode qemu executes the threads with a single-core model,
     so you will NOT see reordering there. That is a lesson about emulators,
     not about Arm.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- relaxed: 8.8% of trials saw both zeros. acquire/release: 24.6%. Both
    are "impossible" under SC and both happen constantly, because on x86
    relaxed and acq/rel compile to the same plain mov: neither prevents a
    store from being buffered past a later load. (The different rates are
    timing artifacts of the two runs; the point is both are far from 0.)
  - seq_cst: 0 in a million. The xchg makes the store globally visible
    before the load issues, so at least one thread must observe the
    other's store. This is the Dekker / Peterson pattern: two flags, each
    thread sets its own then checks the other's. Mutual exclusion built
    on that pattern REQUIRES seq_cst (or an explicit full fence between
    the store and the load); acquire/release is not enough, no matter how
    it reads.
  - Everything else you write (producer/consumer, publish-then-flag,
    reference counts, queues) needs only acquire/release, because those
    patterns order a store BEFORE a load in the OTHER thread through the
    same variable, which is what acq/rel promises. The store-buffer
    pattern needs a store in each thread to be ordered before a load of a
    DIFFERENT variable in the same thread: only a full fence does that.

THE RULE OF THUMB YOU CAN DEFEND IN AN INTERVIEW:
  "Does my correctness depend on two threads agreeing on the order of
  stores to two DIFFERENT variables?" If yes: seq_cst (or a seq_cst
  fence between the store and the load). If no: acquire on the load that
  consumes, release on the store that publishes. And on AArch64 the
  answer is the same and the instructions are the same (ldar/stlr are
  RCsc), so this test gives 0 there for acq/rel too; the relaxed row
  would still show reordering, and more of it.

S1. x86 reorders exactly one thing: a store followed by a load of a
    different address. Everything you cannot see on x86 you WILL see on
    Arm; everything you can see on x86 you can see everywhere.
S2. seq_cst on x86 costs an xchg per store (~20-40 cycles); use it where
    S1 matters, acq/rel elsewhere.
S3. Write litmus tests for your own lock-free code: a million trials
    across two pinned cores finds in seconds what code review misses.

labs.evidence: relaxed 8.8%, acq/rel 24.6%, seq_cst 0% of 1M trials show r1==r2==0; seq_cst stores are xchg

labs.title: malloc is not slow, it is UNPREDICTABLE
labs.teaches:
The argument against allocation on a latency-critical path is not the
median cost of malloc (tens of ns) but its tail and its dependence on
allocator state you do not control: size classes, the mmap threshold,
trimming, first-touch page faults. Each iteration allocates, touches
one byte, frees, and is timed individually (serialized TSC), 200k times:
  32 B                 tcache fast path
  4 KiB                above tcache, small-bin path
  1 MiB (default)      what glibc does out of the box
  1 MiB (forced mmap)  the threshold pinned so every block is mmap/munmap
  1 MiB (heap)         threshold raised and trimming disabled
  pool 64 B            a free list over pre-faulted memory (what you ship)

blocks.output:
label                       min      p50      p90      p99    p99.9      max       mean   (ns per alloc+touch+free)
malloc 32 B                  28       36       43       49       51    13215       36.7
malloc 4 KiB                 43       52       56       60       64     8088       52.2
malloc 1 MiB (default)       38       41       42       43       44     5458       41.0
malloc 1 MiB (forced mmap)     4068     4184     4413    10345    14810   205867     4578.7
malloc 1 MiB (heap, no trim)       38       41       42       44       48     7255       41.2
pool 64 B                    14       16       18       18       18     3971       16.4

59.59    1.420996           7    200003           munmap
 40.38    0.962921           4    200010           mmap
Two syscalls per allocation, plus a page fault on the touch (fresh
mmap memory is unmapped until first write) and the kernel zeroing the
page. p50 4.2 us, p99 10 us, max 206 us: that is the "malloc is slow"
people remember, and it is the mmap path, not malloc.

tryIt.text:
1. Run `small` under `ltrace -c -e malloc+free`: ltrace adds ~100 us per
     call (it stops the process at each PLT entry). Tools change what
     they measure; use ltrace for counts, never for timing.
  2. Allocate from two threads at once (each its own sizes): the first
     contended malloc creates a second arena (mmap of 64 MB): find it in
     the histogram.
  3. Add `mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE)` at startup and rerun
     `large-mmap`: faults disappear, mmap/munmap remain.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- 32 B: p50 36 ns, p99.9 51 ns, but max 13 us. The median is a tcache
    hit (a per-thread free list: pop, push). The max is one iteration
    that hit something else: a page fault, a timer interrupt, a
    migration. Even the fast path has a tail you cannot budget for.
  - 4 KiB: 52 ns. Above the tcache limit (1032 bytes by default), so the
    request goes through the arena's bins with a lock (uncontended here).
  - 1 MiB (default): 41 ns and a 5 us max. Surprise: glibc's mmap
    threshold is DYNAMIC. The first 1 MiB block is mmapped (that is the
    max), and when it is freed glibc raises the threshold so later blocks
    of that size come from the heap. Your program's allocation history
    changes the cost of the next allocation. Nothing about that is under
    your control unless you pin it with mallopt.
  - forced mmap: mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, 512 KiB) disables the dynamic
    behaviour: every 1 MiB block is mmap + fault + munmap: 100x slower.
  - heap, no trim: raising M_MMAP_THRESHOLD and M_TRIM_THRESHOLD keeps the
    blocks on the heap and stops free() from returning memory to the OS
    (a madvise/brk you would otherwise pay later). 41 ns, tight tail.
  - pool: 16 ns, p99.9 18 ns, and even its max (4 us) is an interrupt,
    not the allocator. Pre-allocated, pre-faulted, one pointer swap each
    way. This is the shape of every allocator in a trading system.

WHAT MAKES ALLOCATION UNPREDICTABLE (the list to recite):
  size-class boundaries (tcache 1032 B, mmap threshold 128 KiB default and
  dynamic up to 32 MiB), first-touch page faults, arena locks between
  threads, trimming (free returning memory via brk/madvise), fragmentation
  over a long run, and the allocator's own metadata cache misses.

H1. No malloc/free on the hot path. Pools, arenas, free lists, ring
    buffers, sized at startup, pre-faulted (MAP_POPULATE / touch) and
    mlocked.
H2. If you must use malloc, pin its behaviour: mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD),
    mallopt(M_TRIM_THRESHOLD, huge), mallopt(M_TOP_PAD), and verify with
    strace -c that steady state makes no mmap/munmap/brk calls.
H3. Measure allocation cost as a DISTRIBUTION per size class in your
    process, after warm-up; the median tells you almost nothing.

labs.evidence: 36 / 52 / 41 ns medians; forced mmap 4.2 us p50 (200k mmap+munmap); pool 16 ns

labs.title: What a system call costs, and what only looks like one
labs.teaches:
"Avoid syscalls on the hot path" needs a number. Seven calls, one
million times each: a vDSO call that never enters the kernel, the
cheapest possible real syscall, reads and writes of one byte through
the VFS, a scheduler entry, and a path lookup. Then the same program
under strace, to see that the tool that counts syscalls makes each one
~100x slower.

blocks.output:
clock_gettime(MONOTONIC)         37.9 ns   vDSO: no kernel entry
getpid()                        142.5 ns   the cheapest real syscall: pure user<->kernel transition
syscall(SYS_getpid)             142.3 ns   same, via the generic wrapper
read(/dev/zero, 1 byte)         217.7 ns   transition + VFS + copy_to_user
write(/dev/null, 1 byte)        184.5 ns   transition + VFS
sched_yield()                   333.5 ns   transition + scheduler (nothing else runnable)
open+close(/dev/null)          1667.0 ns   path lookup + fd table: two syscalls

clock_gettime(MONOTONIC)         29.6 ns   vDSO: no kernel entry              <- unchanged: not a syscall
getpid()                      23629.7 ns   ...                                <- 166x slower
sched_yield()                 29032.6 ns
open+close(/dev/null)         62196.2 ns
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
 33.12    6.532653           3   2000000           getpid
 23.76    4.686517           4   1000000           sched_yield
 21.80    4.299017           4   1000001           write

tryIt.text:
1. `perf stat -e syscalls:sys_enter_getpid ./bin/02_syscall_cost` (needs
     tracepoint access; may require root here): the low-overhead way.
  2. Boot parameter `mitigations=off` (root, a VM is a good place) and
     rerun: getpid drops; that difference is the security tax.
  3. Replace getpid with `gettid` via syscall(): same cost. Replace with
     `getcpu()`: vDSO on x86-64: ~vDSO speed.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- clock_gettime is ~38 ns and strace does not see it: the vDSO maps a
  page of kernel code and data into every process, and the time is read
  from that page (TSC + a scale factor) with no mode switch. Use it
  freely for microsecond timing; use rdtsc for nanosecond timing
  (perf lab 04: 12 ns).
- getpid is the floor: ~140 ns for the transition into the kernel and
  back on this CPU with its mitigations (Spectre/Meltdown-era entry code
  added a lot to this number across the industry; it used to be ~50 ns).
  Anything a syscall does is on top of this.
- read/write of one byte: +40-75 ns for the VFS layer and the copy.
  Real reads of real data are dominated by the data, not by this.
- sched_yield: 330 ns to enter the scheduler and find nothing to switch
  to. A REAL context switch (another thread runs, caches cool, TLB
  partially flushed) is 1-5 us of direct cost and more of indirect.
- open+close: 1.7 us. Path lookup (dcache), permission checks, fd table.
  Anything with a path is expensive; keep files open.
- Under strace every syscall becomes a ptrace stop: two context switches
  to the tracer and back. strace -c is for COUNTING what you call, never
  for timing it. (Same for ltrace, lab 01.) For low-overhead syscall
  accounting use `perf trace` or bpftrace (root), or just count with
  strace and measure without it.

sections.title: WHY THIS MATTERS ON A LATENCY-CRITICAL PATH

blocks.text:
140 ns is not the problem; a syscall's VARIANCE is. Entering the kernel
means the scheduler may run, an interrupt may be serviced, a lock may
be taken. That is why the hot path does no syscalls at all: no
logging (write), no clock_gettime when rdtsc will do, no
epoll_wait (busy-poll instead, lab 03), no malloc (mmap, lab 01), no
locking that can sleep (futex, concurrency lab 04).

Y1. Know the floor on your machine (getpid). Everything else is floor + work.
Y2. vDSO calls (clock_gettime, gettimeofday, getcpu) are not syscalls;
    real syscalls in a hot loop show up in `strace -c` counts and in
    `perf stat -e context-switches` when they sleep.
Y3. Count syscalls with strace; time them without it.

labs.title: UDP round trip on loopback — blocking vs epoll vs busy-poll
labs.teaches:
The cost of WAITING. A client and a server exchange 50k UDP datagrams
over loopback, the client timing each round trip. Both sides wait for
data the same way:
  block   recvfrom() blocks; the kernel puts the thread to sleep and wakes it
  epoll   epoll_wait() then recvfrom(): the event-loop pattern
  spin    recvfrom(MSG_DONTWAIT) in a loop: the thread never sleeps
The network stack cost is identical in all three; the difference is
entirely what happens between "packet arrived" and "thread runs".
labs.build:
(cd systems && ./build.sh)   -> bin/03_udp_pingpong [block|epoll|spin]
Client pins to CPU 2, server to CPU 4 (two P-cores). Ports 40001/40002.

commands: for m in block epoll spin; do ./bin/03_udp_pingpong $m | tail -1; done

tryIt.text:
1. Run `spin` with both threads on SMT siblings (change the pins to 2
     and 3): the two spinners fight for one core's resources.
  2. Add `SO_BUSY_POLL` (setsockopt; may need CAP_NET_ADMIN for large
     values) to the `block` mode: the kernel spins on your behalf for N us
     before sleeping: a middle ground.
  3. Increase the datagram to 1400 bytes: the stack cost grows slowly
     (copies); the wake-up cost does not change.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- spin: 8.7 us per round trip = two one-way trips through the loopback
  stack at ~4.3 us each (sendto: socket -> IP -> loopback device ->
  softirq -> socket queue; then the receiver's recvfrom copies it out).
  That is the kernel network stack's cost on this box, with nobody
  sleeping. p99.9 17.7 us, max 42 us.
- block: 18.5 us p50, 2.1x. The extra ~10 us is two WAKE-UPS per round
  trip: the packet arrives, the kernel marks the sleeping receiver
  runnable, sends an IPI to its (idle) core, the core leaves its idle
  state, the scheduler switches in the thread, and it returns from
  recvfrom. Each is ~5 us here, and worse: the tail is 5x longer
  (p99.9 77 us, max 687 us) because a wake-up can hit a core that is in a
  deep sleep state, a timer tick, or a scheduler decision.
- epoll: the same wake-up plus the epoll_wait bookkeeping: 19.9 us. The
  event loop is not free, but its tail was better than plain blocking
  in this run (max 485 vs 687 us); those maxima are single events and
  vary from run to run. The medians are the stable story.

sections.title: WHAT A TRADING SYSTEM DOES WITH THIS

blocks.text:
It spins. On an isolated core, a thread polling the socket (or, with
kernel bypass, the NIC's receive ring directly) sees a packet in ~1-2 us
of its arrival with a tight tail; a blocking thread sees it in 5-10 us
with a fat tail. The price is one core at 100% and the requirement that
the core really is dedicated (a spinning thread that gets preempted is
worse than a sleeping one). Control-plane threads (logging, config,
monitoring) keep sleeping on epoll; only the hot path spins.

N1. Waiting costs more than working at this scale: a wake-up is ~5 us
    with a tail to hundreds of us; the whole UDP stack traversal is ~4 us.
N2. Spin only on a dedicated, pinned core; measure the tail, not the mean.
N3. Loopback numbers are an UPPER bound on what the stack costs and a
    LOWER bound on what a real NIC costs (no wire, no DMA, no interrupt
    coalescing). Use them to compare wait strategies, not to predict
    production latency.

labs.title: Nagle + delayed ACK — the 40 ms stall, and TCP_NODELAY
labs.teaches:
The most expensive default in TCP for request/response traffic. A
client sends each 16-byte request as TWO writes (a 4-byte header, then
a 12-byte body) and waits for the 16-byte reply. Nagle's algorithm
holds the second small write until the first is acknowledged; the
server's delayed-ACK timer holds that acknowledgment for up to 40 ms
because it hopes to piggyback it on data that never comes (the server
is waiting for the body). Result: every request takes ~40 ms on a link
whose real latency is ~40 us. One setsockopt fixes it.

blocks.output:
label                       min      p50      p90      p99    p99.9      max       mean   (request ns)
default (Nagle)          326199 41089598 42030664 43227964 44547930 44547930 41187428.2
requests slower than 1 ms: 499 of 500

TCP_NODELAY               33648    41461    65339   189330   947555   947555    50857.6
requests slower than 1 ms: 0 of 500

tryIt.text:
1. Combine the header and body into one write and rerun without
     TCP_NODELAY: fast again. The pattern, not the flag, is the bug.
  2. Set TCP_QUICKACK on the SERVER socket before each read instead of
     TCP_NODELAY on the client: also fast (the ACK is not delayed). Which
     side owns the fix in a real system?
  3. `tcpdump -i lo -ttt port 40003` while running the default mode: read
     the ~40 ms gaps.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- Default: p50 = 41.1 ms. Not 41 us: 41 MILLISECONDS, a thousand times
    the loopback round trip, on 499 of 500 requests. The first request
    (min 326 us) escaped because there was no unacknowledged data yet.
  - The mechanism, step by step: write(hdr) goes out immediately (nothing
    in flight). write(body): Nagle sees unacknowledged data (the header)
    and a segment smaller than the MSS, so it QUEUES the body until the
    header's ACK arrives. The server has the header but needs 16 bytes,
    so it keeps reading; its delayed-ACK logic waits (up to 40 ms on
    Linux) to send the ACK with the reply. Deadlock until the timer
    fires. Two sensible optimizations, each fine alone, deadly together.
  - TCP_NODELAY: p50 41 us, p99 189 us, worst 948 us: the body goes out at
    once and the exchange completes at loopback speed.

THE ALTERNATIVES (know all three):
  1. TCP_NODELAY on the socket: send every write immediately. The
     standard choice for request/response and for anything latency-
     sensitive; every exchange gateway client sets it.
  2. Do not write-write-read: build the message in one buffer and write
     once (or writev / sendmsg). Then Nagle has nothing to hold. Good
     practice regardless: fewer syscalls (lab 02), one segment.
  3. TCP_CORK: the opposite tool: hold partial writes on purpose until
     you uncork, for bulk senders that want full segments.

sections.title: WHY THIS IS AN INTERVIEW FAVOURITE

blocks.text:
It tests whether you know what the kernel does between write() and the
wire, whether you can explain an interaction of two features, and
whether you measured (a 1000x regression that shows up only under a
specific write pattern is the kind of thing a profile does not explain:
the CPU is idle the whole time).

G1. Latency-sensitive TCP: TCP_NODELAY, always, and one write per message.
G2. When a request/response path is slow and the CPU is idle, suspect
    timers: Nagle/delayed ACK (40 ms), retransmit (200 ms+), Nagle on
    the peer.
G3. Watch it happen: `ss -ti` shows per-connection state; `tcpdump -i lo
    port 40003` shows the 40 ms gap between the header and the body.

labs.title: Kernel receive timestamps — how long a packet waits for you
labs.teaches:
You cannot fix latency you cannot locate. Linux will stamp every
received packet with the time the kernel took it from the driver
(SO_TIMESTAMPNS, delivered as ancillary data with recvmsg). With a
send-time timestamp inside the payload, one receive gives you two
numbers per packet:
  send -> kernel rx stamp   the sender's stack + loopback delivery
  kernel stamp -> user      how long the packet sat in the socket queue
                            before your code got it: the WAIT
A sender thread emits 20k packets 50 us apart; the receiver is either
blocking in recvmsg or busy-polling.

(cd systems && ./build.sh)   -> bin/05_timestamps [spin]
Receiver pins to CPU 2, sender to CPU 4. Port 40004.

send -> kernel rx stamp     2261     5228     6949     8762    27931    59774     5244.2
kernel stamp -> user       4871    16971    98493  1206926  2763328  3334524    61065.3

receiver: busy-poll (MSG_DONTWAIT loop)   (20000 packets, 50 us apart)
send -> kernel rx stamp     1889     1989     2415     5874    14225    63690     2180.8
kernel stamp -> user       2312     2762     3340     7282    12925    48161     2960.4

1. Change the sender's spacing to 5 us and to 500 us: the blocking
     receiver's wait gets worse at LOWER rates (it sleeps more deeply).
  2. Use SO_TIMESTAMPING with SOF_TIMESTAMPING_TX_SOFTWARE on the sender
     to get a transmit stamp too, and split send -> stamp into "sendto
     call -> driver" and "driver -> receive".
  3. Run the spinning receiver with an unpinned, busy machine (compile
     something in another terminal): watch p99 climb; then pin to an
     otherwise idle core.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- The wait, blocking: p50 17 us, p90 98 us, p99 1.2 ms, max 3.3 ms.
  With a packet every 50 us the receiver keeps falling asleep and being
  woken; a wake-up that lands badly (idle state exit, a scheduler tick,
  the sender thread's own usleep timer sharing the timer wheel) leaves
  packets queued for hundreds of microseconds. Nothing in the network
  stack was slow; the packet was READY and nobody was there to take it.
  A profile of this program would show the receiver idle.
- The wait, spinning: p50 2.8 us, p99 7.3 us, max 48 us. That is the
  floor for "kernel queued it -> recvmsg returned" with the copy and the
  ancillary data. 6x better median, 165x better p99.
- send -> stamp also improved (5.2 -> 2.0 us). On loopback the sender's
  CPU runs the receive-side processing in the same softirq, and with a
  sleeping receiver that path includes the work of waking it; an idle
  receiving core also responds more slowly to everything. Verify with
  `perf sched` / ftrace sched_wakeup events (root) if you need the
  breakdown; the point here is that the stamp separates "stack" from
  "wait" without guessing.

sections.title: WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT TOOL

blocks.text:
Application-level timing (before and after recv) cannot distinguish a
slow network from a slow receiver. Kernel timestamps can, at a few
hundred ns of cost per packet. NIC hardware timestamps
(SO_TIMESTAMPING with SOF_TIMESTAMPING_RX_HARDWARE, PTP-synchronized)
extend the same idea to the wire: then you know arrival-on-wire ->
driver -> stack -> socket -> user, per packet, in production, all the
time. Every serious feed handler records these and alerts on the
percentiles.

P1. Instrument the path, do not infer it: kernel (and NIC) receive
    stamps plus a timestamp in the payload give per-stage latency for
    free.
P2. On a latency-critical receiver, the dominant cost is the wait, and
    the fix is not to wait (spin on a dedicated core), lab 03.
P3. Report the wait as p50/p99/max over a long run under realistic
    packet rates; a mean of 61 us here hides a 3.3 ms worst case.

labs.title: The same C, read on x86-64 and AArch64
labs.needs: tools/a64.sh (clang cross target + sysroot), asm only
labs.teaches:
Reading AArch64 assembly when you grew up on x86: seven small functions
compiled for both targets (and for armv9-a, which changes nothing
here). What to look for: the calling convention (x0-x7, two-register
returns), the frame (stp/ldp of x29/x30), predication with csel/cset,
immediates that need several instructions, scaled addressing, and the
NEON registers showing up in a plain integer loop.
labs.build:
(cd aarch64 && ./build.sh)   -> bin/01_x86.s, bin/01_a64.s, bin/01_a64_v9.s

SIDE BY SIDE (from the .s files; noise stripped):

  clamp(x, lo, hi) = x<lo ? lo : x>hi ? hi : x
    x86:   movl %edx,%eax ; cmpl %edx,%edi ; cmovll %edi,%eax ; cmpl %esi,%edi ; cmovll %esi,%eax ; retq
    a64:   cmp w0, w2 ; csel w8, w0, w2, lt ; cmp w0, w1 ; csel w0, w1, w8, lt ; ret
    Same shape. csel is AArch64's cmov: `csel dst, a, b, cond` = cond ? a : b.
    The `w` registers are the 32-bit views of the 64-bit `x` registers.

  big_const() = 0x1234567890ABCDEF
    x86:   movabsq $1311768467294899695, %rax ; retq          (one 10-byte instruction)
    a64:   mov  x0, #52719                      // 0xcdef
           movk x0, #37035, lsl #16            // 0x90ab
           movk x0, #22136, lsl #32            // 0x5678
           movk x0, #4660,  lsl #48            // 0x1234
    Fixed 32-bit instructions cannot carry a 64-bit immediate: four
    16-bit chunks (mov + movk). Constants live in code, or in a literal
    pool loaded with adrp+ldr. This is why "just use a magic constant"
    costs more on Arm, and why the compiler prefers bitmask immediates.

  call_leaf(f, x) = f(x) + 1
    x86:   pushq %rax ; movq %rdi,%rax ; movq %rsi,%rdi ; callq *%rax ; incq %rax ; popq %rcx ; retq
    a64:   stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!        // save frame pointer AND link register
           mov x8, x0 ; mov x0, x1 ; mov x29, sp
           blr x8                            // branch-with-link to register
           add x0, x0, #1
           ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16 ; ret
    AArch64 has no push/pop and no return address on the stack: `bl`
    puts the return address in x30 (lr). A function that calls another
    must save x30 itself (stp with pre-index), and `ret` is `br x30`.
    Leaf functions never touch the stack for this: that is why `clamp`
    has no prologue at all.

  swap_pair({lo, hi}) -> {hi, lo}
    x86:   movq %rsi,%rax ; movq %rdi,%rdx ; retq
    a64:   mov x8, x0 ; mov x0, x1 ; mov x1, x8 ; ret
    A 16-byte struct is passed and returned in TWO registers on both
    ABIs (rdi:rsi / rax:rdx vs x0:x1 / x0:x1). Larger structs go through
    memory (x8 holds the return address of a large struct on AArch64).

  spill_many(out, a..i): 9 integer args
    a64:   add x8, x2, x1 ; ldr x9, [sp] ; add x10, x4, x3 ; stp x8, x10, [x0] ; ldr x10, [sp, #8] ...
    Eight argument registers (x0-x7); the 9th and 10th come from the
    caller's stack ([sp], [sp, #8]). x86-64 SysV has six (rdi rsi rdx
    rcx r8 r9), so its spills start at the 7th. Note `stp x8, x10,
    [x0]`: two 64-bit stores in one instruction (store pair).

  sum_scaled(a, n, k): sum of a[i]*k over ints
    a64 inner loop:
           ldp  q5, q6, [x8, #-16]           // two 128-bit NEON loads (8 ints)
           subs x10, x10, #8                 // subtract and set flags
           add  x8, x8, #32
           b.ne .LBB0_5
           ... add v0.2d, v2.2d, v0.2d ; addp d0, v0.2d    // horizontal reduce
    The compiler vectorized with NEON (q/v registers, `.2d` = two 64-bit
    lanes). `subs` + `b.ne` is the loop test: flags are set by the `s`
    suffix, not by a separate cmp. `cbz`/`cbnz` (compare-and-branch on
    zero) handle the n == 0 guard without touching flags at all.

THE ONE-PAGE DECODER RING (x86-64 -> AArch64):
  rax..r15 (16 GPRs)          x0..x30 (31 GPRs) + sp; w-regs = low 32 bits; xzr/wzr = zero register
  rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9 args  x0..x7 args (also x0..x7 returns); x8 = indirect result; x16/x17 scratch (ip0/ip1); x18 platform; x29 fp; x30 lr
  push/pop/call/ret           stp/ldp with pre/post-index; bl/blr set x30; ret = br x30
  cmov                        csel / csinc / csinv / cset / cinc
  test/cmp + jcc              cmp / tst + b.cond; cbz/cbnz and tbz/tbnz branch without flags
  lea                         add with shifted register; `ldr w0, [x1, x2, lsl #2]` scales in the address
  movabs                      mov + movk x3, or adrp + ldr (literal pool)
  xmm/ymm                     v0..v31 (NEON, 128-bit: .16b .8h .4s .2d); z0..z31 + p0..p15 with SVE (lab 02)
  lock xadd / xchg / cmpxchg  ldxr/stxr loops, or ldadd / swp / cas with LSE (lab 03)
  mfence                      dmb ish; acquire/release live IN the load/store (ldar/stlr)

labs.title: NEON vs SVE codegen, and vector-length-agnostic execution under emulation
labs.teaches:
Three loops (vector add, integer sum, float max) compiled twice: for
armv8-a (NEON: fixed 128-bit vectors) and for armv8-a+sve (SVE: the
vector length is decided by the hardware). The SVE binary is ONE
binary that runs correctly at every vector length from 128 to 2048
bits, which qemu lets you prove by changing the length from the
command line. n = 1003 elements on purpose: not a multiple of any
vector length, so the remainder handling is exercised every time.

blocks.output:
vadd  : vectorized loop (vectorization width: vscale x 4, interleaved count: 2)
isum  : vectorized loop (vectorization width: vscale x 2, interleaved count: 2)
fmax_ : vectorized loop (vectorization width: vscale x 4, interleaved count: 1)
main  : vectorized loop (vectorization width: 4, ...)   (the fill loop, fixed width)
`vscale x 4` is LLVM's notation for "4 lanes per 128 bits, times the
runtime multiple vscale = VL/128". The IR type is <vscale x 4 x float>.

blocks.text:
NEON (bin/02_neon.s, vadd): fixed 128-bit q registers, a scalar tail
loop for the remainder:
       ...ldp q0, q1 ... fadd v0.4s ... stp ...           (vector body, 8 floats per step)
.LBB0_4:  fadd s0, s0, s1 ; subs x8, x8, #1 ; b.ne .LBB0_4   (scalar remainder: up to 7 elements)
SVE (bin/02_sve.s, vadd, default epilogue): the main loop uses z
registers with an unpredicated ptrue body and an epilogue.
SVE with tail folding (bin/02_sve_tail, -mllvm -prefer-predicate-over-epilogue=predicate-dont-vectorize):
       whilelo p0.s, xzr, x3                   // p0[lane] = (lane < n)
.LBB0_4:
       ld1w { z0.s }, p0/z, [x1, x10, lsl #2]  // load active lanes, zero the rest
       ld1w { z1.s }, p0/z, [x2, x10, lsl #2]
       fadd z0.s, z0.s, z1.s
       st1w { z0.s }, p0, [x0, x10, lsl #2]    // store active lanes only
       whilelo p0.s, x10, x9                   // recompute the predicate for the next block
No remainder loop at all: the final iteration simply has a partially
true predicate. And no vector length appears anywhere in the code.

labs.title: Atomics on AArch64 — exclusives vs LSE vs outline atomics, run on two emulated CPUs
labs.needs: tools/a64.sh (needs the compiler-rt builtins it installs)
labs.teaches:
The same C11 atomics built three ways, run on a CPU with LSE and on one
without:
  excl     -march=armv8-a -mno-outline-atomics   load/store-exclusive loops; runs anywhere
  lse      -march=armv8.1-a                       single-instruction atomics; SIGILL on old cores
  outline  -march=armv8-a -moutline-atomics       calls a helper that picks at runtime
plus the link error you hit when the helpers' library is missing, which
is the most common "why doesn't my aarch64 build link" question.

steps.title: WHAT THE THREE BUILDS EMIT for atomic_fetch_add(relaxed) / compare_exchange

blocks.text:
excl:    .LBB0_1: ldxr x10, [x21] ; add x10, x10, #1 ; stxr w11, x10, [x21] ; cbnz w11, .LBB0_1
lse:     ldadd x9, x10, [x21]                      casal x19, x8, [x21]
outline: bl __aarch64_ldadd8_relax                 bl __aarch64_cas8_acq_rel
Read it: the v8.0 loop retries until the exclusive store succeeds (w11
== 0). LSE does it in one instruction that the cache system performs
atomically (like x86's lock prefix). Outline atomics call a small
function (in compiler-rt or libgcc) that checks HWCAP once at startup
and then runs the LSE or the exclusive version: portable binaries that
still get LSE where it exists, at the cost of a call. This is the
default for aarch64 Linux in GCC and clang, which is why the helpers
must be linkable.

steps.title: THE LINK ERROR EVERYONE MEETS (before tools/a64-setup.sh installed compiler-rt)

blocks.output:
ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: __aarch64_ldadd8_relax
ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: __aarch64_cas8_acq_rel
The helpers live in libgcc.a (GCC) or libclang_rt.builtins-aarch64.a
(clang). A cross setup without one of them cannot link default aarch64
builds; the fixes are to provide the library (tools/a64-setup.sh fetches
compiler-rt's, root-free), or to build with -mno-outline-atomics, or
to target -march=armv8.1-a+ where LSE is inline anyway.

steps.title: RUN ON A CPU WITH LSE (-cpu max) AND ONE WITHOUT (cortex-a57)

commands: for b in 03_excl 03_lse 03_outline; do a64run -cpu max ./bin/$b; done
blocks.output: HWCAP atomics(LSE)=1 | counter=1000000 | CAS(expect 0) -> failed, observed 1000000    (x3, identical)

commands: for b in 03_excl 03_lse 03_outline; do a64run -cpu cortex-a57 ./bin/$b; done
blocks.output:
03_excl     HWCAP atomics(LSE)=0 | counter=1000000 | CAS(expect 0) -> failed, observed 1000000
03_lse      qemu: uncaught target signal 4 (Illegal instruction) - core dumped
03_outline  HWCAP atomics(LSE)=0 | counter=1000000 | CAS(expect 0) -> failed, observed 1000000

blocks.text:
Read it: the LSE binary dies on a Cortex-A57 (v8.0): `ldadd` does not
exist there. The outline build runs on both and picks LSE on `max`
(HWCAP_ATOMICS set). The exclusive build runs on both, always slow-path.

tryIt.text:
1. `objdump -d bin/03_outline | grep -A12 '<__aarch64_ldadd8_relax>'`:
     read the helper: it tests a global set from HWCAP and branches to
     the ldadd or the ldxr/stxr path.
  2. Add memory_order_seq_cst variants and compare `ldaddal` vs `ldadd`,
     `ldaxr/stlxr` vs `ldxr/stxr` (concurrency lab 03 table).
  3. Run with `-cpu neoverse-n1` and `-cpu cortex-a76` in qemu: both have
     LSE; check HWCAP in the output.
============================================================

blocks.text:
- You control the hardware (a trading box, a phone SoC you target):
  -march for that core (armv8.2-a+... or -mcpu=neoverse-v2), inline
  LSE, no helper calls.
- You ship one binary to unknown Arm servers: outline atomics (the
  default) or a runtime-dispatched build (lab 04). The call costs a few
  cycles per atomic; in a hot spin loop that matters, so hot paths often
  use -march=armv8.1-a with a HWCAP check at startup that refuses to run
  on older cores.
- Never -mno-outline-atomics with armv8.0 on a server: you throw away LSE
  and get retry loops under contention.

X1. Know which of the three shapes your build emits: `grep -E 'ldxr|ldadd|__aarch64_' out.s`.
X2. On a link error for __aarch64_* symbols, the runtime library is
    missing, not your code.
X3. Test with qemu `-cpu cortex-a57` (v8.0) AND `-cpu max` (everything):
    SIGILL on the first is a feature-dispatch bug that would ship.
