labs.title: Runtime dispatch on CPU features — HWCAP, ifunc, and validating the choice
labs.needs: tools/a64.sh, qemu with -cpu max and -cpu cortex-a57
labs.teaches:
One binary, two implementations of the same kernel (a NEON dot product
and an SVE one), and the two standard ways to pick at run time:
  A. a GNU ifunc: the dynamic loader calls your resolver once, at load
     time, and binds the symbol to the implementation it returns. On
     AArch64 the resolver receives the HWCAP bits as its argument.
  B. a function pointer set at startup from getauxval(AT_HWCAP).
The SVE implementation is compiled with __attribute__((target("sve")))
inside an armv8-a translation unit, so the SVE instructions are present
in the binary but only executed when chosen. Then the part people skip:
the program checks that all three paths agree with a scalar reference.

steps.title: RUN ON A CPU WITH SVE, THEN ONE WITHOUT

blocks.output: HWCAP sve=1 -> chosen: dot_sve  | ifunc=5255.250 ptr=5255.250 neon=5255.250 ref=5255.250 | max abs diff=-0
HWCAP sve=0 -> chosen: dot_neon | ifunc=5255.250 ptr=5255.250 neon=5255.250 ref=5255.250 | max abs diff=-0

blocks.text:
Same binary, different implementation, identical answer, no SIGILL on
the old core (compare aarch64 lab 03's LSE build).

steps.title: WHAT THE RESOLVER AND THE SYMBOL LOOK LIKE

blocks.output:
resolve_dot:
      adrp x8, dot_sve ; add x8, x8, :lo12:dot_sve
      tst  x0, #0x400000                     // HWCAP_SVE is bit 22
      adrp x9, dot_neon ; add x9, x9, :lo12:dot_neon
      csel x0, x9, x8, eq                    // x0 = (hwcap & SVE) ? dot_sve : dot_neon
      ret

commands: llvm-readelf -s bin/04_dispatch | grep -E ' dot$| resolve_dot| dot_sve| dot_neon'
blocks.output:
18: ... FUNC    LOCAL  DEFAULT   14 dot_sve
      19: ... FUNC    LOCAL  DEFAULT   14 dot_neon
      21: ... FUNC    LOCAL  DEFAULT   14 resolve_dot
      40: ... IFUNC   GLOBAL DEFAULT   14 dot
  `dot` has symbol type IFUNC: the loader will call resolve_dot (whose
  address is where a function would be) and patch the GOT/PLT slot with
  the result. After that, calling dot() costs the same as any call
  through the PLT. This is exactly how glibc picks memcpy/strlen variants.

ifunc VS FUNCTION POINTER:
  ifunc: no visible dispatch code at call sites; resolved once; requires
  glibc-style dynamic linking (static-PIE and musl need care), runs before
  main with limited environment (no malloc, no TLS), and is invisible to
  tests unless you also export the variants (as this lab does: dot_neon
  and dot_sve are callable directly).
  function pointer: explicit, testable (call every variant in your test
  suite regardless of the host), works everywhere, and lets a config flag
  or benchmark override the choice. One indirect call per use. Most
  performance libraries (BLAS, codecs) use this or a per-object-file
  variant table for the same reasons.

blocks.text:
VALIDATING A DISPATCH DECISION (the part that matters in real work):
  1. Correctness: every variant against a scalar reference, on inputs
     whose size is not a multiple of any vector length, under qemu at
     several VLs (lab 02) and on the hardware you have. This lab prints
     the max abs difference; a real test uses a tolerance and many inputs.
  2. Benefit: on the target hardware, the chosen variant must actually be
     faster on the sizes the workload uses (small-n overhead, alignment,
     the cost of svwhilelt per iteration). "Has SVE" is not "SVE is faster".
  3. Stability: the choice must not flip between runs (pinned feature
     detection), and must degrade safely (an unknown core gets the
     baseline). Log the decision once at startup.
  That is the checklist for "should this API be redirected to the SVE /
  SME kernel": evidence at each step, not the presence of a feature bit.

tryIt.text:
1. Set n to 4 and to 3: the SVE path's whilelt handles both; compare
     with the NEON path's scalar tail.
  2. Add a dot_sve2 variant with target("sve2") and dispatch on HWCAP2_SVE2;
     run on `-cpu neoverse-v1` (SVE only) vs `-cpu max`.
  3. `LD_DEBUG=bindings a64run -cpu max ./bin/04_dispatch 2>&1 | grep dot`:
     watch the loader bind the ifunc.
============================================================

blocks.text:
D1. Detect with getauxval(AT_HWCAP/AT_HWCAP2) (or /proc/cpuinfo for
    humans); never assume from -march.
D2. Keep variants callable and tested individually; dispatch is a thin
    layer on top.
D3. Prove the chosen variant is correct AND faster on the real target
    before wiring the dispatch; keep an override for benchmarking.

labs.title: SME first look — streaming mode, the streaming vector length, an outer product
labs.needs: tools/a64.sh (clang 21 with +sme, compiler-rt builtins, qemu -cpu max)
labs.teaches:
The Scalable Matrix Extension in the smallest program that exercises
its three new ideas:
  1. Streaming SVE mode: a CPU mode (smstart/smstop) with its OWN
     vector length (SVL), possibly different from the normal SVE VL,
     and a different set of legal instructions.
  2. ZA: a matrix accumulator of SVL x SVL bytes, stored as tiles.
  3. The outer product: `fmopa` multiplies a column vector by a row
     vector and accumulates the whole tile in ONE instruction: the
     core of every SME matmul kernel.
Under qemu you can vary the streaming VL and watch the tile change
size; on a CPU without SME the program says so instead of dying.
labs.build:
(cd aarch64 && ./build.sh)   -> bin/05_sme, bin/05_sme.s
__arm_locally_streaming and __arm_new("za") are the ACLE keywords; clang
inserts smstart/smstop and the ZA lazy-save calls (__arm_tpidr2_save)
that compiler-rt's builtins provide: without that archive the link
fails on `__arm_tpidr2_save`, which is how you learn that SME code has
a runtime ABI, not just instructions.

steps.title: RUN AT THREE STREAMING VECTOR LENGTHS (bytes: 16, 32, 64)

commands: for vl in 16 32 64; do $A64_QEMU -cpu max,sme-default-vector-length=$vl -L $A64_SYSROOT ./bin/05_sme; done
blocks.output:
SME present. streaming VL = 128 bits -> ZA tile is 4 x 4 f32
trace of outer(x, ones) over the tile = 10 (expected sum 1..4 = 10)
SME present. streaming VL = 256 bits -> ZA tile is 8 x 8 f32
trace of outer(x, ones) over the tile = 36 (expected sum 1..8 = 36)
SME present. streaming VL = 512 bits -> ZA tile is 16 x 16 f32
trace of outer(x, ones) over the tile = 136 (expected sum 1..16 = 136)

no SME on this CPU (HWCAP2_SME clear); nothing to run
Read it: x = (1, 2, 3, ...), y = (1, 1, 1, ...); outer(x, y)[r][c] = x[r]
so the trace (diagonal sum) is 1 + 2 + ... + N with N = SVL / 32 bits.
10, 36, 136 at N = 4, 8, 16: the single fmopa did the whole N x N
product each time, and the code never mentioned N.

2 smstart sm        // enter streaming mode (per __arm_locally_streaming function)
      2 smstop  sm
      1 smstart za        // enable the ZA storage
      1 smstop  za
      2 zero {za}         // svzero_za()
      1 fmopa za0.s, p0/m, p0/m, z0.s, z1.s     // the outer product, predicated on both axes
      4 rdsvl x, #1       // read the STREAMING vector length (svcntsb/svcntsw)
  `rdsvl` is not `rdvl`: streaming and non-streaming lengths are separate
  registers of the machine, and code that mixes them up computes wrong
  loop bounds on hardware where they differ.

WHAT TO KNOW BEFORE TOUCHING A REAL SME KERNEL:
  - Streaming mode changes what is legal: many NEON and some SVE
    instructions are not available in streaming mode (unless sme_fa64);
    calling a normal function from streaming code costs smstop/smstart
    around the call unless it is marked streaming-compatible.
  - ZA is caller-saved via a lazy scheme (TPIDR2_EL0 + __arm_tpidr2_save):
    the ABI, not you, saves the tile when a non-ZA function is called.
    Keep hot loops free of calls.
  - Tiles: ZA holds SVL/8 x SVL/8 bytes; as 32-bit floats that is 4 tiles
    (za0.s..za3.s) of (SVL/32)^2 elements. A matmul kernel keeps several
    tiles live and streams panels of A and B through them: fmopa per K
    step, then reads rows out (svread_hor_za32) to store C.
  - Validation: outer products on small integer-valued inputs (exact in
    float), at multiple SVLs under qemu, against a scalar reference; then
    on real SME hardware for performance (Apple M4, and Armv9.2 cores with
    SME2). qemu is again correctness-only.
  - The dispatch checklist of lab 04 applies with more force: an SME
    kernel wins only above some problem size (mode switches and tile
    load/store are not free), so "has SME" must never mean "use SME".

tryIt.text:
1. Change x to (1, 2, 3, ...) and y to (2, 2, 2, ...): trace doubles.
     Then use svmopa with the two predicates restricted (svwhilelt_b32(0,3))
     and see only a 3x3 corner accumulate.
  2. Accumulate two fmopa calls (K = 2) before reading the tile: the
     trace doubles again. That is the K loop of a matmul.
  3. Read the ZA tile row by row with svread_hor_za32 into a C array and
     print it as a matrix at SVL 128: the outer product laid bare.
============================================================

blocks.text:
Z1. Streaming VL != SVE VL. Use svcntsw()/rdsvl inside streaming code.
Z2. No calls inside the ZA-live hot loop; mark helpers
    __arm_streaming_compatible where possible.
Z3. Correctness at several SVLs under qemu first; then measure the
    crossover size on real hardware before dispatching to SME.

labs.title: BIGCODE LAB #01: Build topology — how a 7,500-file C++ project is put together
labs.markdown:
# BIGCODE LAB #01: Build topology — how a 7,500-file C++ project is put together

**TRACK:** bigcode | **DIFFICULTY:** 2 | **NEEDS:** a CMake + Ninja build directory (here: the local LLVM 23 build), `jq`

## What this teaches

Before you can profile, fix or even read a large codebase you need three answers: **what gets built from what, with which flags, and how do I rebuild just one piece**. CMake writes those answers into the build directory; Ninja and `compile_commands.json` let you query them without reading a single `CMakeLists.txt`. Every command below ran on `~/thats_me/llvm-project/build` (Release, Ninja, 7,568 translation units).

## STEP 1 — How big is it, and what are the entry points?

```
$ cd ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build
$ ninja -t targets all | wc -l
61629
$ ninja -t targets | grep -E "^(clang|opt|llc|check-clang|check-llvm|FileCheck)[: ]"
FileCheck: phony
check-clang: phony
check-llvm: phony
clang: phony
llc: phony
opt: phony
```

61,629 build edges; the names you type (`ninja clang`, `ninja check-llvm`) are **phony** targets that fan out to the real ones. `ninja -t targets all` lists everything; `ninja -t targets rule CXX_COMPILER__…` lists by rule; `ninja -t browse` (if built with it) serves a graph in a browser.

## STEP 2 — The compile database: every TU's exact command

```
$ ls -la compile_commands.json | awk '{print $5" bytes"}'
12376961 bytes
$ jq 'length' compile_commands.json
7568
$ jq '.[] | select(.file | endswith("/lib/Support/APInt.cpp")) | .command' compile_commands.json | cut -c1-600
"/usr/lib64/ccache/c++ -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -D_GNU_SOURCE -D__STDC_CONSTANT_MACROS -D__STDC_FORMAT_MACROS -D__STDC_LIMIT_MACROS
 -I/home/.../llvm-project/build/lib/Support -I/home/.../llvm-project/llvm/lib/Support -I/home/.../llvm-project/build/include
 -I/home/.../llvm-project/llvm/include -I/home/.../llvm-project/llvm/../third-party/siphash/include -I/home/.../llvm-project/llvm/../libc
 -fPIC -fno-semantic-interposition -fvisibility-inlines-hidden -Werror=date-time -Wall -Wextra -Wno-unused-pa…
```

Read one command completely once: the **compiler actually used** (`/usr/lib64/ccache/c++`: GCC through ccache, not clang: this LLVM was built with g++), the **defines** (`_GNU_SOURCE`, the `__STDC_*_MACROS`), the **include paths** in order (build dir first: generated headers shadow source headers), and the **codegen flags** (`-fPIC -fno-semantic-interposition -fvisibility-inlines-hidden` are the LLVM shared-library hygiene set).

Aggregate questions are one `jq` away:

```
$ jq -r '.[].command' compile_commands.json | grep -oE ' -O[0-3s]' | sort | uniq -c
   7568  -O3
$ jq -r '.[].command' compile_commands.json | grep -c ' -g'
0
```

Every TU is `-O3` and none has `-g`: a pure Release build. If a profile of this clang showed only addresses, this is why (lab 02, lab 04). The same two lines answer "is anything built without `-fPIC`?", "which TUs get `-fno-exceptions`?", "who uses `-march`?".

## STEP 3 — What does target X consist of, and how is one object built?

```
$ ninja -t query lib/libLLVMSupport.a | head -6
lib/libLLVMSupport.a:
  input: CXX_STATIC_LIBRARY_LINKER__LLVMSupport_Release
    lib/Support/BLAKE3/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupportBlake3.dir/blake3.c.o
    lib/Support/BLAKE3/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupportBlake3.dir/blake3_dispatch.c.o
    lib/Support/BLAKE3/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupportBlake3.dir/blake3_portable.c.o
    lib/Support/BLAKE3/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupportBlake3.dir/blake3_neon.c.o
$ ar t lib/libLLVMSupport.a | wc -l
180
$ ninja -t commands lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o | tail -1 | cut -c1-300
/usr/lib64/ccache/c++ -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -D_GNU_SOURCE ... -o lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o -c /home/.../llvm/lib/Support/APInt.cpp
$ ninja -t deps lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o | grep -c "\.h"
258
```

`-t query` = inputs and outputs of any edge (the archive is 180 objects, including a `blake3_neon.c.o` that exists on x86 too: dispatch code). `-t commands` = the exact commands to rebuild a target, last line being the compile itself: copy it, add `-ftime-trace` or `-S` or `-E`, and you have reproduced one TU outside the build (lab 05 does exactly this). `-t deps` = the header dependency list Ninja recorded: 258 headers for one file, which is the number to reduce if compile time hurts.

## STEP 4 — Rebuild one thing, see what would rebuild

```
ninja lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o     # just that object
ninja -n clang | head                                        # dry run: what is out of date and why
ninja -d explain clang 2>&1 | head                           # WHY each edge is dirty (timestamp, missing, flags changed)
ninja -v lib/libLLVMSupport.a                                # print commands while building
```

`-d explain` is the tool for "why does everything rebuild after I touched one header": it names the dirty input.

## The procedure for an unfamiliar CMake/Ninja tree

1. `ninja -t targets | grep -i <thing>` to find the target name.
2. `jq` the compile database for the flags of the file you care about; note the real compiler and the include order.
3. `ninja -t query <target>` down to objects; `ninja -t commands <obj> | tail -1` to reproduce one compile by hand.
4. `ninja -t deps <obj>` for its header fan-in; `-d explain` for rebuild surprises.
5. Only then open `CMakeLists.txt`, searching for the target name (`rg "add_llvm_component_library\(LLVMSupport"`), because now you know what you are looking for.

Other build systems map onto the same questions: Android/Soong (`m <module>`, `out/soong/build.ninja` is Ninja underneath: `ninja -f out/combined-*.ninja -t query`), Bazel (`bazel query`, `bazel aquery` for commands), plain Make (`make -n`, `make -p`).

## Try this yourself

1. Which TUs include the most headers? `for o in $(ninja -t targets rule CXX_COMPILER__LLVMSupport_Release); do echo "$(ninja -t deps $o | grep -c .h) $o"; done | sort -rn | head`.
2. Find every TU compiled with `-fno-exceptions` vs with exceptions in `compile_commands.json` and explain the split (hint: `LLVM_ENABLE_EH`).
3. Touch `llvm/include/llvm/ADT/StringRef.h`, then `ninja -n clang | wc -l`: how much of the world depends on one header?

labs.title: BIGCODE LAB #02: ELF forensics — what kind of binary is this, and where are its symbols?
labs.markdown:
# BIGCODE LAB #02: ELF forensics — what kind of binary is this, and where are its symbols?

**TRACK:** bigcode | **DIFFICULTY:** 2 | **NEEDS:** `file`, `readelf`, `nm`, `ldd`, `ar`, `size`, `objdump`

## What this teaches

Before profiling or debugging someone else's binary you must know its shape: executable or shared object, PIE or fixed address, static or dynamic, stripped or not, and where its code really lives. Two clangs on this machine make a perfect contrast: Fedora's `/usr/bin/clang-21` and the locally built `~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang`.

## STEP 1 — `file` says most of it

```
$ file -L /usr/bin/clang-21 ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1 /usr/lib64/libc.so.6 /usr/bin/ls
/usr/bin/clang-21:              ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ...
.../build/bin/clang:            ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (GNU/Linux), dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ...
/lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1:         ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, dynamically linked, BuildID[sha1]=621e6ac6...
/usr/lib64/libc.so.6:           ELF 64-bit LSB shared object, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ...
/usr/bin/ls:                    ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked ...
```

- **pie executable** = position-independent, loaded at a random base each run (ASLR); addresses in a profile or a crash are *offsets* from that base. `/usr/bin/clang-21` and `ls` are PIE (distro default).
- **executable** (no "pie") = fixed load address (0x400000 here); the local clang and the lab binaries are built this way by this clang's defaults (`-fno-pie` is the default for the local build's linker invocation). `readelf -h` shows `Type: EXEC` vs `DYN`.
- **shared object** = a library, or a PIE (both are `DYN`); `libc.so.6` even has an interpreter because it can be executed to print its version.
- "dynamically linked" tells you there is a NEEDED list; "statically linked" would mean everything is inside.

## STEP 2 — What does it depend on, and how big is it really?

```
$ ls -la /usr/bin/clang-21 | awk '{print $5}'
157400
$ ldd /usr/bin/clang-21 | grep -E "clang-cpp|libLLVM"
        libclang-cpp.so.21.1 => /lib64/libclang-cpp.so.21.1
        libLLVM.so.21.1 => /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1
$ ls -la /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1 | awk '{print $5}'
145147968
$ readelf -d ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang | grep NEEDED
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libzstd.so.1]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libstdc++.so.6]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libm.so.6]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libgcc_s.so.1]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libc.so.6]
 0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [ld-linux-x86-64.so.2]
$ size ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang | tail -1
   text	   data	    bss	    dec	    hex	filename
208996649	3870420	 888480	213755549	cbda69d	.../build/bin/clang
```

Fedora's `clang-21` is a **157 KB launcher**: the compiler is in `libclang-cpp.so` and the 145 MB `libLLVM.so`. The local `clang` is a **209 MB monolith** that links every LLVM component statically and needs only the system C/C++ runtime. Same source, opposite packaging, and it matters for everything downstream: symbols, startup cost (lab 04: the loader relocating 145 MB of shared library costs real milliseconds), profiling attribution (samples land in `libLLVM.so` vs in `clang`), and deployment.

## STEP 3 — Where are the symbols?

```
$ nm --defined-only /usr/bin/clang-21 | grep -c " [Tt] "
0
$ nm -C --defined-only ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang | grep -c " [Tt] "
207389
$ nm -D --defined-only /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1 | grep -c " T "
28916
$ nm -D --defined-only /lib64/libclang-cpp.so.21.1 | grep -c " T "
26985
```

- The distro launcher has **no** symbol table (`nm` finds 0 text symbols): stripped, as packages are. Its debug info lives in a separate `debuginfo` package, fetchable on demand via **debuginfod** (`DEBUGINFOD_URLS` is set on this box: gdb and perf can download symbols for distro binaries without root).
- The local clang has **207,389** text symbols: an unstripped Release build (symbols but no DWARF; lab 03).
- The distro libraries have their **exported** symbols in `.dynsym` (`nm -D`): ~29k in libLLVM. perf can name any sample that lands in an exported function; internal (hidden-visibility) functions show as the nearest exported symbol or as an address unless debuginfo is present.

Which tool for which table: `nm` reads `.symtab` (full, stripped away by `strip`); `nm -D` reads `.dynsym` (what the dynamic linker needs, survives stripping); `readelf -s` shows both with section indexes; `nm -C`/`c++filt` demangle.

## STEP 4 — Inside a static archive, and the stripped/debug pair

```
$ ar t ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/lib/libLLVMSupport.a | head -3; ar t .../libLLVMSupport.a | wc -l
blake3.c.o
blake3_dispatch.c.o
blake3_portable.c.o
180
$ readelf -n perf/bin/03_hot_function.stripped | grep -A1 "Build ID"        # from the perf track
$ readelf -p .gnu_debuglink perf/bin/03_hot_function.stripped | grep -o "03_hot_function.debug"
03_hot_function.debug
```

A `.a` is just a bag of `.o` files (`ar t` lists, `ar x` extracts one; `nm` works on the whole archive). The link pulls in only the members that resolve an undefined symbol, which is why link order matters and why `--whole-archive` exists. A stripped binary keeps a **build-id** note and, if the packager did it right, a `.gnu_debuglink` naming the file with the DWARF: perf, gdb and `llvm-symbolizer` follow both (perf lab 03).

## The identification checklist for an unknown binary

| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| kind, arch, PIE, stripped? | `file -L bin`; `readelf -h bin \| grep Type` |
| what does it load? | `ldd bin` (or safer, `readelf -d bin \| grep NEEDED`; `ldd` executes the loader) |
| where is the code? | `size bin`; `readelf -S bin \| grep -E "\.text\|\.data\|\.bss"` |
| which symbols exist? | `nm --defined-only`, `nm -D`, `readelf -s` |
| is there debug info? | `readelf -S bin \| grep debug_info`; `llvm-dwarfdump --debug-info bin \| head` |
| can I get debug info? | build-id (`readelf -n`) + debuginfod / `.gnu_debuglink` / distro `-debuginfo` package |
| what will run at startup? | `readelf -d` (INIT_ARRAY count, RUNPATH), `LD_DEBUG=libs ./bin` |
| what compiled it? | lab 03 |

## Try this yourself

1. `readelf -S /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1 | grep -E "\.text|\.rela\.dyn|\.gnu\.hash"`: the relocation section is what the loader processes on every start (lab 04 measures it).
2. `LD_DEBUG=statistics /usr/bin/clang-21 --version 2>&1 | grep relocations`: how many relocations at startup.
3. Build one lab binary with `-static` and compare `file`, `ldd` and `size`.

labs.title: BIGCODE LAB #03: Flags archaeology — which compiler, which flags, produced this binary?
labs.markdown:
# BIGCODE LAB #03: Flags archaeology — which compiler, which flags, produced this binary?

**TRACK:** bigcode | **DIFFICULTY:** 2 | **NEEDS:** `readelf`, `llvm-dwarfdump`, `clang -frecord-command-line`, a compile database

## What this teaches

"The build is `-O2`" is a belief until you read it off the binary. Binaries carry evidence of their origin in four places; each answers a different question and each can be missing. This lab reads all four on real files.

## STEP 1 — `.comment`: which compiler *linked the objects*

```
$ readelf -p .comment ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang | grep "\]" | head -3
  [     0]  GCC: (GNU) 15.2.1 20260123 (Red Hat 15.2.1-7)
$ readelf -p .comment /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1
readelf: Warning: Section '.comment' was not dumped because it does not exist
```

Surprise number one: the *clang* binary in the local build was compiled by **GCC 15**. Lab 01's compile database said `/usr/lib64/ccache/c++`; `.comment` confirms it from the artifact alone. Surprise number two: the distro library has no `.comment` at all: Fedora strips it. `.comment` collects one string per object file's compiler; a binary built from mixed toolchains shows several.

## STEP 2 — `DW_AT_producer`: compiler *and flags*, per compilation unit, when there is DWARF

```
$ llvm-dwarfdump --debug-info perf/bin/03_hot_function | grep -m1 DW_AT_producer
              DW_AT_producer	("clang version 21.1.8 (Fedora 21.1.8-4.fc43)")
$ llvm-dwarfdump --debug-info ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang | grep -m1 DW_AT_producer
(nothing: the Release build has no DWARF)
```

With `-g`, every compilation unit records its producer. Clang records the version by default and adds the flags with `-grecord-command-line` (GCC: `-grecord-gcc-switches`, on by default in some distro configurations): then `DW_AT_producer` reads like `clang version 21.1.8 -O2 -march=x86-64-v3 -g ...`. Without `-g` there is nothing here, which is the case for this Release LLVM and for most shipped binaries.

## STEP 3 — `-frecord-command-line`: the whole command line, even without `-g`

```
$ clang -O2 -g -march=x86-64-v3 -frecord-command-line -c perf/01_noise_floor.c -o /tmp/rc.o
$ readelf -p .GCC.command.line /tmp/rc.o | grep "\]" | cut -c1-200
  [     1]  /usr/bin/clang-21 --gcc-triple=x86_64-redhat-linux -O2 -g -march=x86-64-v3 -frecord-command-line -c -fcolor-diagnostics -o /tmp/rc.o perf/01_noise_floor.c
```

The `.GCC.command.line` section (the name is a GCC convention that clang honours) stores the exact driver command line. Note what the *driver* added that you did not type: `--gcc-triple`, `-fcolor-diagnostics`. If you own the build, turn this on for release binaries: it costs a few hundred bytes per object and ends every "what flags was this built with" argument. It survives linking (sections are concatenated, one entry per object) but not `strip --remove-section`.

## STEP 4 — Build-id and debuglink: the handle to everything else

```
$ readelf -n perf/bin/03_hot_function.stripped | grep -A1 "Build ID"
    Build ID: 7ba4afdee8cb58b4f09b12d6547ad57353ac7865           (from the perf-track build)
$ readelf -p .gnu_debuglink perf/bin/03_hot_function.stripped | grep -o "03_hot_function.debug"
03_hot_function.debug
```

The build-id is a hash of the linked contents. It identifies the exact build across machines: perf's cache (`~/.debug/.build-id/`), debuginfod servers, crash reporters and symbol servers all key on it. If you keep the unstripped binary or the `.debug` file for every build-id you ship, you can symbolize any crash or profile from the field.

## STEP 5 — The driver's own testimony

For a binary you are about to build, ask the compiler what it will do before it does it:

```
clang -O2 -march=native -### -c x.c 2>&1 | tail -1      # the exact cc1 invocation: -target-cpu, -target-feature, defaults you did not specify
clang -O2 -march=native -E -dM - </dev/null | grep -E "__AVX2__|__FMA__|__OPTIMIZE__"   # what the preprocessor sees
clang -v -c x.c 2>&1 | grep -A20 "#include <...>"         # the include search order actually used
clang -print-search-dirs                                  # where libraries and crt files come from
```

`-###` is how you discover that `-march=native` on this laptop means `-target-cpu alderlake` with a list of `-target-feature +avx2 +fma ...`, that `-ffp-contract=on` is implied (codegen lab 02's FMA surprise), and that `-fPIE` may or may not be default.

## Putting it together: the "what am I looking at" checklist

| Evidence | Where | Present when | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.comment` | `readelf -p .comment` | not stripped of it | compiler(s) and versions that produced the objects |
| `DW_AT_producer` | `llvm-dwarfdump --debug-info` | built with `-g` | compiler per CU; flags too with `-grecord-command-line` |
| `.GCC.command.line` | `readelf -p .GCC.command.line` | built with `-frecord-command-line` | the exact driver line per object |
| build-id + debuglink | `readelf -n`, `readelf -p .gnu_debuglink` | almost always (build-id), if packaged well (debuglink) | which build; where its debug info is |
| compile database | `compile_commands.json` | you have the build tree | everything, but only for that tree, not for the binary in your hands |
| ISA actually used | `objdump -d bin \| grep -cE "vfmadd\|vpgather\|zmm"` | always | did `-march` reach the code? |

The last row is the one people forget: flags describe intent; the disassembly describes the result. A binary "built with `-march=native`" that contains no AVX instruction in its hot loop was built with something else, or the hot loop did not vectorize (codegen lab 02).

## Try this yourself

1. Add `-frecord-command-line -grecord-command-line` to `perf/build.sh`, rebuild, and read both sections back.
2. `objdump -d /lib64/libLLVM.so.21.1 | grep -c vpgatherdd` versus the same for `~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang`: which build targets a newer ISA? (Fedora builds for x86-64 baseline; check your local build's `-march` in the compile database.)
3. Find a binary on the system with a `.GCC.command.line` section: `for f in /usr/bin/*; do readelf -S "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -q GCC.command && echo "$f"; done | head`.

labs.evidence: The local clang was built by GCC 15 (from .comment); the exact driver line recovered from an object's .GCC.command.line

labs.title: BIGCODE LAB #04: The hot function is in a shared library you did not build — profile the compiler itself
labs.markdown:
# BIGCODE LAB #04: The hot function is in a shared library you did not build — profile the compiler itself

**TRACK:** bigcode | **DIFFICULTY:** 3 | **NEEDS:** perf, the distro clang (`libclang-cpp.so` + `libLLVM.so`), the LLVM source tree, `rg`

## What this teaches

The realistic case: the program you are profiling is a thin executable whose time is spent inside big shared libraries (here `clang-21` → `libclang-cpp.so.21.1` + `libLLVM.so.21.1`, lab 02). You need to (1) profile the right process, (2) read the right PMU section, (3) attribute samples to library symbols, and (4) map a hot symbol back to a source tree you did not build from. And you get to make, and recognise, the two mistakes everyone makes first.

The workload: compiling `heavy.cpp` (a small file that instantiates `std::regex`, `std::map` and `std::unordered_map` a few times; ~3.2 s at `-O2`) and `llvm/lib/Support/APInt.cpp` from the LLVM tree with its real Release flags (~2.9 s).

## MISTAKE 1 — You profiled ccache

```
$ which clang++
/usr/lib64/ccache/clang++
$ perf record -o cc.data clang++ -O2 -c heavy.cpp -o /dev/null
$ perf report -i cc.data --stdio --sort dso | head
    33.34%  ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
    21.15%  libzstd.so.1.5.7
    17.58%  ccache
    14.07%  libstdc++.so.6.0.34
```

`clang++` on this box is a **ccache wrapper**, and the file had been compiled before: the "compile" was a cache hit. The profile is the dynamic loader (`do_lookup_x`, `_dl_relocate_object`), zstd decompressing the cached object, and ccache's own hashing. The compiler never ran. Signs: the DSO list contains no compiler library, and the run was suspiciously fast. Fix: `CCACHE_DISABLE=1` or call the real binary (`/usr/bin/clang++`), and always check `which` for wrappers (ccache, distcc, sccache, `icecc`) before trusting a profile of a build tool.

## MISTAKE 2 — You read the wrong PMU section

On this hybrid CPU, perf records events from both PMUs (`cpu_core` and `cpu_atom`) and `perf report` prints **one section per PMU, the small one first**:

```
$ perf report -i apint4.data --stdio --sort dso | head -4
# Samples: 69  of event 'cpu_atom/cycles/Pu'
    67.06%  ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
    29.01%  libclang-cpp.so.21.1
```

69 samples on an E-core (the process started there for a few milliseconds before migrating), and a "profile" that says the loader and Sema dominate. Reading only `head` of the report gave a conclusion that contradicted the compiler's own `-ftime-trace` (lab 05). The real data is the *next* section:

```
$ perf report -i apint4.data --stdio --sort dso | awk '/Samples:.*cpu_core/{on=1} on' | head -6
# Samples: 11K of event 'cpu_core/cycles/Pu'
    71.32%  libLLVM.so.21.1
    19.74%  libclang-cpp.so.21.1
     8.10%  libc.so.6
     0.67%  libstdc++.so.6.0.34
     0.11%  ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
```

Rule: look at the **sample count** before the percentages. 69 samples is noise; 11K is a profile. On hybrid machines pin the workload (`tools/pin.sh`) or filter the report to one PMU.

## STEP 1 — The real profile, per library

```
$ perf record -F 4000 -o cc4.data /usr/bin/clang++ -O2 -c heavy.cpp -o /dev/null
$ perf report -i cc4.data --stdio --sort dso | awk '/cpu_core/{on=1} on' | head -6
# Samples: 12K of event 'cpu_core/cycles/Pu'
    61.24%  libLLVM.so.21.1
    28.82%  libclang-cpp.so.21.1
     8.87%  libc.so.6
     0.75%  libstdc++.so.6.0.34
     0.23%  ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
```

Two thirds of a `-O2` compile of a template-heavy file is the optimizer and code generator (libLLVM), a third is the front end (libclang-cpp), a tenth is `malloc`/`free`. That split alone tells you where a compile-time fix would have to land (lab 05 confirms it with `-ftime-trace`: Backend 2.2 s, Frontend 1.0 s).

## STEP 2 — Symbols inside the libraries

```
$ perf report -i cc4.data --stdio --no-children --sort dso,sym | awk '/cpu_core/{on=1} on' | head -10
     3.08%  libc.so.6             [.] _int_malloc
     1.53%  libLLVM.so.21.1       [.] llvm::FoldingSetBase::FindNodeOrInsertPos(llvm::FoldingSetNodeID const&, void*&, ...)
     1.03%  libc.so.6             [.] malloc
     0.85%  libLLVM.so.21.1       [.] llvm::AnalysisManager<llvm::Function>::getResultImpl(llvm::AnalysisKey*, llvm::Function&)
     0.84%  libclang-cpp.so.21.1  [.] clang::Sema::LookupName(clang::LookupResult&, clang::Scope*, bool, bool)
     0.81%  libLLVM.so.21.1       [.] llvm::InstCombinerImpl::run()
     0.78%  libclang-cpp.so.21.1  [.] clang::Lexer::Lex(clang::Token&)
     0.77%  libc.so.6             [.] cfree@GLIBC_2.2.5
     0.74%  libLLVM.so.21.1       [.] llvm::InlineFunction(llvm::CallBase&, llvm::InlineFunctionInfo&, ...)

$ cd ~/thats_me/llvm-project && rg -n --type cpp -m3 '\bFindNodeOrInsertPos\b\s*\(' llvm/lib llvm/include | head -4
llvm/lib/Analysis/ScalarEvolution.cpp:557:  if (const SCEV *S = UniqueSCEVs.FindNodeOrInsertPos(ID, IP)) return S;
llvm/lib/Analysis/ScalarEvolution.cpp:582:  if (const SCEV *S = UniqueSCEVs.FindNodeOrInsertPos(ID, IP))
llvm/lib/Analysis/ScalarEvolution.cpp:1195:        if (const SCEV *S = UniqueSCEVs.FindNodeOrInsertPos(ID, IP))
llvm/lib/IR/LegacyPassManager.cpp:638:    if (auto *N = UniqueAnalysisUsages.FindNodeOrInsertPos(ID, IP))
```

`FindNodeOrInsertPos` is the hash-consing lookup of `FoldingSet`, used by many uniquing tables (SCEV, attributes, metadata). `rg` lists the call sites; which of them is hot is an *inference* until a call graph confirms it, but the profile's neighbours (`getRangeRef`, `getAddExpr`) point at `ScalarEvolution`'s `UniqueSCEVs` for the APInt compile, while for heavy.cpp the run script's `rg` shows `Attributes.cpp` first: same symbol, different hot caller. The version mismatch trap: the library is 21.1.8 and the tree is a 23-git checkout; line numbers drift, names mostly do not. When you must be exact, check out the tag that matches `DW_AT_producer` or the package version (lab 03).

## The procedure (memorize)

1. `which` the tool: wrappers (ccache, distcc) mean you may profile a cache hit.
2. `perf record -F 4000` the real binary; on hybrid CPUs pin it or read the `cpu_core` section; check the sample count.
3. `--sort dso` first: which library owns the time? Then `--sort dso,sym`; expect a flat profile in a compiler-like program and aggregate.
4. Names come from `.dynsym`; hidden functions need debuginfo (debuginfod, `-debuginfo` packages, or your own build with `-g`).
5. Map symbol → source with `rg` in the matching version of the tree; confirm callers with a DWARF call graph.
6. Decide whether the finding is about the code (a hot loop) or about the workload (the input drives a whole subsystem): compilers, databases and interpreters are usually the second kind.

## Try this yourself

1. Profile `opt -O3` on the `.ll` of `heavy.cpp` (`clang++ -O0 -S -emit-llvm heavy.cpp`): the front end disappears and the optimizer's flat profile remains.
2. `perf report --sort dso,sym --children` on the same data: read the inclusive tree from `main` down to `PassManager::run`.
3. `LD_DEBUG=statistics /usr/bin/clang-21 --version 2>&1 | grep -E "relocations|time"`: measure the loader cost that mistake 1 exposed; then compare `time ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/bin/clang --version` (static monolith) with `time /usr/bin/clang-21 --version`.

# BIGCODE LAB #05: Why does this file take three seconds to compile? — `-ftime-trace`

**TRACK:** bigcode | **DIFFICULTY:** 3 | **NEEDS:** clang `-ftime-trace`, `jq`, a compile command from lab 01

## What this teaches

Compile time is a performance problem like any other, with a better instrument than most: clang's `-ftime-trace` writes a Chrome-trace JSON of every phase, every header parsed, every template instantiated, every function optimized, with durations. Lab 04's profile said "two thirds in libLLVM"; this lab says *which passes, on which functions*, and *which headers and instantiations* in the front end.

## STEP 1 — Get the trace for a real TU

Take the command from the compile database (lab 01), swap the compiler for clang (this tree was built with g++), add the flags:

```
$ CMD=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.file | endswith("/lib/Support/APInt.cpp")) | .command' ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build/compile_commands.json)
$ CMD2=$(echo "$CMD" | sed 's|/usr/lib64/ccache/c++|/usr/bin/clang++|; s| -o [^ ]*| -o /tmp/APInt.o -ftime-trace -ftime-trace-granularity=500 -Wno-unknown-warning-option|')
$ cd ~/thats_me/llvm-project/build && /usr/bin/time -f "%es %MKB" bash -c "$CMD2"
3.12s 150228KB
$ ls -la /tmp/APInt.json | awk '{print $5" bytes"}'
453906 bytes
```

`-ftime-trace-granularity=N` (µs) drops events shorter than N; use 0 to see every header and instantiation (bigger JSON). Open the JSON in `chrome://tracing` / Perfetto for the flame view; `jq` for the numbers.

## STEP 2 — The phase split

```
$ jq -r '.traceEvents[] | select(.ph=="X" and (.name|startswith("Total")|not) and .name!="ExecuteCompiler") | "\(.dur/1000|floor) \(.name) \(.args.detail // "")"' /tmp/APInt.json | sort -rn | head -10
2238 Backend
1189 Optimizer
1047 OptModule /home/.../llvm/lib/Support/APInt.cpp
1047 CodeGenPasses
819 Frontend
744 ModuleInlinerWrapperPass [module]
742 ModuleToPostOrderCGSCCPassAdaptor [module]
398 ModuleToFunctionPassAdaptor [module]
107 OptFunction _ZN4llvm8APIntOps26SolveQuadraticEquationWrapENS_5APIntES1_S1_j
57 PerformPendingInstantiations
```

Read it as a tree: `ExecuteCompiler` (3.1 s) = `Frontend` (0.82 s: parse + Sema + IR generation) + `Backend` (2.24 s) = `Optimizer` (1.19 s) + `CodeGenPasses` (1.05 s: instruction selection, register allocation, emission). Inside the optimizer, the **inliner and the CGSCC pipeline** account for 0.74 s. This matches lab 04's DSO split (71% libLLVM) and refines it: for this `-O3` TU, compile time is *optimization and codegen*, and the front end is a quarter. A "make the build faster" effort on APInt.cpp would look at `-O2` vs `-O3` for this library, or at the biggest `OptFunction` entries, not at headers.

```
$ jq -r '.traceEvents[] | select(.ph=="X" and .name=="OptFunction") | "\(.dur/1000|floor) \(.args.detail)"' /tmp/APInt.json | sort -rn | head -4 | c++filt
107 llvm::APIntOps::SolveQuadraticEquationWrap(llvm::APInt, llvm::APInt, llvm::APInt, unsigned int)
36 llvm::APInt::divide(unsigned long const*, unsigned int, unsigned long const*, unsigned int, unsigned long*, unsigned long*)
30 llvm::APIntOps::GreatestCommonDivisor(llvm::APInt, llvm::APInt)
25 llvm::APInt::sdivrem(llvm::APInt const&, llvm::APInt const&, llvm::APInt&, llvm::APInt&)
```

One function costs 107 ms of optimizer time: the biggest single item in the file. (Lab 04's flat profile could never have named it; the trace attributes by *what the compiler was doing*, the profile by *which compiler code ran*. You need both views.)

## STEP 3 — A front-end-bound TU for contrast

The `heavy.cpp` from lab 04 (a few `std::regex` / `std::map` instantiations, `-O2`):

```
$ /usr/bin/clang++ -O2 -c heavy.cpp -ftime-trace -ftime-trace-granularity=200 -o /tmp/heavy.o
$ jq -r '... same query ...' heavy.json | sort -rn | head -10
2160 Backend
1368 Optimizer
1014 ModuleInlinerWrapperPass [module]
1003 ModuleToPostOrderCGSCCPassAdaptor [module]
984 Frontend
790 OptModule heavy.cpp
790 CodeGenPasses
473 PerformPendingInstantiations
281 InstantiateFunction std::basic_regex<char>::basic_regex
280 InstantiateFunction std::basic_regex<char>::_M_compile
```

Half a second of `PerformPendingInstantiations`, with `std::basic_regex` alone costing 0.56 s to instantiate, then a 1 s inliner run over the code those instantiations produced. This is what "`<regex>` is expensive to compile" looks like in numbers, and the fixes are in the source (avoid instantiating it in every TU; explicit instantiation in one; a lighter library), not in the build flags.

## What each event kind means (the vocabulary you need)

| Event name | What it measures | Where the fix lives |
|---|---|---|
| `Frontend` | lex, parse, Sema, IR emission | headers, templates, constexpr, PCH/modules |
| `Source` | parsing one included file (visible with granularity 0) | include hygiene, forward declarations, PCH |
| `PerformPendingInstantiations`, `InstantiateFunction`, `InstantiateClass` | template instantiation | fewer instantiations, explicit instantiation, type erasure |
| `Backend` = `Optimizer` + `CodeGenPasses` | LLVM passes and machine code emission | `-O` level, function size, `-fno-inline-functions` for diagnostics, `-ffunction-sections` no help here |
| `OptFunction NAME` | optimizer time on one function | that function's size and inlining (`-Rpass-missed=inline` to see why it grew) |
| `RunPass`, `ModuleInlinerWrapperPass`, ... | individual passes | mostly informational; a pathological pass on one function is a compiler bug report |
| `ExecuteCompiler` | the whole thing | the sum |

## Aggregating across a build

One TU is a data point; the build is the target. `ClangBuildAnalyzer` (open source, from the author of `-ftime-trace`) reads every `.json` in a build tree and reports the most expensive headers, templates and functions across all TUs. Without it, `jq` over `find build -name '*.json'` gives the same totals in a few lines. For GCC the equivalent is `-ftime-report` (per-TU, text). For Ninja-level attribution (which TUs took longest, wall clock) use `ninja -d stats` and the `.ninja_log` (`ninjatracing` turns it into the same Chrome-trace format).

## The procedure

1. Reproduce the one slow TU by hand (`ninja -t commands`), add `-ftime-trace`.
2. Phase split first: Frontend vs Backend. That decides which half of this table you are in.
3. Front-end heavy: top `Source` and `Instantiate*` entries; fix at the header/template level.
4. Back-end heavy: top `OptFunction`; check the `-O` level the TU actually uses (lab 01: all `-O3` here); look at the biggest functions and what inlined into them.
5. Prove it: the same command after the change, same machine, same flags, three runs; report seconds and the trace's phase numbers.

## Try this yourself

1. Rebuild APInt.cpp with `-O2` instead of `-O3`: how much of the 2.2 s Backend survives? And with `-O0`?
2. Run with `-ftime-trace-granularity=0` and list the ten slowest `Source` events for heavy.cpp: which header dominates?
3. Add `-ftime-report` and compare its pass table with the trace's `Total <Pass>` events.

# capstones — end-to-end investigations

A capstone is the whole skill in one artifact: an unfamiliar codebase, a
performance question, evidence gathered with the tools from every track, one
change, and proof. Capstone 0 below is worked in full on this machine so you can
calibrate what "done" looks like. Capstones 1 and 2 are templates you fill in
with public code, on your own time, and can publish.

Rules for every capstone (they are the rules of the whole lab):
- Public or synthetic code only. Nothing derived from employer work.
- Every number comes with the command that produced it and the machine state
  (`tools/pin.sh` banner, governor, what else was running).
- The write-up follows the template at the end; the "surprise" line is mandatory.

---

## Capstone 0 (worked): "Why does `APInt.cpp` take three seconds to compile, and what would make it faster?"

**Subject.** `llvm/lib/Support/APInt.cpp` in the local LLVM tree, compiled by the distro `clang++ 21.1.8` with the exact Release flags from the compile database (`-O3`, no `-g`). Machine: i7-1260P, pinned P-core, powersave, no turbo.

**Step 1 — Reproduce one TU outside the build** (bigcode/01):
`ninja -t commands lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o | tail -1`, compiler swapped to `/usr/bin/clang++` (the tree was built with g++ via ccache; `which clang++` is a ccache wrapper, so the real binary is used). Wall time 2.8–3.1 s, 150 MB RSS, three runs.

**Step 2 — Where does the time go, by library** (bigcode/04):
`perf record -F 4000`, reading the `cpu_core` section (11K samples; the 69-sample `cpu_atom` section is discarded):

| DSO | share |
|---|---|
| libLLVM.so.21.1 | 71.3% |
| libclang-cpp.so.21.1 | 19.7% |
| libc.so.6 (malloc/free) | 8.1% |
| ld-linux | 0.1% |

Flat profile: top symbol `_int_malloc` 2.5%, then `ScalarEvolution::getRangeRef` 1.4%, `getAddExpr` 1.2%, `FoldingSetBase::FindNodeOrInsertPos` 1.1%, `computeKnownBits` 1.0%, `Lexer::Lex` 0.9%, `MachineCopyPropagation` 0.8%, `SelectionDAGISel::SelectCodeCommon` 0.8%, `InstCombinerImpl::run` 0.8%.

**Step 3 — Where does the time go, by work** (bigcode/05):
`-ftime-trace`: ExecuteCompiler 3.1 s = Frontend 0.82 s + Backend 2.24 s (Optimizer 1.19 s of which the inliner/CGSCC pipeline 0.74 s; CodeGenPasses 1.05 s). Largest single function in the optimizer: `APIntOps::SolveQuadraticEquationWrap` 107 ms; then `APInt::divide` 36 ms, `GreatestCommonDivisor` 30 ms, `sdivrem` 25 ms.

**Step 4 — Interpretation.**
The two instruments agree: this TU's compile time is three quarters optimization and code generation of a mathematically heavy file at `-O3`, with SCEV (loop analysis) and the inliner prominent, and ~8% in the allocator. The front end (0.8 s, 258 headers) is not the lever.

**Step 5 — The experiment that would follow** (left as the reader's step; the method is what matters):
compile the same TU at `-O2` and at `-O3 -fno-inline-functions`, three runs each, and compare wall time and the Backend phase; then check whether the produced code's speed matters for this library (it is `APInt`: probably yes, so a per-file `-O2` would need a benchmark of APInt-heavy passes before being proposed). Report either "keep `-O3`, the 2.2 s is the price of the code quality" with the benchmark, or "`-O2` saves N% at no measured runtime cost".

**Surprise.** Two convincing wrong answers preceded the right one: a profile of a ccache *hit* (dynamic loader + zstd), and the E-core PMU section (69 samples) read as if it were the profile, which claimed the front end dominated. The `-ftime-trace` phase split is what exposed the second mistake.

---

## Capstone 1 (template): a public x86 codebase, profile → fix → prove

Pick something with a build, a benchmark or a reproducible workload, and a hot loop you can reason about. Good sizes: 10k–200k lines. Candidates that are public and neutral: `zstd`, `lz4`, `xxHash`, `simdjson`'s tests, `sqlite` with a query workload, `jq` on a large JSON, `cJSON`, a `libpng` encode, `bzip2`.

1. **Build topology** (bigcode/01): how is it built, with which flags, how do you rebuild one file.
2. **Baseline** (perf/01, perf/04): a pinned, repeatable workload; min/p50/p99 of the end-to-end time; `perf stat` cycles and instructions.
3. **Locate** (perf/02, perf/03): counters → is it branchy, memory-bound, compute-bound? `perf record` → hot symbol → hot line, through inlining.
4. **Explain** (cache/*, codegen/*): what is the line bound by? A dependency chain, a miss pattern, a mispredict, a missing vectorization, a call across a TU?
5. **Change one thing**: layout, a `restrict`, a pragma, an algorithmic batch, a flag (`-march`, LTO, PGO), or a rewrite of the loop. One change per measurement.
6. **Prove**: same workload, ABAB interleaved, three runs; counters before and after; the assembly diff (`tools/asmdiff.sh`); correctness checks (tests, checksums).
7. **Write it up** with the template below; if the change is real, send it upstream as a PR with the numbers.

## Capstone 2 (template): NEON vs SVE kernel selection, validated

Using the aarch64 track's toolchain (correctness under qemu at several vector lengths; performance by `llvm-mca` and, if you have access, real Arm hardware):

1. Take a kernel (dot product, saxpy, a reduction, a small GEMM) in three versions: scalar reference, NEON intrinsics, SVE intrinsics (aarch64/04 shape).
2. **Correctness** at VL 128/256/512/2048 under qemu with sizes that are not multiples of any VL, against the scalar reference with a tolerance.
3. **Codegen**: `-Rpass=loop-vectorize` on the auto-vectorized C version for both targets; compare with the intrinsics versions; `llvm-mca -mcpu=neoverse-v1` (SVE 256) and `-mcpu=neoverse-n1` (NEON only) throughput per element.
4. **Dispatch**: an ifunc or function-pointer selection on HWCAP (aarch64/04), plus an override for benchmarking.
5. **Decision**: a table of predicted cost per element by core and size, the crossover size below which NEON (or scalar) wins, and the sentence "on hardware X we measured …" only if you measured it. Without hardware, say so; the model-based answer with the validation matrix is still a complete deliverable.
6. Extend to SME (aarch64/05) as a stretch: the outer-product tile version of the GEMM, correct at three streaming VLs.

---

## The write-up template

```
title:      one sentence: what was slow and what you found
subject:    repo, commit, build flags, workload, machine (tools/pin.sh banner)
question:   the performance question in one line
baseline:   min/p50/p99 of the workload; cycles, instructions, IPC
location:   hot symbol -> hot line; the counters that classify it
mechanism:  what the line is bound by, with the lab that taught it
change:     the one change (diff or flag)
proof:      before/after table, ABAB, three runs; counters; asm diff; correctness evidence
residual:   what is still slow and why you stopped
surprise:   the thing you did not expect (mandatory; if there was none, you did not look hard enough)
```

# capstones — end-to-end investigations

A capstone is the whole skill in one artifact: an unfamiliar codebase, a
performance question, evidence gathered with the tools from every track, one
change, and proof. Capstone 0 below is worked in full on this machine so you can
calibrate what "done" looks like. Capstones 1 and 2 are templates you fill in
with public code, on your own time, and can publish.

Rules for every capstone (they are the rules of the whole lab):
- Public or synthetic code only. Nothing derived from employer work.
- Every number comes with the command that produced it and the machine state
  (`tools/pin.sh` banner, governor, what else was running).
- The write-up follows the template at the end; the "surprise" line is mandatory.

---

## Capstone 0 (worked): "Why does `APInt.cpp` take three seconds to compile, and what would make it faster?"

**Subject.** `llvm/lib/Support/APInt.cpp` in the local LLVM tree, compiled by the distro `clang++ 21.1.8` with the exact Release flags from the compile database (`-O3`, no `-g`). Machine: i7-1260P, pinned P-core, powersave, no turbo.

**Step 1 — Reproduce one TU outside the build** (bigcode/01):
`ninja -t commands lib/Support/CMakeFiles/LLVMSupport.dir/APInt.cpp.o | tail -1`, compiler swapped to `/usr/bin/clang++` (the tree was built with g++ via ccache; `which clang++` is a ccache wrapper, so the real binary is used). Wall time 2.8–3.1 s, 150 MB RSS, three runs.

**Step 2 — Where does the time go, by library** (bigcode/04):
`perf record -F 4000`, reading the `cpu_core` section (11K samples; the 69-sample `cpu_atom` section is discarded):

| DSO | share |
|---|---|
| libLLVM.so.21.1 | 71.3% |
| libclang-cpp.so.21.1 | 19.7% |
| libc.so.6 (malloc/free) | 8.1% |
| ld-linux | 0.1% |

Flat profile: top symbol `_int_malloc` 2.5%, then `ScalarEvolution::getRangeRef` 1.4%, `getAddExpr` 1.2%, `FoldingSetBase::FindNodeOrInsertPos` 1.1%, `computeKnownBits` 1.0%, `Lexer::Lex` 0.9%, `MachineCopyPropagation` 0.8%, `SelectionDAGISel::SelectCodeCommon` 0.8%, `InstCombinerImpl::run` 0.8%.

**Step 3 — Where does the time go, by work** (bigcode/05):
`-ftime-trace`: ExecuteCompiler 3.1 s = Frontend 0.82 s + Backend 2.24 s (Optimizer 1.19 s of which the inliner/CGSCC pipeline 0.74 s; CodeGenPasses 1.05 s). Largest single function in the optimizer: `APIntOps::SolveQuadraticEquationWrap` 107 ms; then `APInt::divide` 36 ms, `GreatestCommonDivisor` 30 ms, `sdivrem` 25 ms.

**Step 4 — Interpretation.**
The two instruments agree: this TU's compile time is three quarters optimization and code generation of a mathematically heavy file at `-O3`, with SCEV (loop analysis) and the inliner prominent, and ~8% in the allocator. The front end (0.8 s, 258 headers) is not the lever.

**Step 5 — The experiment that would follow** (left as the reader's step; the method is what matters):
compile the same TU at `-O2` and at `-O3 -fno-inline-functions`, three runs each, and compare wall time and the Backend phase; then check whether the produced code's speed matters for this library (it is `APInt`: probably yes, so a per-file `-O2` would need a benchmark of APInt-heavy passes before being proposed). Report either "keep `-O3`, the 2.2 s is the price of the code quality" with the benchmark, or "`-O2` saves N% at no measured runtime cost".

**Surprise.** Two convincing wrong answers preceded the right one: a profile of a ccache *hit* (dynamic loader + zstd), and the E-core PMU section (69 samples) read as if it were the profile, which claimed the front end dominated. The `-ftime-trace` phase split is what exposed the second mistake.

## Capstone 1 (template): a public x86 codebase, profile → fix → prove

Pick something with a build, a benchmark or a reproducible workload, and a hot loop you can reason about. Good sizes: 10k–200k lines. Candidates that are public and neutral: `zstd`, `lz4`, `xxHash`, `simdjson`'s tests, `sqlite` with a query workload, `jq` on a large JSON, `cJSON`, a `libpng` encode, `bzip2`.

1. **Build topology** (bigcode/01): how is it built, with which flags, how do you rebuild one file.
2. **Baseline** (perf/01, perf/04): a pinned, repeatable workload; min/p50/p99 of the end-to-end time; `perf stat` cycles and instructions.
3. **Locate** (perf/02, perf/03): counters → is it branchy, memory-bound, compute-bound? `perf record` → hot symbol → hot line, through inlining.
4. **Explain** (cache/*, codegen/*): what is the line bound by? A dependency chain, a miss pattern, a mispredict, a missing vectorization, a call across a TU?
5. **Change one thing**: layout, a `restrict`, a pragma, an algorithmic batch, a flag (`-march`, LTO, PGO), or a rewrite of the loop. One change per measurement.
6. **Prove**: same workload, ABAB interleaved, three runs; counters before and after; the assembly diff (`tools/asmdiff.sh`); correctness checks (tests, checksums).
7. **Write it up** with the template below; if the change is real, send it upstream as a PR with the numbers.

## Capstone 2 (template): NEON vs SVE kernel selection, validated

Using the aarch64 track's toolchain (correctness under qemu at several vector lengths; performance by `llvm-mca` and, if you have access, real Arm hardware):

1. Take a kernel (dot product, saxpy, a reduction, a small GEMM) in three versions: scalar reference, NEON intrinsics, SVE intrinsics (aarch64/04 shape).
2. **Correctness** at VL 128/256/512/2048 under qemu with sizes that are not multiples of any VL, against the scalar reference with a tolerance.
3. **Codegen**: `-Rpass=loop-vectorize` on the auto-vectorized C version for both targets; compare with the intrinsics versions; `llvm-mca -mcpu=neoverse-v1` (SVE 256) and `-mcpu=neoverse-n1` (NEON only) throughput per element.
4. **Dispatch**: an ifunc or function-pointer selection on HWCAP (aarch64/04), plus an override for benchmarking.
5. **Decision**: a table of predicted cost per element by core and size, the crossover size below which NEON (or scalar) wins, and the sentence "on hardware X we measured …" only if you measured it. Without hardware, say so; the model-based answer with the validation matrix is still a complete deliverable.
6. Extend to SME (aarch64/05) as a stretch: the outer-product tile version of the GEMM, correct at three streaming VLs.
